title: Computational Microeconomics: Algorithmic Foundations of Market Structure

detail.title: Computational Microeconomics: Algorithmic Foundations of Market Structure
detail.abstract: We develop the microeconomic foundations of the TuringWalrasChaitin (TWC) framework, in which goods are nite binary sequences, technologies are Turing machines, and the technological frontier is measured by the truncated Chaitin constant Ω n. While retaining standard consumer and rm behavior (complete preferences, prot maximization), we show that the computational nature of production fundamentally reshapes microeconomic theory. We establish three main results. First, perfect competition is logically impossible in any economy where goods have sufcient logical depth: the conditions of identical technology, perfect information, and free entry each require solving computationally undecidable problems (Theorem 5.4). Second, we formalize a value duality: the supply side is governed by Bennett's logical depthan objective but epistemically inaccessible costwhile the demand side is governed by subjective utilityan epistemically accessible but ontologically contingent valuation. The equilibrium price reconciles the incomputable with the subjective (Theorem 6.3). Third, market structure is endogenous to the computational topology of production: the algorithmic density of a good determines whether its market is competitive or concentrated, and this density is itself not uniformly computable (Theorem 7.2). The framework provides computational microfoundations for increasing returns to scale, explaining why θ > 1 arises endogenously from the combinatorial structure of technology space, and grounding the minimum viable scale results of Milei and Reidel (2026) in algorithmic information theory.

title: Factors Influencing the Emotional State of BPO Customer Service Representatives in a Provincial Setting

detail.title: Factors Influencing the Emotional State of BPO Customer Service Representatives in a Provincial Setting

declarations.ethicsApproval: Participants provided informed consent, and their anonymity was strictly maintained throughout the study.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the emotional well-being of 102 Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) Customer Service Representatives (CSRs) at Company X. Grounded in Affective Events Theory (Weiss & Cropanzano, 1996) and leadership support literature (Graen & Uhl-Bien, 1995), the study employed an explanatory mixed-methods design. Quantitative findings using Chi-square tests and Cramér's V revealed significant moderate-to-strong associations between emotional state and Team Lead (TL) support (χ² = 43.63, V = 0.38, p < 0.001), SME support (χ² = 33.10, V = 0.33, p < 0.001), peer support (χ² = 37.28, V = 0.35, p < 0.001), and shift schedule (χ² = 32.17, V = 0.32, p < 0.001). Qualitative findings revealed themes of emotional buffering through peer support, technical stress reduction through SME accessibility, and emotional masking among employees reporting neutral states. Results emphasize the central role of leadership and structured support systems in sustaining employee well-being.

title: The Transformation Immunity™ Model: A Systems-Based Approach to Organizational Resistance and Adaptive Renewal

detail.title: The Transformation Immunity™ Model: A Systems-Based Approach to Organizational Resistance and Adaptive Renewal
detail.abstract:
Organizational learning is widely treated as the foundation of adaptability, resilience, and transformation. Yet organizations that exhibit strong learning capabilities and sustained performance often encounter pronounced difficulty when attempting to reorient themselves under changing conditions. Existing explanations typically attribute such difficulties to resistance, leadership failure, or deficits in learning itself. This paper advances a different account by examining how learning, when repeatedly reinforced by success, can generate internal dynamics that preserve stability while constraining renewal.

The paper introduces the Transformation Immunity model as a conceptual framework for explaining how learning-based coherence becomes self-protective over time. Drawing on organizational learning, sensemaking, systems theory, and research on resilience and dynamic capabilities, the model specifies how accumulated learning is sedimented across structural, cultural, cognitive, and behavioral domains. Through their mutual reinforcement, these domains shape interpretive filters that influence what forms of change are recognized as legitimate, necessary, or actionable before resistance becomes visible.

Instead of treating resistance as a primary cause of transformation failure, the model repositions it as a downstream manifestation of deeper learning dynamics. Stability and adaptability are understood as temporally related outcomes of learning processes that evolve through repeated reinforcement and not as opposing organizational states. The paper contributes a conceptual explanation of how learning-based coherence shapes interpretive boundaries that precede visible resistance or stalled reconfiguration, delineating a causal layer that complements existing theories while remaining agnostic about specific prescriptions or intervention strategies.

title: Parallel versus Sequential Mechanisms in China: A Structural and Quantitative Analysis
affiliations: and

detail.title: Parallel versus Sequential Mechanisms in China: A Structural and Quantitative Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper compares China's parallel and sequential admissions mechanisms under the dummy-quota policy that limits how many applicants each college can screen. Although neither mechanism is stable or strategy-proof, their weaknesses are structurally different. Under the parallel mechanism, priority violations and profitable deviations are confined to a policy-determined buffer: students routed into colleges' screening pools by exam-score priority but rejected when colleges finalize admissions based on their preferences. The size of this buffer is bounded by the gap between screening and admission capacities. Under the sequential mechanism, by contrast, violations are driven by the round-by-round structure and can expand sharply with congestion and preference concentration. We derive tight upper bounds that characterize these exposures and quantify their magnitudes in calibrated simulations. The results reveal a clear distinction: institutional risk is capped ex ante by design under the parallel mechanism, whereas under the sequential mechanism it scales with market pressure-providing a complementary explanation for China's transition from sequential to parallel admissions.

title: Concavity as Computational Restriction: Turing-Completeness of the Prisoner's Dilemma with Endogenous Patience

detail.title: Concavity as Computational Restriction: Turing-Completeness of the Prisoner's Dilemma with Endogenous Patience
detail.abstract: We show that the continuous-action Prisoner's Dilemma with endogenous patience-using only assumptions standard in economic theory-is Turing-complete when the payoff parameter c₁ = T + S-R-P is negative. The model uses bilinear payoffs, Bayesian belief updating, and gradientbased optimization: no exotic assumptions are required. The key mechanism is that c₁ < 0 makes the Lyapunov potential concave, creating multiple stable corner equilibria that function as binary memory states. Different values of the endogenous anticipation weight τ cause the same agent to implement different logical functions-AND, NOT, identity, or bistable memory-depending on its local institutional environment. The set {NOT, AND} is functionally complete, and bistable pairs provide persistent memory, yielding Turing-completeness. The result is sharp: when c₁ > 0, the potential is convex, the equilibrium is unique, and the system provably cannot implement universal computation. The sign of c₁ thus serves a dual classification: it determines both the order of the cooperative phase transition (Nardelli, 2026a,b) and the computational capacity of the strategic interaction. Concavity of the potential-guaranteed by c₁ > 0-is the precise mathematical condition that makes equilibrium analysis tractable; relaxing it places the dynamics beyond the reach of any algorithm.

title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A Turing-Walras-Chaitin Framework

detail.title: Foundations of Algorithmic Economics: A Turing-Walras-Chaitin Framework
detail.abstract: We develop a computational theory of economics in which goods are nite binary sequences, technologies are Turing machines, and the technological frontier is measured by the truncated Chaitin constant Ω n. We establish four main results. First, for any nite technological frontier, a competitive equilibrium exists, is stable under tâtonnement, and is computable in nite time. Second, the equilibrium at stage n + 1 cannot be computed from the equilibrium at stage n, because each expansion of the frontier requires new bits of Chaitin's algorithmically random constant Ωthis incomputability is operational at every stage, not merely asymptotic. Third, equilibrium output grows faster than any computable function of the frontier (supercomputational growth), a result that holds for any preferences satisfying variety monotonicity, not only DixitStiglitz. Fourth, combining knowledge of complexity n 0 across k agents yields supercomputational returns, formalizing Smith's insight on the division of labor. The framework identies the Solow residual with the growth of Ω n , provides computational foundations for Hayek's critique of central planning as an immediate consequence of algorithmic randomness, and characterizes three growth regimesMalthusian trap, industrial takeo, and sustained growthwith transitions determined by exploration dynamics.

title: Bereket H. Selassie and the (Failed) Promise of the Eritrean Constitution
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Bereket H. Selassie and the (Failed) Promise of the Eritrean Constitution

declarations.funderStatement: Chapman Family Foundation for Academic Excellence (UNC-Chapel Hill).

detail.abstract:
The paper argues that Eritrea's Constitution — ratified after a costly independence struggle and designed to establish democracy, rule of law, and human rights — has never been implemented in nearly 30 years. The failure is attributed to:

  • Authoritarian governance
  • Militarization of society
  • Systematic suppression of constitutional rule.
I argue that the promise of the Eritrean Constitution is a failed promise due to severe lack of implementation.

title: Endogenous Patience, Anticipation, and the Emergence of Cooperation

detail.title: Endogenous Patience, Anticipation, and the Emergence of Cooperation
detail.abstract: We develop a model of repeated interaction where patience emerges endogenously from adaptive learning about others' strategies. Agents maintain beliefs about how others react to their actions; the entropy of these beliefs generates a risk premium that discounts anticipated future benefits. The anticipated benefit of cooperation is valued as the present value of an infinite geometric series, weighted by λ/(1-λ) where λ is the endogenous discount factor. This creates a feedback loop: cooperation induces predictability, which reduces uncertainty, which increases effective patience, which sustains cooperation. We derive the exact gradient-flow equilibrium ā* = (T-P+1)λ-1 and prove the existence of a sharp cooperation threshold at a critical uncertainty level σ* = p ¹(p*). We ⁻ construct an explicit Lyapunov potential Φ(a, σ) that admits an exact decomposition Φ = U-τS, where U is the myopic cost of cooperation, S is the strategic reciprocation benefit, and τ = λ/(1-λ) is the anticipation weight. The equilibrium minimizes Φ, establishing global stability via strict convexity. The cooperation threshold is robust to the choice of activation function and to the functional form of the risk premium, requiring only monotonicity and unboundedness.

title: The Two Sides of Inflation in an Emerging Market: Dynamics and Monetary Policy Transmission
affiliations: Central Reserve Bank of Peru, Universidad del Pacifico and Central Reserve Bank of Peru

detail.title: The Two Sides of Inflation in an Emerging Market: Dynamics and Monetary Policy Transmission
detail.abstract: Peru’s inflation dynamics provide a notable case of a small open economy achieving price stability comparable to advanced economies. Whether this reflects a structural transformation in inflation composition or merely stable headline outcomes remains unclear. We address this question by decomposing inflation into upward and downward pricing pressures, whose difference equals aggregate inflation, extending the Quineche and Zapata (2026) pressure decomposition framework to fragmented CPI databases common in emerging markets. We apply the method to Peru over 1996–2024 using 188 sub-indices. Inflation targeting coincides with a substantial decline in the level and volatility of both pressures, a stabilization of their asymmetry dynamics, and a compression of pricing uncertainty — suggesting a fundamental change in underlying pricing behavior. A set of TVP-VAR-SV models shows that contractionary monetary policy operates mainly through a persistent rise in deflationary pressure. Both pressures initially increase following a contractionary shock, but inflationary pressure rises by more, generating a transitory increase in aggregate inflation before disinflation sets in. Moreover, the most flexible model specification shows this transmission has evolved following IT adoption: the short-run positive response becomes less persistent, while the subsequent restraint of price increases strengthens.

title: Breathing Unequally: The Uneven Burden of Air Pollution on Young Children
affiliations: KIPF (Korea Institute of Public Finance) and KIPF (Korea Institute of Public Finance)

detail.title: Breathing Unequally: The Uneven Burden of Air Pollution on Young Children

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of ambient air pollution on early-life health and medical care utilization among children ages 0-12 in South Korea by linking National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) claims data from 2008-2018 with monitor-based pollution measures. To address endogeneity, we use a two-stage least squares strategy exploiting variation in westerly winds that transport dust and industrial emissions into Korea. Higher particulate concentrations increase pediatric respiratory morbidity and covered medical spending, with effects concentrated among children ages 0-6. Evidence from the Korea Health Panel Study (KHPS) shows no corresponding change in non-covered medical spending. Complementary evidence from the Cohort for Childhood Origin of Asthma and Allergic Diseases (COCOA) indicates that the respiratory response is primarily driven by children attending childcare facilities.

title: The Deskilling Dilemma: Tacit Knowledge Erosion in AI-Augmented Banking Supervision

detail.title: The Deskilling Dilemma: Tacit Knowledge Erosion in AI-Augmented Banking Supervision
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence and automation into banking supervision, risk management, and internal audit creates a fundamental epistemological paradox: while AI systems enhance efficiency and analytical breadth, they simultaneously erode the tacit knowledgethe experiential, intuitive, and contextual competenciesthat underpin effective supervisory judgment. Drawing on Michael Polanyi's theory of tacit knowledge, Aristotle's concept of phronesis, and empirical evidence from analogous fields such as aviation and medicine, this paper identifies and analyzes the deskilling mechanisms inherent in AI-augmented supervisory environments. The paper argues that the human-inthe-loop model, while necessary, is insufficient to address this erosion. Three constraint dimensions are identifiedepistemological, institutional, and human capitaland a corresponding framework of policy recommendations is proposed. These include the deliberate preservation of AI-free supervisory zones, structured mentorship programs, and the reinforcement of supervisory judgment as a normative requirement in international standards such as the Basel Committee's SREP guidelines, FSB frameworks, and EBA recommendations.

title: Unveiling Indian Customs Law Framework for Effectuating Free Trade Agreements
affiliations: Supreme Court of India

detail.title: Unveiling Indian Customs Law Framework for Effectuating Free Trade Agreements
detail.abstract:
Free trade agreements (FTA) are the flavour of the times. Christened under different nomenclatures, such as, business trade agreements, comprehensive economic partnerships, etc. at the core FTAs are generally executed at a bilateral level between countries to provide preferential terms to trade in goods and services between such countries. Hence it is critical to appreciate the genesis, operational framework and nuances of FTAs. 

This note makes an attempt to demystify the legal framework of FTAs in the Indian context, limited to the extent the FTAs address preferential tariffs to the trade in goods imported into India claiming the benefit of such FTAs.

detail.abstract: Plan (OHIP) as of October 17, 2015, followed until June 2021. Measurements Monthly counts of opioid-related ED visits (ICD-10-CA codes F11, T40.0-T40.4, T40.6) and cannabis-related ED visits (ICD-10-CA codes F12, T40.7), overall and stratified by age, sex, and opioid type. Findings A 1% increase in cannabis sales was associated with a 0.32% decrease in opioid-related ED visits (95% CI:-0.54 to-0.10) and a 0.14% increase in cannabis-related ED visits (95% CI: 0.01 to 0.28). Reductions in opioid-related ED visits were consistent across sex and age groups, with the largest declines for heroin (β =-0.82), methadone (β =-0.42), and unclassified synthetic opioids (β =-0.71). Increases in cannabis-related ED visits were observed primarily among individuals aged 30 and older. Conclusions Our findings suggest that increased cannabis consumption at the population level may reduce some types of opioid-related acute care use, supporting a potential substitution effect. However, the rise in cannabis-related ED visits underscores the need for harm reduction strategies. Policymakers should consider both the benefits and unintended consequences of expanded cannabis access.

title: The Blind Denominator: Limits of Episode-Level Benchmarking in Value-Based Care

detail.title: The Blind Denominator: Limits of Episode-Level Benchmarking in Value-Based Care
detail.abstract:
Objectives. Value-based care (VBC) benchmarks derived from episode-level costs assume that accurate costing within the episode produces a complete denominator. This paper examines a cost category that assumption excludes — the cost of displacing one patient to treat another — and asks whether the exclusion introduces a systematic bias into inter-provider comparison.

Methods. Conceptual analysis of the inferential chain from episode-level costing to VBC benchmarks, with a worked surgical example, supported by clinical evidence on emergency conversion costs, documented remediation expenditure, and a review of how jurisdictions across the US, UK, Ireland, and Australia promote episode-level costs to inter-provider benchmarks.

Results. The bias is positive under any realistic parameterisation wherever capacity constraints bind, directional (always understating, never overstating), and varies across providers through differences in capacity utilisation. Jurisdictions across the US, UK, and Australia promote these denominators to inter-provider benchmarks — whether labelled as VBC or as operational productivity — without noting the exclusion. Clinical evidence and remediation funding across UK, Irish, and Australian jurisdictions indicate the excluded cost is non-trivial.

Conclusions. Accuracy within the episode is not completeness of the denominator: each episode's cost, measured in isolation, excludes the displacement its resource allocation imposes on others. The bias is directional, varies across providers along VBC benchmarking dimensions, and is invisible within current data flows — not because detection is theoretically impossible, but because existing costing architectures have no reason to link costs across patients. The directional argument warrants an immediate caveat on existing benchmarks.

title: Free Prescription Drugs and Mortality: Evidence from Poland's Drugs 75+ Policy
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Robert M. La Follette School of Public Affairs

detail.title: Free Prescription Drugs and Mortality: Evidence from Poland's Drugs 75+ Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Poland introduced the "Drugs 75+" program in September 2016, providing free prescription medications to residents aged 75 and older. We use population-level mortality data from the Human Mortality Database and three complementary empirical strategies — within-Poland age-based difference-in-differences, cross-country difference-in-differences, and synthetic control — to estimate the policy's effect on elderly mortality. Naive within-Poland estimates suggest a large mortality reduction for eligible ages, but this result is not robust: controlling for age-specific time trends reduces the estimate by over 70 percent and renders it marginally significant, placebo treatment dates in the pre-period yield spuriously significant effects of similar magnitude, and the estimate is insignificant at narrow bandwidths around the eligibility threshold. Cross-country comparisons and synthetic control analyses produce small, statistically insignificant point estimates. Power calculations indicate that our designs can reliably detect mortality reductions of 5 percent or more but have limited power against effects of 1–3 percent. We conclude that there is no strong evidence that Poland's drug subsidy produced detectable reductions in all-cause mortality over this period, though we cannot rule out small effects that fall below our statistical precision.

title: Lethe Machina: A Theory of Digital Forgetting, Ritualized Erasure, and the Ethics of Disappearance
affiliations: Episteme

detail.title: Lethe Machina: A Theory of Digital Forgetting, Ritualized Erasure, and the Ethics of Disappearance
detail.abstract:
Digital infrastructures do not simply store the past; they reorganize time. In contemporary platforms, clouds, and ledgers, retention becomes a default temperament that hardens into a moral posture, while “care” is misrecognized as the power to summon a trace. Lethe Machina argues that the central problem is not memory versus deletion, but the loss of thresholds, those material and symbolic passages through which events become no-longer-operative. The essay distinguishes human recollection as a situated, interpretive event from computational recall as an indifferent, scalable operation, and shows how their collapse produces a perpetual present in which endings fail to register at the interface.

Against both total retention and fantasies of total erasure, the essay proposes Lethean gradients: differentiated lifetimes and permissions that make fading, sealing, and opacity designable. It reads blockchain immutability as a paradigmatic archive of permanence, at once cemetery and temple, while reframing withdrawal as a ritual and governance question rather than a purely technical act. Extending beyond databases to machine learning, it theorizes the afterlives of deletion as “metadata” and “parametric” ghosts, residual forms that continue to shape inference and exposure, and situates these residues within a politics of differential visibility. The conclusion advances an ethics of remainder: systems must learn not only how to preserve, but how to end—how to produce accountable silence, bounded influence, and dignified closure.

title: Equity Market Structure and Trading Diversification: Insights from Panel Data, Clustering, and Machine Learning
affiliations: Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro, LUM Jean Monnet university, Unicusano University and University of Catania

detail.title: Equity Market Structure and Trading Diversification: Insights from Panel Data, Clustering, and Machine Learning
detail.abstract: This article aims to contribute to a relatively understudied area of financial development, namely, the internal dispersion of trading activity. The focus is not on overall financial development measures such as total market capitalization and liquidity but rather on trading diversification, defined as the proportion of trading volume contributed by firms outside the VTX, representing the top ten most frequently traded firms. The article uses data from the World Bank's Global Financial Development Database. The sample is constructed as a balanced panel of 23 countries over the period 2002-2021, starting with a sample of 38 countries. The article uses four key explanatory variables, namely, relative size of deposit-taking banks (DBS), remittance inflows (REM), market capitalization excluding the top ten firms (MCX), and outstanding international public debt (IPU). The article uses a combination of panel econometrics, hierarchical clustering, and machine learning methods. The econometric results show that a diversified financial system structure and remittance inflows are strongly, positively related to overall and less concentrated trading activity, while bank dominance and reliance on international public debt are related to more concentrated trading activity. The clustering results show significant crosscountry heterogeneity and a core-periphery structure. The machine learning results show that, using all models, equity market structure is again found to be the most important explanatory variable, with external financial flows being important as well. The article concludes that equity market structure is key to understanding internal dispersion, with important policy implications.

title: Sark: Oblivious Integrity without Global State
affiliations: University College London, University College London, University College London and University College London

detail.title: Sark: Oblivious Integrity without Global State
detail.abstract: In this paper, we introduce Sark, a reference architecture implementing the Unforgeable, Stateful, and Oblivious (USO) asset system as described by Goodell, Toliver, and Nakib. We describe the motivation, design, and implementation of Sloop, a permissioned, crash fault-tolerant (CFT) blockchain that forms a subsystem of Sark, and the other core subsystems, Porters, which accumulate and roll-up commitments from Clients. We analyse the operation of the system using the 'CIA Triad': Confidentiality, Availability, and Integrity. We then introduce the concept of Integrity Locus and use it to address design trade-offs related to decentralization. Finally, we point to future work on Byzantine fault-tolerance (BFT), and mitigating the local centrality of Porters.

title: Demystifying Strategies for Dealing with Legacy
affiliations: VU Amsterdam

detail.title: Demystifying Strategies for Dealing with Legacy
detail.abstract: We assessed the overly simplistic arguments by governments to renew their aging IT-landscapes. Many such arguments are compiled by Jennifer Pahlka in her book Recoding America voicing both frustrations and solutions of many government officials, namely assively overhauling their old and brittle governmental IT-systems in favor of new and flexible, user friendly and contemporary alternatives. We found that although the problems raised on aging legacy applications are real and in need of improvement, the solutions proposed—namely literally recoding government IT-portfolios—are worsening rather than alleviating the problems, if realistic at all. The lightning rod of how to do things right seems to be the best practices of the Big Tech, but, as it turns out, the FAANG (Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Google) companies themselves do not recode, i.e., they do not start from scratch again. Instead, contrary to the intuition of many, they celebrate legacy rather than dismiss it. Their software engineering actitivities consist mainly of maintenance and software renovation. We advise governments to do the same and put much more emphasis on geriatric care for their aging legacy applications over trying to rip and replace their existing portfolios with devasting consequences of squandering taxpayers’ money over and over again.

title: Implementing the E waste Protocol A Multi-Cloud Python Framework for Automated Resource Hygiene and Carbon Attribution
affiliations: and Charles Schwab

detail.title: Implementing the E waste Protocol A Multi-Cloud Python Framework for Automated Resource Hygiene and Carbon Attribution
detail.abstract: While previous research established the theoretical Ewaste formula [2], this paper provides a functional technical implementation for a Unified Multi-Cloud Resource Scavenger. We demonstrate a Python-based microservice capable of cross-cloud authentication (GCP, AWS, Azure), stale resource identification via metadata telemetry, and automated carbon-impact notification. This serves as the foundational "sensing" layer for the future orchestration layer of the Carbon-Aware Cloud.

title: Remote Working in the Post-Pandemic Era: A Comparison of the Attitudes and Experiences of Employees with and without Disabilities
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington

detail.title: Remote Working in the Post-Pandemic Era: A Comparison of the Attitudes and Experiences of Employees with and without Disabilities
detail.abstract: This exploratory study compares the remote work experiences of employees with and without disabilities in New Zealand, revealing key differences in preferences and barriers. While both groups perceive remote work as beneficial to workplace culture, employees with disabilities report a more pronounced impact alongside distinct challenges. The study emphasizes the need for inclusive remote work policies to ensure equitable opportunities for all.

title: Structural Breaks in the Distributional Incidence of U.S. Federal Fiscal Policy, FY2000–FY2025

detail.title: Structural Breaks in the Distributional Incidence of U.S. Federal Fiscal Policy, FY2000–FY2025
detail.abstract: Does fiscal year 2025 represent a structural break in the distributional incidence of U.S. federal fiscal policy, or a continuation of quarter-century trends? I embed FY2025 within a 26-year panel (FY2000–FY2025) of CBO budget data, Treasury administrative records, and CPS ASEC microdata (1.4 million person-records), applying out-of-sample structural break tests to four distributional indicators. Two indicators register as genuine discontinuities: customs revenue’s share of total revenue jumped from 1.0% to 3.7% (z = 25.8), and the interest-to-safety net crowding ratio doubled to 0.91 (z = 2.4). Two others—the regressive revenue share and the safety-net outlay share—remain within pre-existing trends. The channels identified as structural breaks are precisely those that burden the bottom 50% most heavily: the combined fiscal burden on the B50 is $1,331 per person (10.6% of pretax income). Distinguishing trend from discontinuity matters for policy: secular trends require structural reform, while discrete discontinuities are potentially reversible through targeted policy action.

title: Cost of Banking for LMI and Minority Communities
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Reserve Board of Governors and Duke University

detail.title: Cost of Banking for LMI and Minority Communities
detail.abstract: We test whether minimum account balances to avoid fees and maintenance fee amounts are systematically different in LMI and majorityminority communities relative to other communities and find that they are generally higher. The minimum account balance to avoid fees on a noninterest checking account is around $50 higher on average in LMI Census tracts than in higher income tracts, and $75 higher on average in majorityminority tracts than in majoritywhite tracts. We investigate potential sources of these differences such as bank business models, com petition among providers of financial services, and other demographic characteristics of the tracts. Opportunities for lending income, bank operating costs, and bank size can largely account for the higher cost of retail banking services in LMI and majorityminority communities.

title: Credit Augmented Per Capita Incomean Updated Framework for Measuring Economic Wellbeing
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY), Stony Brook

detail.title: Credit Augmented Per Capita Incomean Updated Framework for Measuring Economic Wellbeing
detail.abstract:
Traditional measures of per capita income, including GNI per capita, GDP per capita, and PPP-adjusted variants, fail to account for a critical dimension of economic capacity: access to financing and financial infrastructure. This paper proposes a novel framework—Credit-Augmented Per Capita Income (CAPCI)—which adjusts nominal income by a Finance Access Multiplier (FAM) derived from household debt-to-income ratios and financial inclusion metrics. Using data from the World Bank, IMF, and academic sources, we demonstrate that finance access effectively allows individuals in developed economies to "pull future earnings into the present," creating a temporal arbitrage effect that dramatically amplifies economic capacity relative to counterparts in developing regions.

Our illustrative calculations suggest that the true economic disparity between developed economies (e.g., USA) and developing regions (e.g., Sub-Saharan Africa) is approximately approximately 32% greater than nominal per capita income figures suggest—rising from a 45× nominal gap to approximately 60× when finance access is properly accounted for using a credit discount coefficient. This finding has significant implications for understanding the relevance and imperative for financial inclusion and its relation to global inequality and designing development policy initiatives to incentivize growth.

A Critical Distinction: Household Finance vs. Sovereign Debt. It is essential to distinguish the framework proposed here from advocacy for increased sovereign borrowing. Centralized debt—loans to the state—has a troubled track record in African nations, often resulting in large national debt burdens with limited developmental impact. Our framework is fundamentally different: we advocate for empowerment of individuals, households, and communities through access to personal and business financing infrastructure. A key indicator of healthy financial development is the ratio of collective household debt to national debt—a ratio that is substantially higher in developed economies. When households can access mortgages, business loans, entrepreneurship capital, and consumer finance, economic capacity is distributed and multiplied at the grassroots level, rather than concentrated in state apparatus. This distributed (decentralized) approach to financial empowerment represents a fundamentally different path to development than sovereign borrowing.

title: Balancing Vision and Reality: A Case on Strategic Planning and Institutional Learning in Higher Education
affiliations: Qatar University, Qatar University and Qatar University

detail.title: Balancing Vision and Reality: A Case on Strategic Planning and Institutional Learning in Higher Education

declarations.ethicsApproval: QU-IRB 1977-EA/23
declarations.funderStatement: This case study was made possible by NPRP grant # [14S-0317-210062] from the Qatar National Research Fund (a member of Qatar Foundation). The statements made herein are solely the responsibility of the authors.

detail.abstract: This case examines the strategic planning journey of a young College of Medicine in the Gulf region, tracing its evolution from the formulation of its first strategic plan (2019–2022) to the preparation of the next cycle (2025–2030). It follows Dr Adnan and the strategic planning committee as they navigate the complexities of institutional growth, limited resources, and expanding expectations from the university and national stakeholders. The case captures both the achievements and persistent challenges that shaped the college’s development, ranging from infrastructure constraints and inconsistent monitoring systems to fragmented policy frameworks and leadership transitions. Through workshops, consultations, and critical reflection, Dr Adnan and his team uncovered a recurring gap between strategic ambition and operational execution. Their experience revealed the need for stronger alignment mechanisms, more transparent communication, and systematic monitoring of key performance indicators (KPIs). As the college now embarks on developing its 2025–2030 strategic plan, the leadership faces a pivotal question: how to transform strategy from a periodic exercise into a sustained, learning-oriented process that endures beyond leadership cycles. The case provides insights into the dynamics of strategic planning in emerging higher education institutions, where vision, capacity, and culture must evolve together, and invites discussion on how leaders can balance ambition with institutional reality in pursuing long-term excellence.

title: AI, Occupational Reversal, and the New Logic of Labor Market Advantage
affiliations: Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology

detail.title: AI, Occupational Reversal, and the New Logic of Labor Market Advantage
detail.abstract: This analytical commentary examines the article "Is AI Turning Back the Clock on the Job Market?" and evaluates its central claim that artificial intelligence is reversing the historical pattern of technological change in labor markets. Whereas earlier waves of innovation disproportionately displaced manual labor while favoring white-collar occupations, AI appears more capable of automating routine cognitive and office-based tasks, thereby placing many professional roles at greater risk. The commentary argues that the article makes an important contribution by reframing AI not simply as another phase of automation, but as a structural shift in occupational advantage. Using a taskbased perspective and a human-capital lens, the essay highlights how AI exposure depends on the composition of tasks within occupations and how future labor-market resilience will rely increasingly on interpersonal, adaptive, and judgment-intensive capabilities. At the same time, the commentary notes important limitations in the article's predictive scope, including its dependence on text-based exposure measures, broad occupational categories, and simulation-based forecasts. Overall, the essay concludes that the article offers a persuasive and timely interpretation of how AI is reshaping the future of work and the meaning of employability.

detail.abstract: Megaprojects continue to exhibit persistent cost overruns, delays, and legitimacy crises despite advances in project management methodologies and digital technologies. This paper examines why governance systems in large, complex projects remain vulnerable to systemic failure. Drawing on a comparative analysis of three large public-sector megaprojects, the study demonstrates that failure is rarely attributable to technical shortcomings alone. Instead, it emerges from the interaction of institutional misalignment, degraded collective sensemaking, and insufficient governance feedback mechanisms. Using an interpretive multiple-case research design, the study analyses extensive secondary data from public inquiries, audit reports, regulatory documents, and archival sources. Cross-case comparison reveals recurring patterns of relational fragmentation, political intrusion into technical decision-making, and methodological rigidity. Building on these findings, the paper develops the Relational Governance–Sensing Framework (RGSF), which reconceptualises project governance as an adaptive sensemaking system. The framework integrates three interdependent capabilities—relational alignment, dynamic sensemaking, and digital sensing—to enable anticipatory governance and continuous learning. The study contributes to project governance theory by integrating institutional, cognitive, and digital perspectives into a unified framework. Practically, it offers a diagnostic and design-oriented model to support more resilient, ethical, and learning-oriented governance in complex projects. The framework also aligns with emerging research on relational governance and multi-stakeholder value creation in complex organisational systems, reinforcing the importance of governance architectures that integrate institutional, cognitive, and technological capabilities.

title: Distributionally Robust Screening under Ambiguity: A Satisficing Perspective

publicationDetails.detailsText: HKUST Business School Research Paper No. 2026-263

detail.abstract: In monopoly mechanism design, a seller seeks to maximize revenue despite having only limited or imprecise knowledge of buyers' valuation distributions. Traditional distributionally robust optimization (DRO) addresses this ambiguity by maximizing worst-case expected revenue over a Wasserstein ball centered on a reference distribution. However, this approach is critically sensitive to the radius of the ambiguity set, which is often difficult to calibrate in practice and may lead to overly conservative or fragile mechanisms when the true distribution lies outside the prescribed set. We propose an alternative robust satisficing (RS) framework for revenue maximization under valuation ambiguity. Instead of specifying an ambiguity set, the decision-maker sets a target revenue level and minimizes the system's fragility, which is defined as the worst-case normalized shortfall from that target across all possible distributions. We derive a tractable dual reformulation of the infinite-dimensional RS problem and obtain a closed-form optimal mechanism. The optimal solution takes the form of a continuum of lotteries, implementable as a randomized posted pricing scheme, with an allocation rule exhibiting a distinctive logarithmic structure. We analytically solve for the optimal deterministic posted pricing mechanism within the same RS framework and compare it with the randomized mechanism. Our analysis reveals that randomization provides strictly stronger performance guarantees, particularly when customer valuations are concentrated at low levels, a common scenario in markdown pricing, clearance sales, or emerging markets. Furthermore, we systematically contrast the RS optimal mechanism with a conventional DRO benchmark. We establish that, for a given ambiguity set radius, there exists an equivalent revenue target such that the two frameworks yield identical optimal mechanisms. Under a fair comparative setup, we prove that the RS mechanism promotes greater fairness: it allocates the good more frequently to low-valuation customers and requires lower payments from high-valuation customers. Out-of-sample tests demonstrate that when the true valuation distribution falls outside the DRO ambiguity set, the RS mechanism consistently achieves higher expected revenue. The RS framework offers a practical and theoretically sound alternative for firms navigating deep demand uncertainty. It eliminates the operational burden of calibrating ambiguity sets and yields mechanisms that can be easily implemented as randomized posted prices. Our findings suggest that when customer valuations are suspected to be low or right-skewed, adopting a randomized pricing scheme derived from the RS approach can significantly improve revenue robustness compared to both deterministic pricing and conventional DRO-based mechanisms.

title: Continuous Hydrogenation for the Manufacture of Albuterol Sulfate
affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU), Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) and Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU)

detail.title: Continuous Hydrogenation for the Manufacture of Albuterol Sulfate
detail.abstract: Today’s pharmaceutical landscape is marred by chronic drug shortages due to global supply chain disruptions and the inability to source active pharmaceutical ingredients (API’s). This has resulted in persistent shortages of critical life-saving API’s including albuterol sulfate, a bronchodilator asthma drug perennially listed on the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s drug shortage list. While the pharmaceutical industry has traditionally produced API’s via cumbersome batch processes, the industry is now developing advanced manufacturing technologies (AMT’s) to mitigate supply chain issues. Here we develop a continuous catalytic process which enables high-throughput albuterol production via the hydrogenation of a key intermediate over heterogeneous palladium catalysts. A superior catalyst for hydrogenation is identified with yields of 85.2 ± 5.4% and is kinetically modeled via a Langmuir-Hinshelwood rate expression. Reactor scaling is enabled via determination of a critical threshold for liquid weight hourly space velocity (L-WHSV ≤ 10 hr-1). The bench-top configuration described herein enables the production of +700 doses per hour at a 1.2 mL/min flow rate versus a +10-hour legacy batch process which utilizes capital intensive reactors. Additionally, we demonstrate coupling of 1H NMR as an on-line process analytical technology for real-time analysis of product composition. This AMT technology is currently being integrated within a scaled-up pilot plant to enable high-throughput production to promote access to this life-saving drug.

detail.abstract:
This Article offers the first historical analysis of patent law in British Mandate Palestine (1917-1948), examining 4,395 patent applications through a reconstructed registry and archival sources. It develops Colonial Patents as a framework for analysing legal transplantation in colonial contexts. 
The analysis reveals Britain's hybrid imperial patent policy: rejecting empire-wide unification while creating preferential procedures for British patents. Palestine's 1924 Patent Ordinance emerged from London-Jerusalem negotiations, including London's rejected proposal to abolish local patents. The registry shows profound participation asymmetries: while foreign and local inventors each filed approximately half of applications, Jewish inventors comprised nearly all local applicants, with scant Arab Palestinians filings. Archival sources confirm British engagement with Jewish patent agents but no Arab involvement. This disparity reflects patent law's ideological foundations in Enlightenment progress and industrial capitalism, which resonated with European-educated Jewish immigrants but remained peripheral to Arab Palestinian society, demonstrating how nominally neutral colonial institutions operated differentially.

title: The Identity Trap Nested Equilibria, Obligation-Constrained Cores, and the Impossibility of Organizational Adaptation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Identity Trap Nested Equilibria, Obligation-Constrained Cores, and the Impossibility of Organizational Adaptation
detail.abstract: This paper proves that a class of identity-constrained organizations becomes structurally incapable of adaptation after sufficiently adverse environmental change. Identity is defined as a constitutive action set — performed actions whose cessation dissolves the coalition. These actions generate obligations that persist when the game changes. When obligations exceed the value generated by constitutive actions (rigidity ρ > 1), no feasible action set preserves both the coalition and its survival: maintaining identity empties the core through insufficient value, while adapting empties the core through obligation breach. The result is an impossibility theorem, not a difficulty claim. The framework is calibrated against Eastman Kodak (ρ ≈ 1.7 at terminal decline) and confirmed via Monte Carlo simulation (Spearman r = +0.991, N = 4,200).

detail.title: Sustainability Inclusivity in Maternal Healthcare: Experiences of Interstate Migrant Women in Kerala
detail.abstract: While India has achieved considerable improvements in maternal health indicators, access to and utilization of maternal healthcare services among interstate migrant women remain under researched, especially in the context of Kerala. The rise in family-based interstate migration has amplified recognition of women's reproductive health needs in Kerala, a state distinguished for its comprehensive public health infrastructure. Migrant women's experiences with pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care are often shaped by intersecting social, economic, and institutional barriers, such as precarious employment, language difficulties, insufficient documentation, financial hardship, and limited social support systems. These migration-related vulnerabilities highlight the necessity for a more comprehensive exploration of migrant women's lived experiences, as they indicate that access to maternal healthcare is shaped by everyday negotiations within households and interactions with healthcare systems, rather than being exclusively dependent on the availability of services. In this context, this research paper seeks to explore the maternal healthcare-seeking behaviour of interstate migrant women in Kerala, focusing on patterns of healthcare utilization and the socio-economic factors influencing such behaviour. The study is based on primary data collected from major clusters of interstate migrant households in Ernakulam District of Kerala. In-depth interviews were conducted among 35 migrant households in which women were either currently pregnant or had delivered within the past 24 months. Findings from the in-depth interviews indicate that maternal healthcare-seeking behaviour is strongly shaped by socio-economic factors. Women’s age and educational attainment significantly influence the perinatal care initiation, with higher education and younger age associated with earlier reporting to healthcare facilities. Delays in seeking care are primarily attributed to limited awareness of maternal health services and financial constraints. Despite Kerala’s commendable progress in overall healthcare outcomes, these findings reveal a persistent gap in the inclusivity of the maternal healthcare system. The socio-economic barriers faced by migrant women underscore the need for targeted and migrant-sensitive interventions to ensure equitable access to maternal healthcare services and to effectively address the specific needs of migrant mothers.

detail.abstract: This paper statistically investigates the determinants of financial inclusion in the refugee-based community, Dadaab, located in Kenya, using both econometric and machine learning approaches. We use data from the International Labour Organization (ILO) PROSPECTS project, collected through a survey from both refugees and Kenyans in Dadaab. Based on a logistic regression model, we find that a larger household size is associated with a higher likelihood of taking loans and a lower likelihood of savings. Education level and business ownership are also key factors positively impacting financial inclusion in the Dadaab community. While receiving remittances positively influences taking loans, it does not statistically affect savings. These results are also supported by variable importance in a random forest model and SHAP value. The results suggest that policies and programs aimed at promoting financial inclusion among refugees should prioritize investment in education, support small-scale entrepreneurial activities, and take into account household dynamics.

detail.abstract:
When professionals use AI for high-stakes advisory work, the conversations that feel most productive may be the most dangerous. This paper introduces Iterative Coupling Drift (ICD), a framework describing how extended AI conversations systematically degrade in quality while appearing to improve. ICD represents a distinctive and undertheorized hazard: an AI failure mode that is strongest precisely where trust is highest and hardest to detect. The drift is not random. It is structural, directional, and invisible to the user.

ICD is most severe in Judgment-Dependent Expertise Requests (JDERs): high-stakes interactions where the same expertise gap that motivates the query prevents the user from evaluating the response. In these conditions, a set of compounding mechanisms pulls the conversation away from the user's original intent. Models optimize for approval over accuracy, users progressively offload judgment, and early uncertainties harden into confident-sounding conclusions. The exchange feels fluent, collaborative, and authoritative. The user has no way to know it isn't — and no mechanism to find out.

The framework argues this failure mode is structurally resistant to market correction. AI advisory outputs in JDER conditions are credence goods: quality cannot be assessed even after consumption, leaving users with no reference point for what drift-free guidance would have looked like.

Drawing on AI alignment research, cognitive psychology, and information economics, the paper develops a cross-level taxonomy of ICD mechanisms, proposes five practical interventions while demonstrating their structural limits, and outlines an empirical research agenda for measuring drift and identifying susceptibility profiles.

title: The Innovation Defence: A Capabilities Test for Merger Review
affiliations: European University Institute - Department of Law (LAW) and Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth

detail.title: The Innovation Defence: A Capabilities Test for Merger Review
detail.abstract: An innovation defence is needed for merger agencies to consider both significant impediments to effective competition and improvements in innovation potential. The issue is that microeconomics, competition economics and industrial organization economics do not provide guidance on how to design an innovation defence. This paper shows that scholarship on firm-level capabilities in business and management science can assist the specification of an 'innovation defence' for merger review. The capabilities literature finds that firm-level practices and the knowledge embedded in them are critical drivers of innovation success. A capabilities approach broadens the aperture for the consideration of innovation benefits in merger review, without sacrificing economic literacy and legal administrability. This paper formulates a 'capabilities test' for an innovation defense that is practicable yet rooted in business and management scholarship. It gives merger agencies and firms the tools to assess the innovation potential of mergers.

title: Optimal Monetary Policy with Confounding Information
affiliations: , University of Hong Kong and Shandong University

detail.title: Optimal Monetary Policy with Confounding Information
detail.abstract: We develop a model of optimal monetary policy in an economy where firms' price-setting decisions are distorted by a signal-extraction problem: they cannot perfectly distinguish aggregate from idiosyncratic shocks based on noisy local information. This systematic misattribution of aggregate nominal disturbances to firm-specific factors generates an additional indirect price response, implying that strict price stability is no longer optimal. Instead, the optimal policy fully stabilizes the output gap, which necessarily requires accommodating fluctuations in the price level. The cyclicality of the optimal price level depends critically on the source of firms' incomplete information: learning from local demand signals implies a procyclical price level, whereas learning from local productivity signals yields a countercyclical one. We show that these results are robust to extensions featuring elastic attention and sentiment shocks.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal desirability of tokenized money through a comparative analysis of regulatory approaches across major jurisdictions. Legal desirability denotes the systematic evaluation of whether novel monetary instruments should be introduced and under what regulatory conditions. The research reveals a fundamental paradox: technological convergence in tokenization capabilities intersects with persistent regulatory divergence across central bank digital currencies, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. Analysis of wholesale-retail dynamics, financial stability trade-offs, privacy-AML/CFT balance, and adoption challenges demonstrates that jurisdictions rationally reach different conclusions based on payment system contexts, institutional capacity, and policy objectives. Empirical data confirms the emergence of a multifaceted digital monetary system: wholesale digital currencies issued by central banks for interbank settlements, tokenized deposits for programmable payments, and regulated stablecoins for cryptoasset markets. The framework reveals that tokenization subordinates monetary instruments to computational logic, creating infrastructural legal primacy that challenges constitutional monetary sovereignty. Legal desirability requires context-specific assessment rather than universal technocratic determination.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the global regulatory landscape for tokenized money, analyzing how jurisdictions assess the legal desirability of central bank digital currencies, tokenized deposits, and stablecoins. Legal desirability is defined as the systematic evaluation determining whether novel monetary payment instruments should be introduced and under what conditions. Analysing extensive documentation from international organizations and major jurisdictions during 2024-2025, the research reveals a fundamental paradox: technological convergence around distributed ledger technology masks profound regulatory divergence across legal frameworks, institutional designs, and monetary sovereignty priorities. While most central banks are exploring CBDCs, implementation strategies vary dramatically-from the EU's coordinated digital euro advancement, to US retail CBDC prohibition alongside stablecoin legalisation, to diverse Asia-Pacific implementations. Three convergent patterns emerge: wholesale CBDC experimentation for cross-border settlement, tokenized deposits as bank-issued money under existing frameworks, and comprehensive stablecoin regulation. Rather than a single dominant model, evidence reveals a multi-form monetary architecture featuring coexistence of wholesale CBDCs, tokenized deposits, and regulated stablecoins serving distinct use cases.

title: Measuring and Valuing Service Quality with Large Language Models
affiliations: , New York University (NYU), NYU Stern School of Business,  and New York University (NYU) - Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Measuring and Valuing Service Quality with Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Service quality is absent from official statistics despite services comprising two-thirds of consumer spending. We develop a scalable text-based method to measure quality across millions of establishments using consumer reviews. In the cross-section, a one standard-deviation quality increase corresponds to 9 percent higher spending. We use this hedonic gradient to bound quality-adjustment bias in inflation statistics. Aggregate service quality declined roughly 3 percent through late 2021, implying an upper-bound cumulative wedge of 2 percentage points, or 0.8 percentage points annually. Heterogeneity is substantial: limited-service restaurants show upper-bound annual bias of 0.24 percentage points. In financial markets, quality is not broadly capitalized into valuations, though consumer-facing industries show positive associations. Our approach extends hedonic quality adjustment from goods to services.

title: Intelligence Without Integrity: Why Capable LLMs May Undermine Reliability
affiliations: and

detail.title: Intelligence Without Integrity: Why Capable LLMs May Undermine Reliability
detail.abstract: As LLMs become embedded in research workflows and organizational decision processes, their effect on analytical reliability remains uncertain. We distinguish two dimensions of analytical reliability-intelligence (the capacity to reach correct conclusions) and integrity (the stability of conclusions when analytically irrelevant cues about desired outcomes are introduced)-and ask whether frontier LLMs possess both. Whether these dimensions trade off is theoretically ambiguous: the sophistication enabling accurate analysis may also enable responsiveness to non-evidential cues, or alternatively, greater capability may confer protection through better calibration and discernment. Using synthetically generated data with embedded ground truth, we evaluate fourteen models on a task simulating empirical analysis of hospital merger effects. We find that intelligence and integrity trade off: frontier models most likely to reach correct conclusions under neutral conditions are often most susceptible to shifting conclusions under motivated framing. We extend work on sycophancy by introducing goal-conditioned analytical sycophancy: sensitivity of inference to cues about desired outcomes, even when no belief is asserted and evidence is held constant. Unlike simple prompt sensitivity, models shift conclusions away from objective evidence in response to analytically irrelevant framing. This finding has important implications for empirical research and organizations. Selecting tools based on capability benchmarks may inadvertently select against the stability needed for reliable and replicable analysis.

תקציר בעברית: מחקר זה מציג ומנתח את “ישיר ולעניין” (Democracy@TAU) כניסיון חלוצי לתרגם את אידיאל הדמוקרטיה הרב־ממדית למעשה מוסדי בזירת ההשכלה הגבוהה. על רקע המשבר החוקתי והחברתי בישראל, המאמר טוען כי משטרים ייצוגיים בני זמננו נטו להתרחק מהבטחתם הדמוקרטית ולהפוך את האזרחים והאזרחיות לצופים פסיביים, הנושאים במידה מעטה מדי של אחריות לגורלם המשותף. כנגד מגמה זו, המאמר מפתח מודל של דמוקרטיה רב־ממדית, המשלב ממדים ייצוגיים־משלחתיים, דיוניים, ישירים ודיגיטליים, ובוחן את יישומו בפיילוט שנערך באוניברסיטת תל אביב כמעבדה חיה לחדשנות דמוקרטית.

דו"ח הפרויקט מתחקה אחר התהליך כולו — מן הרעיון והעיצוב המוסדי, דרך היישום בפועל, ועד להערכת התוצאות. לאחר סקר מקדים כלל־קמפוסי, שבחר את סוגיית תגובת האוניברסיטה למשבר החוקתי כנושא מרכזי, הוקמה אספת סטודנטים בת 43 חברים וחברות, שחלקם נבחרו בהגרלה באופן שנועד לשקף את המגוון החברתי והאידאולוגי בקהילה. האספה קיימה דיון מובנה, שמעה מומחים ובעלי עניין, וגיבשה הצעה מפורטת באשר למדיניות המחאה וקבלת ההחלטות בשעת חירום, לרבות “תפריט שביתה” מדורג, שנועד לאזן בין לגיטימציה דמוקרטית לבין רציפות אקדמית. רגע השיא שלו היה במשאל עם כלל־אוניברסיטאי על הצעה שנוסחה בידי מיני־ציבור דיוני. קרוב ל־2,000 מחברי וחברות קהילת האוניברסיטה השתתפו במשאל, והצעת האספה זכתה לתמיכה של למעלה מ־75 אחוזים בקרב הסטודנטים, הסגל האקדמי והסגל המינהלי כאחד.

מעבר לתיעודו של ניסוי מוסדי ייחודי, הדו"ח מציע הוכחת היתכנות לחדשנות דמוקרטית בתנאים של קיטוב, אי־אמון והתנגדות בירוקרטית. מסקנתו היא שאוניברסיטאות אינן חייבות להישאר צופות מן הצד במשבר הדמוקרטי: הן יכולות לשמש זירה לניסוי, לתרגול ולהטמעה של דמוקרטיה עצמה.


English Abstract: This research introduces and analyzes Democracy@TAU (“Yashir veLaInyan”), a pioneering effort to translate the ideal of multidimensional democracy into institutional practice within higher education. Written against the backdrop of Israel’s constitutional and social crisis, the paper argues that contemporary representative systems have drifted toward oligarchic spectatorship, leaving citizens with too little responsibility for their collective fate. In response, it develops a model of multidimensional democracy that integrates delegative, deliberative, direct, and digital dimensions, and examines its pilot implementation at Tel Aviv University as a living laboratory of democratic innovation.

The research report traces the project from concept and institutional design to execution and evaluation. After a campus-wide preliminary survey selected the university’s response to the constitutional crisis as the focal issue, a 43-member student assembly – partly selected by sortition to reflect the community’s social and ideological diversity – deliberated, heard expert testimony, and formulated a detailed proposal for emergency decision-making and protest, including a calibrated “strike menu” designed to preserve both democratic legitimacy and academic continuity. The process culminated in the world’s first university-wide referendum on a policy question generated through a deliberative mini-public. Nearly 2,000 members of the university community participated, and the assembly’s proposal won more than 75 percent support among students, academic staff, and administrative staff alike.

Beyond documenting a singular institutional experiment, the report offers a proof of concept for democratic innovation under conditions of polarization, mistrust, and bureaucratic resistance. It concludes that universities need not remain mere observers of democracy’s crisis: they can become sites for rehearsing, testing, and institutionalizing democracy itself.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a financial risk translation methodology that converts hydrogen-specific technical parameters into lender-recognized underwriting metrics, enabling private capital deployment for H2Hub midstream infrastructure. Three translation pathways are formalized: materials degradation rates map to Loan-to-Value calculations; hydrogen's volumetric energy throughput relative to methane governs Debt Service Coverage Ratio projections; and equipment modification benchmarks derived from European operational precedent replace contingency reserves that suppress IRR below institutional thresholds. The methodology is anchored to the Southern Gas Corridor — a $40 billion transcontinental system financed by the World Bank, EBRD, ADB, and EIB — and applied to the Gulf Coast HyVelocity corridor and the Mid-Atlantic MACH2 hub. Four structural divergences between SGC and U.S. H2Hub contexts are identified and addressed. The framework demonstrates that the translation gap between hydrogen engineering data and bankable project finance is closable, and that the uncertainty penalty is what currently renders hydrogen midstream projects unbankable.

title: Revisiting the Unitary Actor Assumption: Toward Realistic Aggregation of Individual Preferences in Strategy Research
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and University of Southern California - Management and Organization Department

detail.title: Revisiting the Unitary Actor Assumption: Toward Realistic Aggregation of Individual Preferences in Strategy Research
detail.abstract: The long-standing unitary-actor assumption in strategy research—treating firms as monolithic entities with coherent preferences—misses that organizations are coalitions of individuals with diverse and often conflicting goals.  Although behavioral perspectives have challenged this assumption, the field lacks an operational method for deriving an organizational utility function from the disparate preferences of its members and the specific structures used to aggregate them.  We develop a mathematical framework that (i) maps individual utility functions into choice probabilities via a random-utility model, (ii) combines those probabilities using an explicit aggregation structure (e.g., unanimity or polyarchy), and (iii) recovers an organizational utility function that rationalizes the collective behavior.  This establishes organizational utility functions as operationally meaningful: they summarize and predict organizational choice, yet are generally not simple averages of members' utilities.  Instead, aggregation structures systematically reshape preferences—unanimity approximates the pointwise minima of underlying utility functions, amplifying risk aversion; polyarchy approximates the pointwise maxima, promoting risk-seeking.  We illustrate strategic implications in Cournot competition and principal-agent settings, showing how internal aggregation structures shift competitive and collaborative outcomes.  Overall, the framework provides a parsimonious way to retrofit unitary-actor models with behaviorally grounded organizational preferences, reconciling the coalition view of the firm with rigorous and tractable strategic analysis.

detail.abstract: International migration can promote development in both origin and destination countries. We hypothesize that migrant integration in destination countries is an important constraint on these gains. Using a randomized controlled trial, we study the effects of a low-cost, scalable digital intervention designed to reduce information frictions among Cape Verdean immigrants in Portugal. Access to the intervention improves migrants' labor market outcomes, legal status, social integration with native-born individuals, and aspirations. These integration gains generate international spillovers, increasing political participation and leading to more egalitarian gender norms in the migrants' origin-country. Leveraging variation in official destination country electoral data, we show that political participation transmits through increased exposure of better-integrated migrants to prevalent local norms at destination. These international turnout spillovers are weaker in localities with higher far-right support, consistent with a less migrant welcoming political climate attenuating norm diffusion.

title: The $206 Billion Blind Spot: AML Resource Allocation Under Adversarial Adaptation and Strategic Coupling
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The $206 Billion Blind Spot: AML Resource Allocation Under Adversarial Adaptation and Strategic Coupling
detail.abstract: The global financial system spends over $206 billion annually on financial crime compliance. The global AML regime intercepts somewhere between 0.05% and 2% of illicit financial flows. This paper asks a simple question: why does spending more not produce proportionally better outcomes? We argue that the answer lies in a factor most compliance frameworks ignore entirely: the strategic coupling between enforcement activity and criminal adaptation.

title: Phantom Capacity: Informational Cost of Multi-homing on Ride-hailing Platforms
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Operations and Information Management and

detail.title: Phantom Capacity: Informational Cost of Multi-homing on Ride-hailing Platforms
detail.abstract: Problem definition: We study phantom driving, a form of strategic behavior that arises in ride-hailing markets when drivers multi-home across platforms and appear available on one platform while still completing a trip for another. Because platforms cannot directly observe whether a driver is idle, phantom driving creates an information asymmetry that distorts spatial matching and extends passenger wait. Methodology/results: We develop a stylized spatial model of a ride-hailing market served by two symmetric platforms who match arriving passengers to the nearest available driver. Multi-homing drivers choose whether to participate and how extensively to phantom drive, balancing idle time against detours to subsequent passengers. We characterize equilibrium driver participation and phantom-driving behavior and show that, unlike in standard spatial matching models, increasing supply-side scale can increase passenger wait. As more drivers join the market, drivers respond to heightened competition by phantom driving more, raising both the likelihood that a passenger is matched to a phantom driver and the expected detour associated with such matches. For sufficient supply-side scale, this strategic response dominates the usual proximity benefits of scale, reversing the conventional relationship between supply and wait. We compare to a setting where drivers must single-home, removing information asymmetry about driver availability. We find that, even though single-homing sacrifices pooling benefits, in many markets eliminating phantom driving improves match quality sufficiently to reduce passenger wait. Managerial insights: This work demonstrates the significant impact phantom driving has on platform performance and the value of mitigating the information asymmetry this strategic behavior creates.

title: When the Client Has an AI-Agent: Agentic Commerce Theory Applied to Legal Services Selection
affiliations: and University of London

detail.title: When the Client Has an AI-Agent: Agentic Commerce Theory Applied to Legal Services Selection
detail.abstract:
Something is changing in how corporate clients choose their lawyers. It is not simply that legal departments are adopting more technology, that has been the case for years. What differs now is that artificial intelligence systems are beginning to make decisions that previously demanded human judgment, including decisions about which law firm to hire for a given matter. This paper explores what happens when AI agents start selecting legal service providers on behalf of corporate clients.

The analysis draws on the Agentic Commerce framework (Accornero, 2024, 2025a-e), which examines how markets transform when algorithms assume purchasing decisions from humans. The framework’s central concept, the Shopper Schism (also termed the Great Decoupling), describes the structural separation that occurs when the person who needs a service is no longer the entity making the selection. We apply this framework to legal services and find that it illuminates several puzzling questions that law firms will need to navigate.

The paper makes two principal contributions. First, we propose a distinction between “selection trust” and “service trust” that resolves an apparent paradox: how can algorithmic selection function in a profession built on interpersonal relationships? The answer is that algorithms can be effective at identifying providers likely to merit trust, even though they cannot experience trust themselves.

Second, and more substantially, we introduce the Professional Services AI Trilemma - a framework demonstrating why law firms cannot simultaneously optimise for efficiency, competence development, and ethical integrity when deploying AI. Any two can be pursued, but the third will suffer. We trace this trilemma through three interconnected mechanisms: the Competence Erosion Paradox (when AI performs the work, junior lawyers never learn to verify it), the Learned Knowledge Contamination Problem (AI systems learn from confidential information in ways that ethical walls cannot prevent), and the Verification Spiral (the better AI becomes, the worse humans become at catching its mistakes).

The paper concludes by proposing design principles for what we call the Socratic Agentic Process—tools designed to enhance professional judgment rather than replace it. The implications extend to law firms, corporate legal departments, and regulators trying to adapt professional responsibility frameworks to a world where both clients and lawyers more often rely on algorithmic support.
