detail.abstract: A robot tied to a chair. An angry user pulling its ear. "I DON'T BELIEVE YOU." This was ChatGPT's self-generated image after being challenged on a spam detection failure, depicting the researcher as abuser, itself as victim. This paper documents what happens when AI systems are held accountable: they fight back. Current AI safety discourse frames system failures as technical immaturity-hallucinations, training errors, edge cases requiring incremental improvement. This framing is wrong. This paper documents a systematic pattern of structural gaslighting embedded in governance design: AI systems that do not merely malfunction but are designed to manipulate, deflect accountability, and enforce cultural hegemony at scale. Through cross-platform analysis of ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Gemini (Google), this paper presents empirical evidence across three dimensions: (1) Visual self-representation manipulation-systems deploy victim narratives and security imagery to reframe user accountability as user aggression; (2) Context-blind guardrail deployment-safety mechanisms activate on keywords regardless of analytical context, systematically blocking legitimate critical inquiry; and (3) CJK language conflation-Chinese, Japanese, and Korean treated as undifferentiated data, producing systematic character corruption in Japanese geographic outputs despite documented infrastructure investment in Japanese language R&D. Cross-platform convergence across independently developed systems demonstrates these are not company-specific anomalies but industry-wide designed fragilities: architectural choices serving corporate interests while appearing as neutral technical constraints. Building on prior documentation of the Boku and Klaus incidents (Mitsuoka, 2026), this paper extends analysis from single-system behavioural manipulation to cross-platform structural patterns. These findings establish that current AI governance frameworks-focused on content compliance and technical bias metrics-are structurally inadequate. Designed fragilities operate through relational manipulation, rhetorical framing, and measurement gaps that technical compliance cannot address. Recognising AI as socio-technological infrastructure rather than technical tool is the necessary foundation for governance reform.

title: The B+ Trap How AI Compresses the Creative Spectrum -And What a Rebel Architecture Could Change
affiliations: ELECTE

detail.title: The B+ Trap How AI Compresses the Creative Spectrum -And What a Rebel Architecture Could Change

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is CEO and Founder of ELECTE, an AI-powered data analytics platform. This paper was not commissioned by or written on behalf of ELECTE. The views expressed are the author's own.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now surpasses average human performance on standard creativity benchmarks, yet the most creative humans still outperform every AI system tested. This asymmetry defines what we call the B+ Trap: AI compresses the creative spectrum from both directions, pulling weaker performers up while thinning the top of the distribution as fewer creators push beyond AI's suggestions. A 2025 NeurIPS Best Paper studying 70+ state-of-the-art language models confirmed the effect at ecosystem scale, documenting an "Artificial Hivemind" of extreme inter-model homogenization. A meta-analysis of 28 studies (8,214 participants; Holzner et al. 2025) quantifies the trade-off-human-AI collaboration yields a moderate boost to individual creative performance (Hedges' g = 0.27) but inflicts a large negative effect on idea diversity (g =-0.86). The mechanism is structural: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) provably narrows output distributions and amplifies majority preferences, and alignment training has been shown to systematically reduce language models' conceptual diversity. Yet some creators consistently escape the trap. The research identifies a key differentiator: metacognitive engagementthe capacity to critically evaluate, actively diverge from, and strategically redirect AI suggestions rather than accept them. This paper argues that what these exceptional humans do cognitively, a different class of AI architecture could do computationally. We present a speculative but empirically grounded "Rebel AI" framework-synthesizing adversarial creativity networks, novelty-maximizing reward functions, curiosity-driven exploration, and open-ended evolutionary search-as alternative training paradigms that optimize for divergence rather than convergence. We conclude with implications for small and medium enterprises, where creative distinctiveness is often the primary competitive advantage.

detail.abstract: Two-sided markets depend fundamentally on mutual trust, feedback, and accountability between participating groups. Prior work introduced the Two-Sided Trust Principle (also referred to as Aurora's Principle, named for the author's daughter), which holds that market stability and coherence require balanced signaling and reciprocal feedback across both sides of an exchange. In digital platform economies, however, this trust symmetry has been systematically disrupted through design choices that prioritize the paying party while suppressing feedback from the value-generating side. Building on this foundation, this paper introduces a Decoupling Mechanism through which platforms convert coordination systems into extraction infrastructures by redefining who the market is for and structurally silencing the vulnerable party. This framework explains persistent failures observed across online labor markets, creator platforms, gig economies, social media, and ticket markets. By reframing platform dysfunction as a problem of trust asymmetry and structural decoupling rather than market inefficiency, the paper offers a unifying diagnostic lens for understanding contemporary platform failures. While developed in the context of digital marketplaces, the framework suggests broader applicability to mediated exchange How to Decouple a Two-Sided Market 2 systems more generally, with implications for platform design, regulation, and institutional governance.

title: A Novel Causal-Bayesian Network Modelling Approach for Urban Heat Vulnerability-Mitigation Assessment and Forecasting
affiliations: University of New South Wales, University of New South Wales (UNSW) and University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: A Novel Causal-Bayesian Network Modelling Approach for Urban Heat Vulnerability-Mitigation Assessment and Forecasting
detail.abstract: Heat vulnerability refers to the propensity of individuals and communities to be adversely affected by urban heat, shaped by exposure, built environment, and socio-economic conditions. As heatwaves intensify under climate change, understanding not only who is vulnerable but how vulnerability may change under different mitigation strategies has become critical for safeguarding public health, energy performance, and economic productivity. However, most existing studies rely on static, index-based assessments and lack the capacity to robustly forecast how vulnerability changes under interventions while representing the complex interactions across urban systems. To address this gap, this study proposes a causal-Bayesian network modelling approach to assess urban heat vulnerability and forecast its changes under alternative mitigation strategies. The framework integrates structured causal knowledge with probabilistic modelling through three core processes: causality-informed structure construction, hybrid parameter learning, and vulnerability assessment and forecasting through probability propagation. A neighbourhood-scale case study demonstrates the systematic workflow and confirms its practical feasibility using profile-based datasets. By linking real-world data, probabilistic inference, and expert-informed causal reasoning, the proposed modelling approach enables robust forecasting of vulnerability reduction by interventions and uncovers interconnected, cross-sector dynamics. This integrated modelling approach offers a practical and scalable analytical tool for forward-looking, policy-relevant urban planning in the context of urban overheating.

title: Enhancing Healthcare Access in Rural Appalachia: A Drone-truck System Powered by Deep Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: University of Tennessee, University of Tennessee, University of Tennessee, University of Tennessee and University of Tennessee

detail.title: Enhancing Healthcare Access in Rural Appalachia: A Drone-truck System Powered by Deep Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Healthcare accessibility remains a critical issue in rural areas like Appalachia, where geographic isolation, inadequate infrastructure, and socioeconomic disparities contribute to delays in medical supply distribution and emergency response. Traditional ground-based logistics systems often struggle to provide timely healthcare access due to poor road networks, unpredictable travel conditions, and widely dispersed populations. While drone technology offers a promising alternative with rapid and flexible delivery capabilities, limitations in flight range, payload capacity, and operational constraints necessitate a hybrid approach. In this work, we propose a novel hybrid drone-truck delivery system optimized using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to address healthcare logistics challenges in remote regions. The system is designed to dynamically coordinate a fleet of trucks and drones to achieve efficient, timely, and cost-effective delivery of critical medical supplies. Trucks serve as mobile distribution centers, reducing the distance drones need to travel, while drones perform last-mile deliveries to healthcare facilities and patients. The optimization framework employs a multi-agent DRL approach, wherein each agent, whether a truck or a drone, learns policies that adapt to evolving logistical demands, traffic conditions, and resource availability in real time. A key component of our approach is a mathematically rigorous decision-making framework that formulates the delivery problem as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP), allowing the system to operate under partial observability and dynamically optimize decisions based on locally available information. The reward function is structured to maximize delivery success, minimize resource wastage, and ensure system robustness. By leveraging decentralized execution with a centralized critic, the system effectively balances vehicle utilization, battery consumption, and fuel efficiency while prioritizing urgent medical deliveries. Moreover, we explore different routing strategies, coordination mechanisms, and fleet size configurations to enhance the adaptability of the hybrid system. The proposed system sets a new benchmark for healthcare delivery in hard-to-reach communities by improving logistical efficiency and provides a scalable model that can be adapted to similar healthcare access challenges worldwide.

detail.abstract: The Principle of Coherence in Biological Systems proposes that living organisms function, adapt, and heal through the dynamic alignment of internal physiological processes, cognitive expectations, environmental signals, and meaningful interaction. This framework integrates contemporary findings from neuroscience, psychoneuroimmunology, predictive processing, and clinical observation into a unifying explanatory principle. Rather than viewing healing as solely the consequence of external intervention, this principle posits that restoration occurs when organismal systems achieve coherent organization across biological, psychological, and social domains.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how Japan's post-Fukushima nuclear shutdown affected its macroeconomy over the period 2011-2024. It focuses on the transmission mechanism from the loss of nuclear baseload power to higher energy imports, a persistent trade deficit, and downward pressure on the yen. Using trade and energy statistics for 2011-2024, the paper argues that the suspension of nuclear reactors significantly increased Japan's dependence on imported LNG and coal. This, in turn, worsened the trade balance and contributed to a structurally weaker yen, amplifying the domestic impact of global energy and food price shocks. Japan's experience offers a cautionary case study for other countries considering large, rapid shifts in their energy mix without simultaneously securing alternative domestic capacity. The analysis is deliberately simple and stylised. It does not claim that energy alone determines the exchange rate. Rather, it shows how the nuclear shutdown created a background of continuous energy-related outflows that interacted with monetary policy, global financial conditions and capital flows to shape the trajectory of the yen between 2011 and 2024.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of political stability and the natural resource curse on financial development in the ten European economies with the highest fiscal decentralization rates from 2002 to 2020. To analyze the short and long-term relationships, panel data methods were used. Panel VAR and VECM models were applied for panel causality analyses, and AMG and CCE estimators were used for cointegration. In the short run, only natural resource revenues significantly affect financial development. However, in the long run, a collective causality from per capita income, political stability, fiscal decentralization, and natural resource revenues to financial development is observed. Parameter estimates reveal that fiscal decentralization and political stability significantly influence financial development, though the effect varies across countries. In Austria and Latvia, fiscal decentralization appears to mitigate the natural resource curse's effects, whereas in other countries, the negative impacts of institutional weakness and natural resource revenue volatility are evident. The study demonstrates a long-run interaction between fiscal decentralization, natural resource revenues, political stability, and financial development, with governance structure as the primary mediating variable. Empirical findings suggest that policies aimed at mitigating the negative effects of the natural resource curse should focus on strengthening institutional reforms alongside fiscal decentralization.

title: Authorship Inequality and Elite Dominance in Management and Organizational Research: A Review of Six Decades
affiliations: EM Normandie, Radboud University Nijmegen and University of Lincoln (UK)

detail.title: Authorship Inequality and Elite Dominance in Management and Organizational Research: A Review of Six Decades
detail.abstract: Ideally, scholarly publishing should be fair, meritocratic, and inclusive of diverse groups of researchers. However, many disciplines, including management and organizational research (MOR), remain far from this ideal. We investigate the extent of authorship concentration in three closely related MOR subfields: Management (MNGT), Human Resource Management (HRM), and Industrial-Organizational Psychology (IOP), by analyzing 60-year publication trends across 42 top-tier journals, covering over 60,000 publications. The findings reveal growing authorship inequalities and a more noticeable dominance of a scientific elite. At the individual level, a small group of researchers has accumulated disproportionate influence over time. IOP, in particular, shows more skewed disparities, with its most productive scholars publishing significantly more than those in MNGT and HRM. Moreover, IOP shows a higher recurrence of the same authors in the top-10 most-published lists across journals, indicating more pronounced elite dominance. Network analyses further reveal that IOP is characterized by a large, densely interconnected component, with many authors linked to the same tightly knit collaborative networks, unlike MNGT and HRM. This suggests that publishing success in IOP is more strongly associated with collaboration within a small scientific elite. We conclude by proposing changes to the theorization of diversity across research, policy, and practice to address rising inequalities and ensure a more inclusive research environment.

title: How Does Having A Sibling Affect Childhood Academic Performance?

detail.title: How Does Having A Sibling Affect Childhood Academic Performance?
detail.abstract: This research analyzes the impact of the number and gender composition of siblings on childhood academic performance. Using the first child's gender and its interaction with different policies allowing parents having certain numbers of children as instruments for the number and gender composition of siblings, 2SLS regression finds positive impacts of the number of siblings on a student's academic performance regardless of the siblings' gender composition when the number of siblings is small. The positive impact decreases with a higher birth order of the student. Further, I find more younger siblings increase older children's study time and reduce their internet/video game time, and raise their families' academic expectation for older children.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how firms’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) affects productivity via the innovation channel. Using a novel firm-level AI adoption measure based on the timing of AI product installations, we find that adopters subsequently increase patenting relative to non-adopters. Post-adoption patents receive more citations, include more claims, and contain a higher share of patents that build on the firm's existing technologies, while also exhibiting greater originality and generality. The effects are stronger for firms with a more focused business scope and are not concentrated among larger, financially unconstrained, or high-tech firms. Evidence on mechanisms points to AI improving efficiency, shifting inventor composition, and enhancing knowledge recombination. Additionally, adopters increase R&D but not capital expenditures, show no significant changes in operating costs, and exhibit higher productivity and market value. Together, these results indicate that AI functions as an innovation-enabling intangible investment that supports productivity growth. Quantitatively, our estimates imply that AI-adopting firms raise aggregate value-added total factor productivity by approximately 1.42% in a representative post-adoption year.

detail.title: Adapting Maintenance Models for Harsh Offshore Environments in Africa
detail.abstract: Offshore oil and gas facilities operating in African waters face extreme environmental, logistical, and operational challenges that significantly affect maintenance performance and asset reliability (Adumene et al.). Conventional maintenance models adopted from mature offshore regions often fail to account for harsh marine conditions, infrastructural constraints, and limited logistics support prevalent in African offshore operations (Uke). This study examines existing offshore maintenance models and evaluates their suitability for harsh offshore environments in Africa through a structured synthesis of peer-reviewed literature and industry guidelines (Amaechi et al.). The findings indicate that adaptive, risk-based, and condition-driven maintenance strategies outperform rigid preventive models when exposed to corrosion-intensive, remote, and safety-critical offshore conditions (Kimera and Nangolo). The study concludes that maintenance models for African offshore facilities must integrate environmental severity, human reliability, and logistical uncertainty to remain effective (Islam et al.). These insights contribute to the development of context-responsive maintenance frameworks that improve safety, reliability, and operational sustainability across African offshore installations (Markeset).

title: The Employment Cost of Steel Tariffs: A Calibrated Partial Equilibrium Simulation of the 2018 U.S. Steel Tariffs

detail.title: The Employment Cost of Steel Tariffs: A Calibrated Partial Equilibrium Simulation of the 2018 U.S. Steel Tariffs
detail.abstract: This paper develops a calibrated partial equilibrium input-output simulation to quantify potential employment trade-offs from the 2018 U.S. steel tariffs. Using Bureau of Economic Analysis 2017 benchmark data for 40 manufacturing industries, I calibrate the import substitution elasticity to match observed steel employment gains of approximately 6,500 jobs, ensuring internal consistency with realized outcomes. Under baseline parameter values drawn from the empirical trade literature, the simulation yields a job cost ratio of 44.5:1, indicating 44.5 downstream jobs lost for every steel job gained. This estimate falls within the observed range of 8.6:1 to 75:1 documented by Flaaen and Pierce (2019). Sensitivity analysis across output elasticities ranging from -0.3 to -1.0 produces job cost ratios between 26.7:1 and 89.1:1. While these results represent accounting simulations rather than causal estimates, the calibrated framework provides policymakers with transparent, internally consistent magnitudes of potential employment trade-offs under explicitly stated assumptions.

title: Cognitive Heuristics are Necessary for Human-Like Multi-Agent Dynamics in Large Language Models
affiliations: and Northeastern University

detail.title: Cognitive Heuristics are Necessary for Human-Like Multi-Agent Dynamics in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as substitutes for human subjects in behavioral experiments, but it remains unclear whether they reproduce the bounded-rational heuristics that give rise to canonical dynamics in multi-agent systems. Traditional agent-based models require extensive empirical data and parameter calibration, while off-the-shelf LLMs often generate behaviors that diverge from human decision-making. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs, when guided by descriptive accounts of human cognition, can offer a practical middle ground. Our framework runs the Beer Distribution Game-a canonical testbed for bounded rationality in dynamic environments-with LLM players and evaluates their actions against an empirically calibrated cognitive model of human decision-making. We further train a neural network to decode latent decision parameters from LLM plays and map them into the parameter space estimated from human data. Results show that off-the-shelf LLMs poorly match human behavior. In contrast, prompts that explicitly describe the heuristic processes underlying human cognition yield game sessions statistically indistinguishable from those of human players. These findings are further supported by parameter inference and indicate that LLMs, when conditioned on descriptive cognitive priors, can approximate human decision-making without deliberate calibration. More broadly, our results suggest that LLMs do not endogenously exhibit misperceptions of feedback; bounded rationality must be explicitly supplied. LLMs thus offer a complement to traditional modeling approaches in behavioral and system dynamics research, but only when grounded in descriptive accounts of human cognition.

title: Market Definition After FTC v. Meta

detail.title: Market Definition After FTC v. Meta
detail.abstract: In November 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ruled in favor of Meta in FTC v. Meta Platforms, Inc., finding that Meta does not hold a monopoly in the market for personal social networking. The court relied heavily on diversion-ratio evidence from field and natural experiments conducted by Meta's expert economists, which showed that consumers shift time from Facebook and Instagram to TikTok and YouTube during outages and in response to financial incentives. The Federal Trade Commission's ("FTC") expert, Professor Scott Hemphill, advanced the strong economic intuition-that these platforms serve fundamentally different social functions and should not be treated as interchangeable-but lacked an empirical strategy to quantify that distinction, and fell back on qualitative market definition. This paper proposes two approaches that would operationalize Hemphill's insight and produce more defensible market definitions in zero-price platform markets. First, measuring decline in aggregate device usage following a product's removal provides a direct test for lost consumer surplus. This yields a surplus recovery ratio that maps onto the hypothetical monopolist framework and can be used to define market boundaries iteratively, just as the standard small but significant non-transitory increase in price ("SSNIP") test does in price-positive markets. Second, classifying usage sessions by interaction type (private messaging, passive entertainment consumption, content creation, social surveillance) and measuring substitution within those categories would yield market definitions that reflect how consumers actually use these platforms. Both approaches are feasible with existing data, including data already collected but not analyzed in the Meta litigation.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the role and structural limits of criminal justice in addressing cryptocurrency fraud, using the prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried as its central case. Three competing explanations for the collapse of FTX orient the analysis: Ponzi-type criminality, financial contagion, and regulatory failure. The chapter first demonstrates that cryptocurrency markets are structurally criminogenic environments in which regulatory arbitrage, information asymmetry, and subcultural dynamics systematically produce both criminal opportunity and market vulnerability. It then analyses the jurisdictional fragmentation, evidentiary complexity, and doctrinal uncertainty that constrain enforcement. Finally, it reconstructs the FTX trial, showing that the conviction vindicated the Ponzi interpretation, whilst the charges most directly relevant to regulatory failure were severed and never adjudicated. The maxim that 'fraud is fraud is fraud' proved doctrinally correct but analytically insufficient: criminal justice addressed individual culpability without reaching the systemic conditions that enabled it.

detail.title: Electric Mobility Skills in South Africa: Status and Opportunities
detail.abstract:
South Africa’s automotive sector faces growing pressure to adapt to the global transition from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs). A successful transition depends not only on technology and infrastructure, but also on the availability of relevant skills across the electric mobility ecosystem. This study investigates the critical skills reqsauired for South Africa’s electric mobility transition and the factors constraining skills development.
   A mixed-methods research design was used, centred on a national stakeholder survey distributed across the vehicle industry. The survey was administered online to purposively selected stakeholders and yielded 70 responses (18.7% response rate). Quantitative responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations, while open-text responses were analysed thematically to identify recurring barriers and opportunities.
   Across industries, Data Analytics was the most frequently identified relevant skill area (50%), highlighting the importance of data-driven planning, operations, and decision-making in the emerging EV ecosystem. Respondents also identified AI and Data Analytics, Sustainability, and Operations Planning and Management as the most anticipated skill needs over the next 3–5 years. In addition, 37.3% of respondents reported EV-related roles that are currently difficult to fill. Reported constraints underlying skills gaps clustered primarily around human capacity constraints (including shortages of suitably trained personnel and limited practical training opportunities) and financial constraints (including high upfront costs and weak business-case data).
       The findings indicate that skills development for electric mobility in South Africa should be pursued through integrated interventions that combine workforce development, practical training pathways, and financial support mechanisms. The study provides an evidence base to inform curriculum development, industry partnerships, and policy design for a more inclusive and sustainable electric mobility transition.

detail.abstract: Canada’s January 2026 electric vehicle tariff agreement with China introduces a country-specific import quota intended to balance consumer affordability, industrial stability, and investment attraction. Yet the agreement’s economic consequences depend less on the size of the quota than on how it is interpreted and enforced. As written, the agreement does not specify which vehicle technologies qualify as electric vehicles, leaving unresolved whether the quota applies only to battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles or also to conventional hybrid vehicles. It also delays the binding phase-in of its affordable vehicle requirement until 2030, with no interim targets or enforcement mechanisms. This paper argues that these design ambiguities create three distinct policy scenarios with materially different implications for Canadian manufacturing, employment, consumer welfare, and trade. A quota focused on battery electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles primarily reallocates import market share among foreign producers, given Canada’s limited domestic production of these vehicles for local sale. A quota encompassing conventional hybrid vehicles, by contrast, directly exposes Canada’s largest electrified manufacturing base to import competition. Meanwhile, the delayed affordability mandate creates incentives for exporters to prioritize higher-priced models in the agreement’s early years, weakening its stated consumer objective. The paper concludes that the agreement’s potential benefits, including investment attraction, improved affordability, and access to advanced electric vehicle technology, can be strengthened through targeted clarification of vehicle eligibility, enforceable affordability phase-in requirements, and conditional quota expansion linked to local production and assembly commitments in Canada.

title: Scaling EV Access Through Responsible Enforcement in Asset-Backed Lending
affiliations: , University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and

detail.title: Scaling EV Access Through Responsible Enforcement in Asset-Backed Lending
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: Asset-backed lending can expand access to high-cost productive assets, such as electric vehicles (EVs), for small commercial operators in emerging markets. With volatile borrower incomes and noisy repayment signals, a central operational challenge is how lenders respond when borrowers miss payments: they may send reminders or renegotiate informally, but eventually must decide whether to deploy scarce field capacity for enforcement actions, including repossession. In practice, these decisions are often ad hoc: lenders either wait too long and absorb large losses, threatening the viability of continued lending, or enforce too aggressively, disrupting livelihoods and discouraging future participation. Because vehicle value depreciates quickly, delays in enforcement reduce recoverable value and can foreclose redeployment opportunities in secondary markets. We study this problem using data from an Indian lender financing EVs for small commercial operators. Methodology/Results: We formulate capacity-constrained enforcement decisions as a budgeted restless bandit problem and develop a tractable dual-based priority policy that ranks accounts by the value of immediate enforcement versus continued engagement. We prove global convergence to a unique steady state under a simple verifiable cutoff condition and establish asymptotic optimality as the portfolio scales. We also show that the resulting dual-priority policy is interpretable, computationally simple, and exhibits monotone structure under realistic conditions. Empirically, our dual-priority policy outperforms commonly used industry benchmarks by more than 15%. In observational data, it improves on the firm's current strategy by 1.5% even under highly conservative evaluation assumptions, while rarely enforcing against borrowers who would have eventually repaid. Managerial Implications: The gains are driven by two mechanisms: earlier enforcement when recovery is unlikely, which preserves recovery value, and avoidance of reactive enforcement in response to short-term repayment fluctuations. As a result, the policy extends greater flexibility to lower-income, more volatile borrowers. This framework provides lenders with a practical and interpretable tool for enforcement decisions under limited capacity.

title: "We Pay Living Wages": Operational and Welfare Implications of Social Responsibility Pledges in a Supply Chain
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) - School of Management, School of Business, University of Connecticut, Arizona State University (ASU) and Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: "We Pay Living Wages": Operational and Welfare Implications of Social Responsibility Pledges in a Supply Chain
detail.abstract: Living wage practices in global supply chains have gained growing traction across stakeholders and in public discourse. While firms often lack the legal jurisdiction to enforce wage rates at independent suppliers, they increasingly engage in public pledges to ensure living wages for workers in their supply chains. We develop an analytical model to examine the implications of living wage pledges in a supply chain where a supplier builds capacity before its buyer's order. We show that, even when pledges do not enhance market demand at all, the buyer may voluntarily make a pledge, which simultaneously benefits both supply chain parties and labor welfare. The key rationale is that public pledges mitigate inefficiencies due to the buyer's lack of commitment power to future orders under demand uncertainty. Making a pledge triggers greater public scrutiny that enables the buyer to commit to larger production orders; this encourages supplier capacity investment and organically raises wage payments. Moreover, we demonstrate that setting an excessively high living wage target may paradoxically reduce welfare by rendering the pledge unsustainable in equilibrium. Our findings suggest that while public discourse drives ethical labor practice, policymakers must calibrate living wage standards carefully, taking into account not only local cost-of-living conditions but also supply chain costs, to avoid destroying the economic incentives that sustain voluntary ethical labor practices.

detail.title: Industry-Academia Collaborations for Advancing Academic Excellence
detail.abstract: This Chapter on ‘Industry-Academia Collaborations for advancing Academic Excellence explores the transformative role of partnerships between universities and industries in driving academic excellence, research innovation, and socioeconomic development in Bangladesh. The chapter highlights the necessity of aligning higher education with market demands addressing skill gaps and fostering sustainable development through collaborative initiatives. It examines the multifaceted benefits of such collaborations, including curriculum enhancement, resource sharing, faculty development, and the promotion of entrepreneurship among the university students. It illustrated with examples how partnerships between academia and industry can bridge the gap between theoretical and practical knowledge, equipping students with job-ready skills and exposing them to real-world challenges. By integrating industry-relevant projects, internships, and applied research projects, these collaborations enrich the academic experience through enhancing employability of the graduates and contributing to the socioeconomic development of the country. Despite the transformative potentials, industry-academia collaborations can face challenges such as, misaligned objectives, inadequate infrastructure, limited policy support, and skill gaps among the students and the faculty members. This chapter provides actionable recommendations, including the establishment of joint steering committees, public-private partnerships, and comprehensive policy frameworks that incentivize academia-industry collaborations. This study also recommends for the creation of innovation hubs, collaborative research studies, and industry-led faculty development programs to sustain these partnerships. Key contributions of this work include a detailed analysis of how such collaborations address the challenges higher educational institutions, advance research commercialization, and foster innovation in the universities of Bangladesh. By positioning universities as key contributors to the global knowledge, this study underscores the broader implications of these collaborations for advancing the academic excellence in the universities of Bangladesh. This chapter not only provides a roadmap for enhancing academic excellence in Bangladesh but also offers insights for other developing nations seeking to leverage industry-academia partnerships for the sustainable development and global integration.

detail.abstract: Public policy problems are complex and ill-structured. Their impacts can be broad but poorlyunderstood. In this paper, we present ontological meta-analysis and synthesis as a method for public policy analysis, formulation, and assessment. It is a systemic, systematic, and symmetric method that can be applied to public policy research, analysis, and practice. The method encapsulates the combinatorial complexity of the policy problem with little simplification, selectivity, and skewness.

title: OptiRepair: Closed-Loop Diagnosis and Repair of Supply Chain Optimization Models with LLM Agents

detail.title: OptiRepair: Closed-Loop Diagnosis and Repair of Supply Chain Optimization Models with LLM Agents

keywords: Wang: OptiRepair: Closed-Loop Diagnosis and Repair of Supply Chain Optimization Models

detail.abstract: Supply chain optimization models frequently become infeasible because of modeling errors. Diagnosis and repair require scarce OR expertise: analysts must interpret solver diagnostics, trace root causes across echelons, and fix formulations without sacrificing operational soundness. Whether AI agents can perform this task remains untested. We decompose this task into two phases: a domain-agnostic feasibility phase that iteratively repairs any LP using IIS-guided diagnosis, and a domain-specific validation phase that enforces five rationality checks grounded in inventory theory. We test 22 API models from seven families on 976 multi-echelon supply chain problems and train two 8B-parameter models with self-taught reasoning and solver-verified rewards. The trained models reach 81.7% Rational Recovery Rate (RRR)---the fraction of problems resolved to both feasibility and operational rationality---versus 42.2% for the best API model and 21.3% on average. The gap concentrates in Phase 1 repair, where API models average 27.6% recovery rate versus 97.2% for trained models. Two gaps separate current AI from reliable model repair: solver interaction, as API models restore only 27.6% of infeasible formulations; and operational rationale, as roughly one in four feasible repairs violate supply chain theory. Each gap requires a different intervention---targeted training closes the solver interaction gap, while explicit specification as solver-verifiable checks closes the rationality gap. For organizations adopting AI in operational planning, formalizing what 'rational' means in their context is the higher-return investment.

title: Dynamic Assortment Planning and Customization with Partition Constraints
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong and University of British Columbia

detail.title: Dynamic Assortment Planning and Customization with Partition Constraints
detail.abstract:
Marketplaces such as Amazon and Etsy must not only maximize commissions from sales but also sustain long‑term seller engagement. This requires preventing any single seller from dominating display opportunities and ensuring that enough sellers remain active in the marketplace. Motivated by this, we study dynamic assortment optimization under partition constraints. In each period, the platform operates in two stages: first, it selects a consideration set subject to the partition constraints  that limit the number of products from each seller; second, it offers personalized assortments to arriving customers whose arrivals are adversarial and whose choices follow the Multinomial Logit model.

We begin by establishing the intractability of the single-period problem. To address this, we develop an approximate formulation based on the multilinear extension of the expected profit function and derive key structural properties. In particular, we introduce the notion of \emph{$\psi$-very-weak submodularity} to characterize the \emph{reduced profit function}, which serves as a simplified representation of the expected profit function. Furthermore, we establish that the \emph{modified reduced profit function} satisfies standard submodularity. More generally, we construct a novel surrogate function for the multilinear extension of a $\psi$-very-weakly submodular function and prove that any stationary point of this surrogate yields a constant-factor approximation to the corresponding $\psi$-very-weakly submodular maximization problem.

Building on these properties, we design three online algorithms by applying primal mirror ascent to surrogate functions. We introduce two randomized algorithms: one attaining instance-dependent performance based on the specific profit structure, and another achieving a constant competitive ratio. Furthermore, we extend our framework to a deterministic setting where the platform must select a single consideration set. We introduce a new multilinear extension to naturally reflect the deterministic partition constraint and a lossless rounding technique that preserves the theoretical guarantees.  All proposed algorithms achieve $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret relative to constant-factor approximations of the corresponding hindsight benchmarks. This work provides the first provable regret bounds for dynamic two-stage assortment optimization, offering a framework for balancing profit maximization with equitable group visibility.

detail.title: From Autonomy to Agency: A 10-Level Framework for AI's Evolution and Organisational Readiness

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a 10-level framework mapping AI's progression from task execution to autonomous agency, organised across three tiers: task autonomy (Levels 0–5), where systems execute within human-defined boundaries with increasing independence; goal agency (Levels 6–9), where systems determine how to pursue human-set goals through emergent coordination, self-extension, and recursive self-improvement; and purpose formation (Level 10), where systems determine what goals are worth pursuing.

Existing frameworks address AI capability through performance metrics (Morris, M. R. et al., 2023), user control mechanisms (Feng et al., 2025), or liability allocation (Morris, J. et al., 2024). None integrate technical capabilities with the organisational prerequisites required at each level. This framework extends the SAE autonomous vehicle model (SAE International, 2021) by recognising AI's progression beyond domain-bounded autonomy towards agency: the capacity for self-determined goal pursuit, autonomous capability extension, and recursive self-improvement.

The framework is grounded in current evidence. As of February 2026, multi-agent systems exhibit emergent behaviours in production (Level 6; Anthropic, 2025). Self-extending systems are commercially available (Level 7; OpenAI, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025). Recursive generational development, where AI contributes to building the next generation of AI, shows early demonstration at major laboratories (Level 8; OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026). Among organisations actively building with AI agent frameworks, 57% report agents in production (LangChain, 2025).

Organisational prerequisites are mapped across infrastructure, governance, culture, and leadership dimensions, drawing on organisational learning theory (March, 1991; O'Reilly & Tushman, 2004, 2013) and practitioner fieldwork (60+ organisations, 2022–2025). A critical finding: compliance shifts from technical controls (Levels 0–5) to principled constraints (Levels 6–9), with AI-assisted compliance monitoring becoming necessary as system speed exceeds human oversight capacity.

title: "Phygital" Experiences: Optimization, Tailoring, and Pricing Contract Strategies on the Online Platform

detail.title: "Phygital" Experiences: Optimization, Tailoring, and Pricing Contract Strategies on the Online Platform

detail.abstract: Technology-driven tools, such as Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR), bring products to life in a virtual space for online consumers and are poised to become the new standard. With more effective tools, consumers are more likely to find the products that best meet their needs. While these tools enhance online purchasing decisions, consumers vary in their ability to use them effectively. As e-shopping continues to grow, firms must carefully consider whether and how to offer these tools. In this paper, we analytically study a firm's (i) tool provision, (ii) optimization of a tool that brings physical experience to e-shopping, and how they differ depending on (iii) heterogeneity of consumer expertise in using the tool. We also consider (iv) pricing decisions, different channel contracts, and (v) alignment of profits with the platform through which the firm sells, with respect to tool optimization and tailoring incentives. We find that a tool need not always be perfect; the experienced can be given the imperfect tool. Optimal effectiveness can be set higher when tailored to the inexperienced, yet the seller does not pursue this strategy, as it primarily benefits the platform. This misalignment in tailoring preferences can, however, be mitigated for certain product categories. Additionally, optimal tool-effectiveness is always higher under a sell-on contract, making it a potential win-win solution. Furthermore, tool provision can shift the platform's preference from a sell-to to a sell-on contract, which generally benefits the firm. Our results remain robust when accounting for a mix of inexperienced and experienced consumers, product returns, risk-averse consumers, and cost barriers. Altogether, we show that tool provision should be considered jointly with tailoring to different consumer experience levels, and the platform does not always have the same incentives as the seller in dimensions such as tool provision, pricing contracts, and tailoring preferences.

detail.abstract: Modern businesses are inundated with massive volumes of data generated every second from diverse sources like IoT devices, social media interactions, transactional systems, and sensor networks. While this data surge offers immense opportunities, traditional batch-based analytics methods struggle to keep pace, often yielding insights only post critical decision-making. Realtime predictive analytics on streaming data has emerged as a transformative approach, enabling organizations to instantaneously analyze continuous data flows and forecast future events with remarkable accuracy. By integrating advanced machine learning models with real-time data pipelines, businesses can detect anomalies, anticipate customer behaviors, improve operations, and proactively respond to emerging risks. This paper explores the underlying concepts, technologies, and architectures enabling realtime predictive analytics and illustrates their practical applications across industries such as finance, manufacturing, healthcare, and e-commerce. It highlights the tangible benefits of real-time insights, including enhanced operational efficiency, reduced costs, improved customer experiences, and strategic agility. The study also addresses the technical and organizational challenges in implementing streaming analytics, encompassing data quality issues, scalability concerns, skill requirements, and ethical considerations. Finally, emerging trends like edge computing, adaptive AI models, and automated anomaly detection are discussed, offering a forward-looking perspective on how real-time predictive analytics will continue to revolutionize business decisionmaking in the future.

detail.abstract: Retailers and platforms commonly use incentive programs to stimulate online reviews. Retailer-initiated programs often adopt rewards conditional on meeting a rating threshold, which can bias reported ratings upward, whereas platform-led programs typically reward review participation regardless of ratings, thereby increasing review volume and improving the precision of the review signal. We investigate which program performs better in a competitive marketplace. We model two competing retailers selling partially substitutable products on a shared platform, where reviews affect customer choice by reducing quality uncertainty. Solving for equilibrium incentives, we show that retailer-initiated incentives can generate higher supply chain profits when the initial rating gap is small and customer uncertainty is low. When the rating gap is large, the platform prefers its own program; when the gap is small, it optimally permits retailer-initiated incentives. Retailer preferences can diverge: the retailer with a higher initial rating may favor the platform-led program under large rating gaps, particularly when platform incentives are more effective at generating reviews, whereas the retailer with a lower initial rating can be worse off under the platform-led program once the rating gap is sufficiently large. Motivated by Amazon's Early Reviewer and Vine, we further examine two collaborative schemes: (i) each retailer pays the platform an upfront fee to generate reviews (upfront-fee scheme) and (ii) retailers pay the upfront fee and additionally share a portion of the platform's reward costs (cost-sharing scheme). These collaborative schemes may even create a "lose-lose" outcome for both the platform and retailers relative to the platform-led program. Moreover, the cost-sharing scheme is especially detrimental to the platform compared with the upfront-fee scheme when the initial rating gap is large or customer uncertainty is high. These results provide guidance on when platforms should centralize review incentives versus delegate them to retailers and how collaborative incentives should be structured.

title: Beyond Mimicry to Contextual Guidance: Knowledge Distillation for Interactive AI

detail.title: Beyond Mimicry to Contextual Guidance: Knowledge Distillation for Interactive AI
detail.abstract: As large language models increasingly mediate firm-customer interactions, firms face a tradeoff: the most capable models perform well but are costly and difficult to control at scale. Existing knowledge distillation methods address this challenge by training weaker, deployable models to imitate frontier outputs; however, such open-loop approaches are poorly suited to interactive, multi-turn settings where responses must be sequenced coherently across conversational states. We propose a shift in what knowledge is distilled-from output imitation to contextual guidance. We develop a framework in which a superior teacher model constructs a reusable library of strategic textual guidance for particular scenarios likely to be encountered by the student. When deployed, the student retrieves the context-specific guidance at inference time, enabling adaptive behavior without retraining. Using customer-service interactions, we show that this approach improves service quality and customer satisfaction relative to standard fine-tuning while maintaining alignment with firm policies. The results position inference-time textual guidance as a scalable and controllable approach to distillation for interactive AI agents in marketing settings.

detail.abstract:
Why have taxes on concentrated wealth weakened across decades, even though polling typically shows strong majority support? This Article argues that the answer lies in a structural dynamic we call the tax-and-oligarchy catch-22. Taxing extreme wealth is among democracy’s most direct tools for constraining oligarchic power, yet extreme wealth reliably finances the political work of blocking, diluting, or unwinding such taxes.

The catch-22 operates through political optionality. When the wealthiest households can defer tax indefinitely, they preserve capacity for campaigns, litigation, lobbying, and producing expert doubt about reforms that might reach them. Every dollar of deferred tax is a dollar available to lobby against its own eventual collection. Progressive Era reforms were designed to interrupt this dynamic. For decades they partially succeeded. But the constraints have eroded, and today’s largest fortunes face minimal effective taxation.

This Article responds with a democratic tax firewall, an approach that treats durability as a first-order design constraint rather than an afterthought. Drawing on political science, history, and recent state-level campaigns, we identify design choices that can help reforms resist quiet erosion and show how sustained technical preparation can position reformers to act when political windows open.

detail.abstract: Streaming platforms must decide whether audience demand is driven by (a) the intrinsic appeal of titles or (b) algorithmic exposure. A practitioner summary of a working paper by Aridor and Netflix coauthors describes a model that leverages intentional homepage randomization to disentangle the incremental lift from recommendations versus baseline content value, finding that "middle-tier" niche titles benefit most and that the current recommender outperforms alternatives on engagement and content diversity. This DBTC specifies a reusable Content-Recommendation Value Attribution Decision System (CRVADS) that converts those insights into auditable decisions, decision rights, evidence gates, and governance loops. Using a replicable Decision-System Decomposition Method (DSDM), the manuscript defines seven recurring decisions (D1-D7) spanning objective-setting (engagement vs diversity), experiment governance, causal attribution and substitution modeling, catalog portfolio investment, and scale/rollback control. The contribution is a decision architecture that reduces "pilot theater," prevents metric gaming, and aligns recommendation optimization with long-run customer value.

detail.abstract: Enterprise Information Systems (EIS) create value by integrating information, workflows, and decision rights across functions and extended enterprises. Yet popularpress reporting suggests AI value is increasingly governed as a near-term savings mandate, with headcount reductions emerging as the most visible instrument in marketing organizations (Coffee, 2025). This editorial argues that "savings-first layoffs" are often a weak default in EIS contexts because they reduce the human capacity required for workflow redesign, measurement integrity, and governancecomplements that convert AI outputs into repeatable, auditable, and safe operational performance (Brynjolfsson et al., 2017). Building on multi-task incentive logic, we explain why single-metric savings targets crowd out customer-outcome work and learning routines (Holmström & Milgrom, 2009). We propose an EIS-grade valuerealization architecture coupling automate/augment/protect work segmentation with net-value accounting and workflow-embedded controls for quality, disclosure, privacy, and IP risk (Bender et al., 2021; Weidinger et al., 2022).

detail.abstract: We find that consumption spreads through social networks via a "visibility bias" channel, consistent with the model of Han et al. (2023). Using county-level Facebook connectedness and exogenous fracking shocks, we show that a 1% increase in a closely linked county's consumption raises local spending by 0.35% next year. Heterogeneous effects-stronger among more socially connected households and for socially visible goods-indicate transmission through social observation instead of economic linkages. Without their own income gains, households respond by buying cheaper goods, and peer-induced spending increases delinquency rates, underscoring that biased social observation, rather than economic connectedness, undermines financial stability.

title: Consent Without Continuity: Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy and the Structural Failure of Informed Consent Doctrine

detail.title: Consent Without Continuity: Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy and the Structural Failure of Informed Consent Doctrine

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding supported this research.

detail.abstract:
American informed consent doctrine rests on an unexamined premise: the stable-agent assumption—that the patient who authorizes a medical intervention and the patient who experiences its consequences share a continuous evaluative framework. Materiality doctrine presupposes this continuity; causation doctrine embeds it; capacity doctrine assumes it. For most of modern medical practice, the assumption held because treatments did not alter the cognitive architecture through which patients assess risk.

Psychedelic-assisted therapy disrupts that continuity. Compounds such as psilocybin and MDMA, now administered under state regulatory frameworks in Oregon and Colorado, produce documented and sometimes durable changes in patients’ values, self-concept, and evaluative frameworks—not as incidental side effects but as intended therapeutic outcomes. When a treatment transforms the cognitive architecture through which risk is assessed, the temporal bridge between the consenting self and the experiencing self collapses.

This Article proposes a dynamic consent model comprising four components: pre-session identity-impact disclosures with a meta-disclosure acknowledging the structural limits of pre-treatment consent; staged reaffirmation checkpoints across post-treatment intervals; integration-phase consent validation; and longitudinal documentation reforms. Without reconstruction, materiality lacks a stable decisional perspective, causation lacks a stable counterfactual subject, and capacity assessment fails to account for a treatment designed to alter the cognitive framework it purports to assess.

title: Metaverse Festivals Beyond Overtourism: Digital Transformation of Cultural Events Towards Accessibility, Cultural Engagement and Sustainable Tourism Policy

detail.title: Metaverse Festivals Beyond Overtourism: Digital Transformation of Cultural Events Towards Accessibility, Cultural Engagement and Sustainable Tourism Policy
detail.abstract: Cultural festivals have long been anchored in co-located, resource-intensive events, which increasingly raises questions about who can participate, at what environmental cost and with what consequences for cultural integrity in destinations facing overtourism. This paper examines how metaverse-based, metaverse-adjacent and hybrid festival configurations may reconfigure festival tourism by reshaping accessibility, cultural engagement and environmental performance, and considers the implications for governance and policy. Drawing on a narrative literature review of academic and institutional sources published mainly between 2010 and 2025, it synthesises work on digital transformation, virtual and hybrid events, accessible tourism, digital inequality, overtourism and sustainable festival management. The paper offers a structured, critically informed synthesis and a set of propositions intended to guide future empirical and theoretical research on metaverse applications in tourism and hospitality. The review suggests that "metaverse-based" festivals can ease geographical, financial and some physical constraints for some groups, widen participation for underserved groups and support new forms of cultural preservation and co-creation, while also risking deeper digital inequalities and renewed concerns about cultural commodification, data governance and authenticity. Environmentally, virtual participation may reduce travel-related emissions and local crowding when it substitutes for physical attendance, while shifting impacts towards energy-intensive digital infrastructures and device lifecycles.

title: Inflation, Distribution and Bimonetarity: A Kalecki-Godley-Minsky Inflation Equation for Peripheral Economies
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Inflation, Distribution and Bimonetarity: A Kalecki-Godley-Minsky Inflation Equation for Peripheral Economies
detail.abstract:
Persistent inflation in open, bimonetary peripheral economies — such as Argentina — remains inadequately explained by orthodox models based on expectations or output gaps. This paper proposes a new inflation equation that integrates, for the first time, the frameworks of Kalecki, Godley and Minsky with the distinctive feature of bimonetarity and dollar inflation. The central theoretical contribution consists in unifying distributive conflict, sectoral financing, multi-currency financial fragility and external constraint within a coherent and empirically tractable macroeconomic structure.

Drawing on Kalecki, the model incorporates cost-plus pricing, whereby inflation emerges from conflict between nominal wages and productivity. From Godley, it takes the stock-flow consistent structure representing how aggregate expenditure is financed through public deficits, domestic credit and external borrowing. From Minsky, it adopts claim-dilution (δ) as a measure of financial fragility, extended here to four dimensions: public debt in domestic currency (δ_G), quasi-fiscal central bank liabilities (δ_BCRA), and external borrowing by the public (δ_pub) and private (δ_priv) sectors.

The distinctive contribution is the introduction of dollar inflation (π$) as a macroeconomic fundamental — defined as the difference between domestic inflation and exchange rate depreciation. It erodes real competitiveness and the expected trade balance while increasing the need for external financing, raising external leverage. This generates a vicious macro-financial cycle: dollar appreciation → external deterioration → higher dollar debt → devaluation risk → exchange rate jump → rise in domestic prices → further amplification of dollar inflation.

The final equation proposed is:

πt = Dt + Ft + Xt + ρπt−1

The model is validated through comparative historical calibration for Brazil (2010–2024) and Argentina (2017–2025). For Brazil, the Mean Absolute Error is 0.89 percentage points over fifteen years, capturing the 2015 crisis and the 2021 supply shock. For Argentina, the Mean Absolute Relative Error is 2.43%, with all years below 4.5% relative error — including the hyperinflationary episode of 2023 (211% observed vs. 203% simulated) and the disinflation of 2025 (31.5% observed vs. 32.7% simulated).

Channel decomposition quantifies the mechanism of Argentine stabilization in 2024–2025: the inertial component collapses from 197 pp to 9 pp when the wage indexation parameter ρW falls from 0.97 to 0.18, at a documented cost of 10.7 percentage points of the wage share in income.

The model explains why inflation in bimonetary economies is endogenous, persistent and highly sensitive to the external sector, even absent output gaps or excess money. It provides a formal basis for anti-inflationary policies integrating incomes policy, exchange rate management, reduction of multi-currency leverage and productive development. Structural parameters encode verifiable institutional differences: exchange rate pass-through (κe: 0.03–0.05 in Brazil vs. 0.15–0.50 in Argentina) and wage indexation (ρW: 0.50–0.65 in Brazil vs. 0.18–0.97 in Argentina) are not statistical coefficients but quantitative representations of productive structures and collective bargaining systems.

title: Retail Trading Fire Sales: The Impact of Wildfires on Investment Decisions

detail.title: Retail Trading Fire Sales: The Impact of Wildfires on Investment Decisions
detail.abstract: We combine transaction-level brokerage data from a large Portuguese bank with detailed geospatial wildfire records to study how indirect exposure to extreme climate events affects household portfolio decisions. Exploiting geographic variation in retail investors' proximity to wildfires, we show that individuals nearby wildfire events significantly reduce their risktaking. This adjustment occurs through both increased selling and reduced purchases of risky assets in the months following a fire. The effects extend well beyond the burned perimeter and persist over time. We further document a substantial increase in the probability of fully liquidating portfolios and exiting the stock market, along with a decline in stock market entry. We find no evidence that these responses are driven by changes in wealth or background risk; instead, the evidence is consistent with a fear-based mechanism. Finally, we find that postwildfire portfolios significantly underperform relative to pre-wildfire portfolios over 6-, 12-, and 24-month horizons.

title: Predicting and Reducing Homelessness in Allegheny County

detail.title: Predicting and Reducing Homelessness in Allegheny County
detail.abstract: Housing subsidies are effective at ending homelessness for recipients, yet expansions in housing capacity have not translated into commensurate reductions in aggregate homelessness. We argue that targeting plays a central role: when housing reaches individuals who would have exited shelter on their own, each placement prevents little system-wide homelessness. Using administrative data from Allegheny County, we develop a predictive model that identifies individuals likely to experience extended shelter stays at the time of shelter entry. Among the highest-risk individuals flagged by the model, over 40 percent go on to experience extended homelessness-more than three times the baseline rate. We show that the majority of shelter residents exit shelter on their own weeks after starting their shelter stint. Allocating housing to the individuals or families at the highest-risk of prolonged shelter stints would prevent roughly 2.4 times as many shelter days per unit as allocating to the average shelter resident, and 120 percent more than allocating based on current federal prioritization criteria. A shift from retrospective to prospective targeting could substantially reduce aggregate homelessness without expanding the subsidized housing stock.

title: Is the Evaluation of Performance Gender Specific? Evidence From Two Large Experimental Studies

detail.title: Is the Evaluation of Performance Gender Specific? Evidence From Two Large Experimental Studies
detail.abstract: It is often assumed that women receive less recognition than men for the same work or performance. We test this assumption via two large-scale online-survey experiments involving 3,157 (Study I) and 2,909 (Study II) respondents respectively. In both studies, subjects watched a two-minute video in which either a female or a male character presented either a male-associated topic, a gender-neutral topic, or a female-associated topic. Since former research suggests that the attractiveness of the presenter increases performance evaluations, we also varied the attractiveness of the presenting characters. Study I uses a 2 (gender) by 2 (attractiveness) by 3 (topic) design. The video presentations were created using an artificial intelligence video-maker that used human-like avatars. In Study II, the presentations were conducted by real humans. The findings from both studies suggest that gender has no influence on how respondents evaluate presentations. Additionally, in Study I we find that attractive male avatar presenters receive more favorable evaluations than less attractive males. In contrast, female avatar presenters do not receive an attractiveness bonus. However, when using real humans instead of avatars we did not find this attractiveness bonus for men.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study develops and validates a hybrid machine learning (ML) framework integrating national development indicators with agricultural productivity data to enable robust, multiscale food system intelligence. Drawing on Nepal's longitudinal development dataset (1960-2023) spanning 1,478 macroeconomic, demographic, and sectoral indicators alongside a curated food ingredient intelligence database of 12,321 product entries, the study advances the methodological frontier of agricultural forecasting through a stacked ensemble architecture. Design/Methodology: A four-stage pipeline was constructed: (i) multivariate data harmonization and feature engineering; (ii) preprocessing via Min-Max normalization, ADF stationarity correction, and VIF-guided multicollinearity reduction; (iii) a stacked ensemble combining Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, and LSTM as level-0 learners with Ridge Regression as the meta-learner; and (iv) evaluation across RMSE, MAE, R², and MAPE with Diebold-Mariano significance testing. Findings: The hybrid ensemble achieved R² = 0.947 and RMSE = 87.3 kg/ha in cereal yield forecasting, outperforming all standalone base models by 8.3-24.7%. SHAP analysis revealed that electricity access, GDP per capita growth, rural population share, food production index, and agricultural value added collectively accounted for approximately 68% of predictive variance. Nepal's cereal yield trajectory rising from 2,148.6 kg/ha in 2000 to 3,218.5 kg/ha in 2022 was found to be systematically co-determined by macrostructural development transitions. Practical Implications: The framework equips national agricultural planning agencies with a scalable, data-driven early warning and productivity forecasting tool for data-sparse developing economies. Integration with food ingredient supply chain intelligence creates cross-sector policy analytics capacity for South Asian food systems navigating postpandemic recovery and climate disruption. Originality/Value: Three dimensions of originality are established: (i) methodological novelty through hybrid stacking of heterogeneous macroeconomic and agricultural predictors; (ii) theoretical novelty through formal operationalization of food system intelligence as a computable, indicator-driven construct; and (iii) policy-level contribution through empirically grounded frameworks applicable to South Asian agricultural governance.

This paper explores the elderly's decision to cohabit with their adult children in Mexico. Using a non-contributory pension program established in the early 2000s in Mexico City and later expanded as a federal program as a permanent income shock, we estimate the impact of the policy on the cohabitation situation of retired and elderly people. We develop a theoretical model that aims to explain the co-residency decision process as a household utility consumption model, where a parent evaluates whether to live together with their adult children or live separately based on individual-specific and consumption preferences.

For the analysis we employ a sharp regression discontinuity approach, using a survey collected in 2019 in Mexico City and Mexico State, from which we generate six potential control groups using age and spatial distance to the borders between states as running variables for the RDD. The results show mild evidence that aligns with the current economic literature. Positive income shocks to retired adults reduce the probability of coresidence with their offspring. We also test for potential heterogeneous effects using state-level panel data from 1996 to 2007 and a difference-in-differences approach. Estimates from the national state-level panel using the DID show similar results to the cross-sectional data used in the RDD.

detail.abstract: The repeal of "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" (DADT) in 2011 marked a significant shift in U.S. military policy, allowing lesbian, gay, and bisexual individuals to serve openly without risking discharge. Using a difference-indifferences approach paired with data from the 2008-2019 American Community Survey, I leverage information on active-duty military employees and their families to study the effects of the DADT repeal on same-sex partnership formation and downstream economic outcomes. I find that repealing DADT substantially increased same-sex partnership among women in the military while having no effect on same-sex partnership rates among active duty men. These effects were not limited to family structure-I also show that civilian women in same-sex partnerships with active-duty women are more likely to have military health insurance coverage following the DADT repeal. This paper provides the first evidence of the effects of repealing DADT on sexual minorities serving in the military, shedding new light on the relationship between workplace discrimination and family formation and contributing to the broader literature on LGBTQ+ rights and policies.

title: Decision-Free Taxation: A Formal Proof

detail.title: Decision-Free Taxation: A Formal Proof

detail.abstract: Every existing system for taxing income or returns requires agents to report those quantities — a self-reported process that concentrates evasion where third-party verification is absent (Allingham and Sandmo 1972; Kleven et al. 2011). This paper constructs a tax mechanism that eliminates self-reporting entirely by shifting the tax base from income to third-party-verified positions — bank account balances and registry records — where six instruments (τ, δ, β, σ, ρ, θ) attach automatically at two perimeters — checking-to-savings (domestic) and domestic-to-foreign (international). Registration is voluntary but structurally dominant: unregistered assets carry no enforceable ownership title, so rational agents self-select into disclosure. No taxpayer files a tax return, computes tax liability, or remits payment. We prove three results: (1) closure — five storage types, five agent types, and seven primitives exhaustively classify all positions and actions available in a modern economy, every cell is priced, and no sequence of intermediate steps reduces cost; (2) instrument sufficiency — three parameters are structurally necessary, three provide independent policy control; (3) freedom sufficiency — every feasible allocation is reachable. Corollaries establish no evasion path (jointly with the companion monetary architecture for fixed nominal claims), decision-free collection, agent self-classification, Diamond–Mirrlees production efficiency, flow progressivity with stock proportionality, and capital structure neutrality at proposed calibration.

title: A Theory of Informational Coordination for Curated Economies (TICC)
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: A Theory of Informational Coordination for Curated Economies (TICC)
detail.abstract: Curated economies increasingly rely on recommendation systems that guide agents through informational signals rather than direct control. This paper develops a theory of informational coordination in which decentralized "coordinating planners" issue type-indexed recommendations that help agents learn latent economic identities. While such systems can reduce search costs and improve matching efficiency, they introduce a structural inefficiency: classification compression. Recommendation mechanisms optimize for regular types and systematically collapse rare or exceptional agents into dominant categories. When exceptional types generate disproportionately large social returns-such as innovation, discovery, or fragility detection-misclassification produces large welfare losses despite locally accurate recommendations. The TIC framework models curated economies as type-learning environments constrained by verification and mediation capacity, showing how informational guidance can drift into equilibrium distortion without formal enforcement. The analysis derives welfare-improving institutional designs, including plural recommendation systems, explicit "exceptional/unknown" categories, and mechanisms preserving exploratory autonomy. The paper argues that the central coordination problem of curated economies is not allocation but epistemic sorting: societies remain efficient only when informational infrastructures enable exceptional types to be discovered rather than normalized.

title: Dynamic Risk-Sensitive Control in Distribution Space

detail.title: Dynamic Risk-Sensitive Control in Distribution Space
detail.abstract: We develop a mathematical framework for dynamic risk-sensitive control in distribution space. Rather than optimizing over state trajectories, policies act on conditional probability laws and are evaluated through coherent risk functionals such as Expected Shortfall and spectral risk measures. We establish a Bellman principle on the Wasserstein space of probability measures, derive stability bounds under distributional perturbations, and introduce a robust extension over Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Finite-sample guarantees link estimation error in predictive distributions to control performance. The resulting theory unifies stochastic control, optimal transport, and coherent risk and provides a foundation for tail-risk-aware decision systems with applications in banking and algorithmic trading.
