title: Farming the Storm: How In-Situ Adaptation shapes Migration decision in Tanzania

detail.title: Farming the Storm: How In-Situ Adaptation shapes Migration decision in Tanzania
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether in-situ agricultural adaptation influences household migration decisions, using nationally representative panel data from Tanzania (LSMS-ISA). The analysis focuses on adaptation practices, commonly known as in-situ adaptation which aims to reduce climate risk by making agricultural practices more resilient such as irrigation, inter cropping, the use of organic fertilizer and herbicide, and the adoption of improved seeds. To address potential endogeneity, an instrumental variable and control function approach are employed. The results show that adaptation increases the likelihood of migration by approximately 47 percentage points, suggesting a complementary relationship between adaptation and migration. Further analysis identifies an income channel, whereby adaptation raises household income and relaxes liquidity constraints, enabling households to afford risk-diversifying migration. Overall, the findings challenge the view that migration and adaptation are mutually exclusive responses or that migration is a failure to adapt. Instead, they indicate that migration can form part of a broader adaptive strategy, with important implications for climate and development policy.

title: Multi-scale and Path Signature-informed Deep Learning for Intraday Volatility Forecasting
affiliations: Jinan University, Jinan University - Finance Department, University of Glasgow - Adam Smith Business School and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Multi-scale and Path Signature-informed Deep Learning for Intraday Volatility Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial data and does not involve human participants. Ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: We investigate how temporal dependencies, path signatures, and cross-sectional commonality can be leveraged to improve intraday realized volatility forecasting. To this end, we develop two recurrent neural network architectures: (i) a multi-scale attention mechanism that captures horizon-dependent dynamics, and (ii) a signature-augmented model that encodes the geometric features of high-frequency price paths. In addition, we introduce a cluster-based training scheme that pools stocks within sectors and conditions on sector-level realized volatility. Using one-minute data for large-cap Chinese A-share stocks, we benchmark our models against standard econometric methods, tree-based learners, and conventional recurrent networks. Our results show that nonlinear models consistently outperform linear specifications, that multi-scale attention and signature augmentation yield systematic gains across short and long horizons, and that cluster-based training delivers the largest and most robust improvements. Diebold-Mariano tests and model confidence set procedures confirm a clear hierarchy among pooling strategies, with sector-cluster-based models outperforming market-augmented, fully pooled, and stock-specific approaches. These findings highlight sector-level comovement as a persistent and exploitable source of predictive power in intraday volatility.

title: The Political Economy of AIIB Lending: Selection, Allocation, and the Evolution of Chinese Influence
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Political Economy of AIIB Lending: Selection, Allocation, and the Evolution of Chinese Influence
detail.abstract: As the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) enters its second decade in early 2026, this study examines the determinants of its lending behavior, focusing on the interplay between Chinese influence and multilateral institutional safeguards. Drawing on a comprehensive dataset spanning 2016-2024, we employ a two-stage empirical approach to distinguish between factors driving loan selection and those determining allocation amounts. Our findings reveal institutional complexity: while loan selection exhibits a "supplementary" logic, where trade integration with China and less democratic governance significantly increase the probability of approval, loan allocation follows a "remedial" logic, characterized by smaller funding amounts for close diplomatic partners and countries heavily indebted to China. Furthermore, the analysis provides evidence of a strategic "division of labor," with the Bank exercising greater caution toward lower-income, less democratic Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) participants. Finally, we observe a temporal shift toward a more pragmatic, trade-oriented focus following the COVID-19 pandemic. These results suggest that the AIIB has matured into a sophisticated multilateral actor capable of balancing shareholder-driven strategic interests with the established norms of multilateral development finance.

title: When Can We Recover Granger/Transfer-Entropy Networks in High Dimensions? Information-Theoretic Limits and Achievable Regimes for VAR Graph Recovery
affiliations: and

detail.title: When Can We Recover Granger/Transfer-Entropy Networks in High Dimensions? Information-Theoretic Limits and Achievable Regimes for VAR Graph Recovery
detail.abstract: We study when directed dependence networks based on linear Granger causality (and hence Gaussian transfer entropy) can be reliably recovered in high dimensions. We provide (i) informationtheoretic lower bounds showing that node-level recovery is impossible below a sample-size regime depending on sparsity, signal strength, and dimension, and (ii) achievable guarantees for rowwise sparse VAR estimation based on penalized regression under stability and regularity conditions. We also explain why certain aggregate network statistics can remain detectable even when node-level structure is not recoverable. Our results yield practical sample-size planning rules and clarify why empirically popular network pipelines may fail at realistic T /N ratios.

title: Preventive Redistribution and Consumption Smoothing in China： Ex-Post Redistribution or Ex-Ante Redistribution?

detail.title: Preventive Redistribution and Consumption Smoothing in China： Ex-Post Redistribution or Ex-Ante Redistribution?

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the limitations of social security and healthcare systems that have traditionally relied on ex-post redistribution, and to propose a new analytical framework centered on preventive redistribution that addresses health risks before they materialize. Using provincelevel panel data from China, it also investigates whether preventive redistribution mitigates the income shocks to consumption and if so, to what extent. After applying an empirically modified full risk-sharing model framework, the results indicate that preventive investment contributes more effectively to consumption smoothing than ex-post measures, particularly in low-income regions, where it alleviates the link between health risks and economic instability, both immediately and over the long term. Further, the findings suggest that such effects are more likely to be sustained when preventive redistribution is implemented as a universal institutional arrangement, than as a selective policy. Thus, this study highlights the need to reposition preventive redistribution, not as a complement to ex-post compensation, but as a core institutional mechanism that integrates economic growth and risk management.

title: Unveiling Diversity: Does Diversity of Uncertainty Influence Corporate Cash Holdings?
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, Pennsylvania State University - School of Graduate Professional Studies (SGPS), NTNU Business School and Thammasat Business School

detail.title: Unveiling Diversity: Does Diversity of Uncertainty Influence Corporate Cash Holdings?
detail.abstract: We explore an important aspect of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) that has been surprisingly overlooked in the literature, i.e., diversity of uncertainty. Firms experience greater diversity of uncertainty when dealing with multiple areas of uncertainty simultaneously. By contrast, when uncertainty is concentrated in one or few areas, there is lower diversity of uncertainty. Coping with several distinct areas of uncertainty is likely more complicated and thus riskier. Consistent with this notion, our results, based on a large sample of almost 300,000 observations over 36 years, suggest that firms are more circumspect and thus hold significantly more cash when grappling with multiple sources of EPU. Greater diversity of uncertainty results in significantly higher cash holdings. Notably, the effect of the diversity of EPU is above and beyond the effect of the level of EPU on cash holdings, suggesting that it constitutes a separate and distinct dimension that warrants careful consideration. Further analysis robustly validates the results, i.e., propensity score matching, entropy balancing, GMM dynamic panel data analysis, and Lewbel's (2012) heteroscedasticity identification.

title: FRTracker: Deterministic Extraction and Structural Modeling of Federal Regulatory Obligations

detail.title: FRTracker: Deterministic Extraction and Structural Modeling of Federal Regulatory Obligations
detail.abstract: FRTracker is a public tool for analyzing the Federal Register and Code of Federal Regulations. It extracts discrete compliance obligations from regulatory text using deterministic, rule-based methods-no artificial intelligence or machine learning is used at any stage of the pipeline. It maps public comments to specific regulatory provisions and links proposed rules to their final versions with structural diffs. A recent extension models external regulatory cross-references as a distinct obligation kind, shifting the system from counting obligations toward mapping the dependency structure of regulatory compliance. All classification is transparent, auditable, and reproducible. This paper describes the system's three core capabilities and its approach to "unrule" detection following Coglianese, Scheffler, and Walters (2021).

title: Pattern Recognition of Artificial Intelligence Hardware in Global Trade Data
affiliations: Asia School of Business in collaboration with MIT Sloan

detail.title: Pattern Recognition of Artificial Intelligence Hardware in Global Trade Data
detail.abstract: This study conducts a strategic audit of semiconductor trade frameworks, specifically analyzing key technology verticals (HS 8542 and HS 8419). By deploying a proprietary 'Physicality Correlation' benchmark, the analysis separates tangible ecosystem development from mere transactional flows. The data highlights a $17.63 billion 'Volume Variance' between projected and realized trade, indicating a higher degree of regulatory alignment than previously forecasted. Additionally, a price correction of-3.3% points toward a 'Legacy Optimization' strategy, where regional entities are recalibrating supply chains around mature technologies rather than restricted frontier systems. These insights provide a robust calibration tool for measuring the reconfiguration of global computing supply chains.

title: Designing the AI-Native Enterprise: From Customer-Value Claims to Coordination Architecture
affiliations: Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology

detail.title: Designing the AI-Native Enterprise: From Customer-Value Claims to Coordination Architecture
detail.abstract: Managerial discourse increasingly labels firms "AI-native," yet the construct often lacks operational meaning because it is not anchored in organization design. This Point of View reframes a CIO.com argument-AI strategy matters only when it improves customer value or reduces cost-as an organization design problem: how to build a coordination architecture that makes AI-driven value repeatable, auditable, and resilient. The CIO.com "two-path" logic (AI as a customer-facing value engine versus AI as an operations-first efficiency foundation) is directionally useful but incomplete because it under-specifies design choices about task modularity and integration, governance and decision rights, and learning loops that connect measurement to redesign. I propose a designable definition of AI-native as a socio-technical coordination architecture and replace the binary "AI-native vs AI-branded" framing with a four-stage maturity continuum (AI-branded, AI-assisted, AIembedded, AI-orchestrated) characterized by distinct structural, systemic, and process levers. I derive six propositions about when frontstage versus backstage AI creates value, how governance centralization and accountability regimes shape performance, and why risk-adjusted evaluation is essential for sustained advantage. A research agenda and managerial design rules are offered to guide organization design scholarship and practice toward measurable, trustworthy AI-enabled organizing.

title: Children Before Profits in the States: Empowering Communities to Constrain Private Equity Profiteering in Local Child Care Markets
affiliations: Open Markets Institute

detail.title: Children Before Profits in the States: Empowering Communities to Constrain Private Equity Profiteering in Local Child Care Markets

declarations.funderStatement: Support for this project came from the Care for All with Respect and Equity (CARE) Fund

detail.abstract: This report looks at policy strategies that policymakers and advocates can deploy at the state and local level to counter the risks that private equity and other profit-maximizing actors pose to child care markets, and to the broader goal of increasing access to affordable, high-quality care across communities. After reviewing existing concerns about private equity in child care, the report looks at strategies to (1)  strengthen guardrails to protect children and workers from harmful profit-maximizing tactics; (2) protect fair and competitive markets so that private equity cannot use their relative market power to harm other stakeholders; (3) equitably increase child care supply by ensuring that diverse types of providers have the resources they need to thrive in child care markets; and (4) ensure corporate accountability to the public good by empowering and mobilizing the diverse stakeholders in child care markets to push back against private equity efforts to put profits before the wellbeing of children and the long-term financial stability of the sector.

title: Default Rules
affiliations: University of Oxford - Institute of European and Comparative Law

detail.title: Default Rules

contentType.other: Forthcoming in the Oxford Handbook of Regulatory Contract Law (ed. by Atamer/Hellgardt)

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in the Oxford Handbook of Regulatory Contract Law (ed. by Atamer/Hellgardt)

detail.abstract: Default rules are legal norms that govern unless parties contract around them. This chapter discusses them as a tool of regulatory contract law. It delineates defaults from mandatory rules and non-binding guides, and shows how parliaments and courts generate, interpret, and recalibrate them across Civil and Common Law traditions. It widens the lens to non-state sources and international regimes to reveal how defaults influence behaviour and markets beyond statute and case law. On design, it distinguishes majoritarian defaults, which mirror hypothetical bargains; purpose-driven defaults, which pursue public policies while preserving justified opt-outs; and penalty defaults, which induce information revelation. A key lever is stickiness, operationalised by altering rules that determine how parties may deviate from the default arrangements. The chapter also addresses semi-defaults common in consumer protection, where deviation is limited in one direction. Finally, the chapter highlights the pervasiveness of defaults by exploring default regimes in cross-border contracting: choice of law and choice of court oftentimes rely on defaults, and party autonomy can even turn domestically mandatory rules into defaults within the limits of the conflict of laws rules and public policy.

title: Legacy of Colonial Education: Unveiling Persistence Mechanisms in the D.R. Congo
affiliations: , Paris School of Economics (PSE) and University of Namur - Centre de Recherche en Economie du Developpement (CRED)

detail.title: Legacy of Colonial Education: Unveiling Persistence Mechanisms in the D.R. Congo

keywords: déduction de la partie impactée par le Pacte d'Excellence JEL Classification : I25

detail.abstract: The mechanisms that contribute to the enduring effects of colonial investments in education on human capital today are not well understood. This paper addresses this gap by examining the case of colonial Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo. We first document the enduring effects of colonial education and then analyze both demand-side channels and supply-side mechanisms. Using detailed contemporary and historical microdata, our results show that exposure to colonial Catholic and Protestant missionary education led to different demand-side mechanisms (intergenerational transmission and educational mobility triggered by missions). However, the quantitative importance of these channels seems limited in this context. On the supply side, we examine the dynamics of school location after independence. Our results suggest that the persistence of educational outcomes is primarily due to the concentration of contemporary schools around historical missions. This agglomeration effect appears to be driven by competition among religious schools of different denominations (and possibly by structural change in the vicinity of Catholic missions). As a result, girls living farther from historical missions have to travel greater distances to reach schools, which affects their enrollment more than that of boys.

title: The Unacceptable Risks of Uninsured Nonbank Stablecoins: Written Testimony Presented to the UK House of Lords' Financial Services Regulation Committee

detail.abstract:
This written testimony was submitted to the Financial Services Regulation Committee of the United Kingdom House of Lords, in response to that Committee’s “Call for evidence” on the “Growth and proposed regulation of stablecoins in the UK,” https://committees.parliament.uk/call-for-evidence/3845/. This testimony provides an overview of the global stablecoin market and the current leading uses of stablecoins. The testimony also describes the unacceptable dangers that uninsured nonbank stablecoins pose to financial stability, economic welfare, consumer protection, monetary policy, regulatory compliance, and law enforcement. The testimony presents the following policy recommendations:

(1) Stablecoins should be regulated in the same way as bank deposits. Only regulated banks should be allowed to issue or distribute stablecoins. Stablecoins should be required to satisfy the same prudential standards and provide the same consumer safeguards – including deposit insurance – as bank deposits.

2) Stablecoins should be issued and recorded exclusively on permissioned distributed ledgers that are controlled and administered by one or more designated banks. The designated banks should have full responsibility and accountability for ensuring that their stablecoins and their distributed ledgers fulfill all legal and contractual obligations.

3) To ensure compliance with AML/BSA/KYC requirements, stablecoin holders should be prohibited from holding their stablecoins in “unhosted” private digital wallets.

(4) Stablecoin reserves should be invested solely in central bank reserves or in government securities with a weighted average maturity of 20 days or less.

(5) If – contrary to the foregoing recommendations – nonbanks are allowed to issue stablecoins, those issuers, crypto exchanges, other crypto trading platforms, and their affiliates and business partners should be prohibited from paying interest, rewards, or any other financial inducements to stablecoin holders for owning stablecoins or keeping their stablecoins at designated locations.

The author also presented oral testimony (via Zoom) to the Committee, available at https://committees.parliament.uk/event/26299/formal-meeting-oral-evidence-session/.

title: Distance Matters: Geographical Proximity and Fiscal Rules Enforcement

detail.title: Distance Matters: Geographical Proximity and Fiscal Rules Enforcement

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW - Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-008

detail.abstract: A reform in the German state of Hesse selectively shifted the responsibility for overseeing and enforcing a balanced budget rule at the municipal level. Oversight was transferred from politically affiliated county administrators to non-political and potentially more impartial fiscal supervisors at a higher administrative layer. We use this institutional change to empirically examine whether enforcement under the former regime was affected by hidden bias related to geographic proximity. We find that municipalities located closer to the former political supervisors reduced their cash loans more strongly under the subsequent neutral regime, consistent with the existence of proximity-related favoritism prior to the reform. This spatial pattern is most evident for smaller municipalities, when supervisors oversee more municipalities, and when mayors and supervisors are not politically aligned.

title: Ownership Friction Index (OFI): Irreversibility and Constraint Asymmetry in Asset Ownership
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Ownership Friction Index (OFI): Irreversibility and Constraint Asymmetry in Asset Ownership

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical and conceptual in nature and does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Assets are commonly evaluated through frameworks that emphasize risk, liquidity, and price dynamics. These approaches implicitly assume that ownership is a reversible financial position whose costs and benefits can be modeled probabilistically. This paper challenges that assumption by introducing the Ownership Friction Index (OFI) as an indexical analytical framework for examining ownership positions as structural conditions rather than market exposures. OFI does not measure liquidity, transaction costs, volatility, or risk. Instead, it examines the degree to which ownership positions impose non-neutrally reversible legal, regulatory, and reputational constraints that accumulate asymmetrically over time and narrow exit optionality independently of asset-level liquidity or price movement. By reframing ownership as a structurally binding condition, OFI explains why owners may become constrained even when markets appear favorable and why exit impairment may occur without price collapse.

title: The Correlation Between Heavy Water usage in Tech and its Effect on Gold

In this paper I will discuss the correlation between the water usage in the US and the spot price day average of gold.

title: The Missing Market For Creative Utility: Missing Markets, Attribution Failure, and the Depletion of the Cultural Utility Stock

detail.title: The Missing Market For Creative Utility: Missing Markets, Attribution Failure, and the Depletion of the Cultural Utility Stock

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of PNAQL, the infrastructure solution proposed in Section VIII of this paper. This relationship is disclosed in the interest of transparency.
declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded. Independent research.

detail.abstract: Creative economies keep producing output. Music is released daily, films are made, buildings go up, and economists point to this as evidence that markets are functioning. This paper argues the inference is wrong. The productive infrastructure of creative economies is depleting under the logic of current architectures, the price signal driving that depletion is structural rather than correctable, and the market that would repair it has never been built. The aggregate scale of what goes unpriced, creative utility generating trillions annually in tourism, property capitalisation, and adjacent economic activity, constitutes a missing market of civilisational scale.Attribution failure is the mechanism of market formation failure. Creative utility depends causally on post-transaction propagation, compounding, and downstream displacement, properties settlement-finality payment architecture cannot incorporate at the time of pricing. Lemmas L1a (Settlement Finality) and L1b (Architectural Stability) establish the formal result: contingent pricing of creative utility is foreclosed by the architecture, and the incumbent system is stable against any unilateral attempt to build an alternative within it. The market cannot assemble spontaneously from within the system it would replace.Three-channel adverse selection is the mechanism of depletion. The paper’s core finding is that wrong price signals consume the reproductive infrastructure of the stock itself; the depletion runs deeper than output mispricing. High-utility creators exit under the worst signal; those who remain substitute toward measurable low-utility production; the entering generation develops its capabilities under that substituted signal and never acquires the craft a corrected market would want. Propositions 1–3 establish each channel formally; Proposition 0 establishes the endpoint. The empirical cases, the music streaming transition and four decades of franchise concentration in film, carry identification strategies and testable predictions. The architecture required to correct the failure prices creative utility across time and downstream markets, routes returns to originators, and intervenes at the point of capability formation rather than only at the point of production choice.

title: Corporations as the State: Urbanisation, Women's Empowerment, and Long-Run Development in the Copperbelt

detail.title: Corporations as the State: Urbanisation, Women's Empowerment, and Long-Run Development in the Copperbelt
detail.abstract: Do corporate labour strategies leave persistent legacies long after the firm disappears? I examine two concessions in the Central African Copperbelt: the Union Minière du Haut-Katanga (UMHK) and the Rhokana Corporation (RC). While both firms extracted resources under comparable profit constraints, the UMHK minimized labour turnover by adopting 'Labour Stabilisation Programmes' that incentivised permanent family settlement. In contrast, the RC maintained a transient, circular workforce. Using a spatial difference-in-discontinuities design, I show that UMHK's policy generated urban agglomeration and persistent development gains: individuals inside the former concession exhibit two additional years of education, 30 percentage points higher literacy, and are one standard deviation wealthier. The RC border displays no discontinuity. By monetising the family unit and formally integrating women into the labour contract, the UMHK left a distinct gendered legacy: women inside the former concession today report greater reproductive autonomy, reduced tolerance for domestic violence, and increased authority over household finances. These findings illustrate how corporate labour institutions determine long-run development trajectories.

title: A Scalar Metric of the Real Quantity of Capital and the Cambridge Capital Controversy

detail.title: A Scalar Metric of the Real Quantity of Capital and the Cambridge Capital Controversy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: In the course of the long capital theory dispute known colloquially as the Cambridge capital controversy, the central claim advanced by post-Keynesian critics of the neoclassical theory of production and distribution was that there does not exist a mathematically consistent and usable scalar metric of the real quantity of capital composed of heterogeneous commodities. Their claim was that heterogeneous commodities can only be aggregated on the basis of their values and that this leads to insoluble problems for the neoclassical theory, including circular dependence of the profit rate and capital price/value, reswitching and capital reversing, and lack of convergence to, and uniqueness of, distribution equilibria. I employ a novel parameterization of a two-good model of production-consumption good and capital good-to compose the well-understood scalar value of capital in consumption good as the product of a necessary price of capital, determined independently of value and quantity, and a real scalar quantity-the "integrated labor time of production of the capital," the labor time required for its production with reproduction of capital inputs. If the post-Keynesians were incorrect about their central claim, that would, at the very least, require reconsideration of their critique to place it on a firmer theoretical footing.

title: Chronic Uncertainty and Momentary Opportunity: A Half Decade of Adaptation among Zambia's Gwembe Tonga
affiliations: University of Kentucky, , California State University,  and

detail.title: Chronic Uncertainty and Momentary Opportunity: A Half Decade of Adaptation among Zambia's Gwembe Tonga
detail.abstract: In Zambia's Southern Province, where a history of climatic and political fluctuation have played out in peoples livelihood choices and ecological impacts, the Gwembe Tonga people have learned to respond to uncertainty by expecting the worst. This outlook emerges from at least 50 years of experience. The building of the Kariba Dam on the Middle Zambezi River in the late 1950s resulted in the forced relocation of Gwembe people. Since resettlement in 1958, Gwembe people have lived under conditions of increasing uncertainty, both environmental and socio-political, that have enormous implications for environmental change. Understanding the environmental change in this region demands an exploration of the social, political and economic context of Gwembe Tonga lives. In looking for broad patterns of adaptation and response, one point emerges clearly. For the Gwembe Tonga, the most recurrent pattern, and most reliable response to living in conditions of extreme uncertainty, is an increasingly opportunistic use of the environment and other resources. This article presents ethnographic data collected over more than 50 years (through the Gwembe Tonga Research Project) in Southern Zambia.

title: Search and Knightian Uncertainty Revisited: Roles of Optimism and Pessimism
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University - Graduate School of Economics, National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies (GRIPS) and Tokyo Center for Economic Research (TCER)

detail.title: Search and Knightian Uncertainty Revisited: Roles of Optimism and Pessimism
detail.abstract: Optimal stopping under ambiguity is central to dynamic decision-making, yet standard models impose uniformly ambiguity-averse preferences that conflict with experimental evidence showing heterogeneous and context-dependent ambiguity attitudes. This paper develops a job search model without recall in which the magnitude of ambiguity is separated from attitudes toward it. Using Choquet expected utility with JP-capacities, we show that the classical prediction that greater ambiguity shortens search holds only when the agent is sufficiently pessimistic; when optimism is high, ambiguity instead lengthens search. Focusing on neo-additive capacities, we further identify how the economic environment shapes this reversal. A key insight is that the discount factor plays a decisive role: even slight contamination of optimism induces ambiguity-seeking stopping behavior when the agent is sufficiently patient. This reveals that patience can fundamentally alter the effect of ambiguity in optimal stopping.

title: On the Devolution of Copyright Scholarship: Part I-Tracing the Digital Copyright Revolution
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law

detail.title: On the Devolution of Copyright Scholarship: Part I-Tracing the Digital Copyright Revolution

publicationDetails.detailsText: UC Berkeley Public Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of California, Berkeley School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
As the digital revolution unfolded in the 1990s and early 2000s, a charismatic hacktivist faction took hold in the copyright legal academy. In its purest form, the copyleft movement celebrated the notion that "information wants to be free" and opposed copyright protection in cyberspace. Some copyleft scholars served as lead counsel in efforts to overturn copyright legislation and immunize filesharing enterprises from copyright liability, blurring the line between interpretive scholarship and policy analysis. Many academic amicus briefs took on the tactics of zealous advocates, selectively and misleadingly presenting empirical, statutory, and doctrinal analysis. 

This Article chronicles the evolution of copyright law while tracing the devolution of copyright scholarship through this tumultuous era. It highlights the origins of the copyleft movement and ways in which many scholars lost sight of essential academic values-independence, objectivity, transparency, scrupulousness, methodological soundness, and analytical rigor-in an effort to persuade courts to remake copyright law through less than forthright and non-democratic means. In the process, they eroded the trust that courts had placed in the legal academy. As the Article shows, the courts have largely remained faithful to the rule of law in copyright cases and this has for the most part promoted cultural, social, and economic progress. 

A follow-on article examines the chasm between judicial interpretation of copyright law and the views of many in the copyright academy through an empirical examination of Supreme Court academic briefs and anthropological analysis of the copyright legal academy. It then assesses the ramifications of the devolution of copyright scholarship for the judiciary, democratic institutions, the scholarly community, and society at large.

title: Digital Transformation and AI in Legal Education
affiliations: The British Institute of International and Comparative Law (BIICL)

detail.title: Digital Transformation and AI in Legal Education
detail.abstract:
● The report outlines key themes from BIICL’s first Legal Training and Technology Workshop, which brought together academics, knowledge lawyers, education specialists, and AI experts. Discussions revealed a profession undergoing rapid transformation as technology — particularly AI — reshapes how lawyers learn and practise. Participants identified the COVID-19 pandemic as a decisive turning point that accelerated digitalisation and forced firms to rethink traditional training models.

● Emergency remote delivery evolved into long-term innovation, including global online programmes, asynchronous learning, and integrated digital workflows. While virtual delivery sometimes improved consistency across offices, hybrid formats often created uneven experiences. The shift also exposed challenges such as reduced engagement and fatigue, underscoring the need for interactive, human-centred, practice-relevant learning design. Digital literacy and virtual practice skills are now core components of professional development.

● A central theme was the expanding role of knowledge lawyers. No longer confined to research support, they now act as strategic intermediaries between legal practice and technology. Their responsibilities include developing AI workflows, curating datasets, designing prompts, delivering training, and contributing to governance. As AI adoption accelerates, knowledge lawyers play a critical role in promoting responsible use and embedding tools consistently with professional standards.

● Participants stressed that effective training must be active and outcome-based. Hands-on exercises, realistic scenarios, and opportunities to test AI tools directly were seen as essential to building confidence and competence. Passive formats were widely regarded as insufficient, particularly in virtual environments.

● Across discussions, there was broad agreement that AI should be treated as an assistant, not a replacement. While AI can summarise and generate drafts, it cannot exercise contextual legal judgment. Case studies demonstrated the risks of persuasive but inaccurate outputs, reinforcing the need for human oversight. Participants also raised concerns about the potential erosion of junior-level training tasks traditionally used to develop foundational skills.

● Safe and effective AI use requires structured training, workflow design, and governance. Lawyers must learn not only how to prompt AI systems but also how to verify outputs, assess limitations, and comply with confidentiality obligations and emerging regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act. Firms increasingly recognise the importance of practice-specific, governed approaches rather than generic tool adoption.

● Finally, the workshop highlighted the importance of collaboration within firms and across the profession. Effective adoption depends on coordination among knowledge teams, IT, innovation groups, and fee-earners, as well as broader dialogue with educators and technologists. Despite competitive pressures, participants emphasised the public interest in responsible AI use and the value of shared learning.

● Together, these discussions reflect a profession at an inflection point, requiring new skills, pedagogical models, governance structures, and sustained collaboration to navigate the digital age effectively. The report concludes by formulating 10 Key Takeaways for the Training of Lawyers, providing practical guidance for firms, educators, and policymakers seeking to design responsible, engaging, and future-oriented training programmes.

title: Employee Online Reviews and Corporate Wage Theft
affiliations: , University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and University of Oklahoma

detail.title: Employee Online Reviews and Corporate Wage Theft
detail.abstract: Wage theft occurs when an employer withholds benefits, such as wages and breaks, to which an employee is legally entitled. This practice is the largest theft crime in the U.S. and remains pervasive despite public and private enforcement efforts. We examine whether workplace transparency created by employee social media disclosures can curb corporate wage theft. Specifically, we test whether employee reports of wage theft on Glassdoor, a major employee review platform, lead firms to reduce future wage theft. Using a sample of over 3.2 million employee reviews from 2008 to 2021, we find that employee disclosures of wage theft concerns are followed by a significant decline in subsequent wage theft at the firm level. This evidence is consistent with managers taking corrective action when wage theft is exposed through anonymous employee reviews. Further analyses show that the disciplining role of employees’ wage theft disclosures is stronger when managers face weaker personal liability for wage theft, indicating that employee disclosures can substitute for formal managerial disincentives. We also show that the relationship between employees’ wage theft disclosures and future wage theft varies systematically with the type of wage theft and with employee characteristics. Overall, our evidence highlights employee online disclosures as an important monitoring mechanism for deterring wage theft. Nonetheless, we caution that managerial opportunism may shift rather than be completely eliminated, as we find that higher rates of employee wage theft disclosure are associated with more financial misreporting.

title: European Funds and Public Investment in Romania: Implications of the wind-up of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) for Economic Growth
affiliations: National Bank of Romania, Romanian Academy - Romanian Academy, National Bank of Romania and

detail.title: European Funds and Public Investment in Romania: Implications of the wind-up of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) for Economic Growth

publicationDetails.detailsText: National Bank of Romania Occasional papers no. 41/2025

detail.abstract: Non-repayable European funds, particularly those associated with the European Union’s Cohesion Policy, have played a key role in fostering the economic and social development of EU Member States over time. Furthermore, the Next Generation EU programme, built around the implementation of National Recovery and Resilience Plans (NRRPs), has provided significant support to economic activity in the aftermath of the public health crisis and the subsequent adverse shocks. This study assesses the macroeconomic impact of European funds related to the EU Cohesion Policy using a panel data model that incorporates data for Romania and ten other Central and Eastern European (CEE) economies. Empirical evidence indicates a contemporaneous impact of around 0.5 percentage points on economic growth following a 1 percentage point increase in European funds as a share of GDP, with spillover effects accumulating over time. For Romania, the analysis is extended by quantifying the impact of the NRRP. Using the synthetic control method, we estimate a cumulative contribution exceeding 1 percentage point to GDP growth over the 2022–2024 period. The study also discusses implications of the wind‑up of the NRRP as a potential investment shock, through the reduction of public investment, as well as the role of alternative compensatory investment programmes, such as the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) programme. The main conclusion is that the impact of European funds depends critically on institutional quality and the pace of project implementation: timely absorption and a front-loaded execution maximize macroeconomic effects, whereas delays generate significant economic costs and constrain Romania’s growth potential.

title: When Markets Never Sleep:  Intraday Liquidity Patterns and Volatility Effects in Cryptocurrency Trading
affiliations: Wroclaw University of Economics and Business and Poznań University of Economics and Business

detail.title: When Markets Never Sleep:  Intraday Liquidity Patterns and Volatility Effects in Cryptocurrency Trading
detail.abstract: This paper examines the microstructure of cryptocurrency markets by analysing liquidity and volatility patterns. Using high-frequency 15-minute data from Binance and Coinbase, we study Bitcoin and Ethereum trading pairs with both fiat currencies and stablecoins. We employ a depth-adjusted spread measure standardised for trade size to identify and statistically validate daily and intraday periodicities in spreads and volatility across trading venues and quote currencies. Our findings reveal that volatility is the primary driver of spread variation, though periodic factors provide additional explanatory power in an integrated model. The identified periodicities enhance out-of-sample spread forecasting performance across several markets, with consistent differences observed between venues and quote currencies.

title: Transforming Water Resource Governance in South Africa Using an ‘untransformed’ Law: The Courts and the National Water Act of 1998

detail.title: Transforming Water Resource Governance in South Africa Using an ‘untransformed’ Law: The Courts and the National Water Act of 1998

declarations.funderStatement: The full study for this paper was partially supported through the University of the Witwatersrand, School of Law Writing Retreats series.

detail.abstract: The South African National Water Act 32 of 1998, praised as a pioneering law setting a global standard for water resource governance, introduced modern concepts for integrated water resources management, efficient water use, and sustainable development. It made water a public resource under state trusteeship, a departure from the colonial and apartheid approach that favoured private rights in a public resource. However, an analysis of recent South African jurisprudence reveals that these theoretical qualities often mask a compromised legal reform process that perpetuates historical inequitable rights. This article argues for targeted policy and legal reforms to the water legislation, the National Water Act 1998, to enable substantive transformation and reallocation, without compromising efficient, beneficial, and sustainable water use.

title: Trading Green: Do Tax Credit Markets Improve Land Conservation?
affiliations: University of Wisconsin at Madison, University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Trading Green: Do Tax Credit Markets Improve Land Conservation?
detail.abstract:
Governments traditionally use top-down regulations to mandate conservation on private land but voluntary, incentive-based Payments for Environmental Services (PES) are an emerging alternative. Critics worry that PES programs subsidize wealthy landowners who would have conserved absent compensation and fail to target lands with high conservation value. 

We ask how conservation incentives can be made more effective in the context of the United States' dominant PES system - conservation easements, covering 38 million acres and funded primarily by tax breaks. We hypothesize that markets for transferable tax credits will expand participation among low-income landowners while also improving conservation outcomes. Using a calculator of federal and state tax codes from 1990-2025 and policy changes in five states allowing transferability, we find that before markets, high-income donors faced a much lower after-tax cost of conservation than low and medium-income donors. Markets shrunk this gap and the donation responses across income levels leading to a greater proportion of easements over farmland under conversion pressure relative to non-working lands hosting second-homes. Markets also increased measures of ecological value and agricultural soil quality across easements. These results demonstrate how decentralized trade in tax credits can improve conservation targeting without subsidy expansion or new ecological mandates.

title: Price Efficiency in Emerging Equity Markets During Recent Crises Periods: Empirical Evidence From Equity Markets in BRICS Countries
affiliations: University of Aberdeen, University of Aberdeen and Independent

detail.title: Price Efficiency in Emerging Equity Markets During Recent Crises Periods: Empirical Evidence From Equity Markets in BRICS Countries
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of increased systematic risk on the efficiency of equity markets in emerging countries, focusing on the BRICS market (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa). We measure market efficiency by analyzing the spot and futures prices of indices in these markets using the futures-spot arbitrage test over recent crisis periods. Our findings suggest that mispricing existed among the major indices of the BRICS market before the crises, but that the crises exacerbated the extent of mispricing. We also find that there are noteworthy variations amongst the BRICS markets in terms of how market efficiency changed during the downturns, highlighting the need for heterogeneous investment strategies for each individual market.

title: The Slope of the Wage Phillips Curve With Heterogeneous Search Efforts

detail.title: The Slope of the Wage Phillips Curve With Heterogeneous Search Efforts
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the slope of the wage Phillips curve through the lens of a search model. The model incorporates heterogeneous search efforts for on-the-job search and the unemployed search. This enables the model to analytically derive a wage equation that yields the wage Phillips curve with Calvo-style wage rigidity. I demonstrate that common estimation approaches, such as the instrumental variable (IV) method, are substantially biased downward due to the cyclicality of four omitted variables: the vacancy rate, the extensive margin of onthe-job search, and the intensive margins of on-the-job search and unemployed search. Based on literature calibrations, I numerically compute theoretical values of the slope and provide evidence for quantifying the downward bias. A hybrid approach combining the structural model and empirical estimation can capture the slope more precisely.

title: Social Concerns Impede Price Competition Among Small Firms: Experimental Evidence from Tanzania

detail.title: Social Concerns Impede Price Competition Among Small Firms: Experimental Evidence from Tanzania

publicationDetails.detailsText: Private Enterprise Development in Low-Income Countries Working Paper, Growth Research Platform

detail.abstract: I run a field experiment with 561 food retailers in urban Tanzania to answer three questions. First, do concerns about social sanctions reduce entrepreneurs’ willingness to undercut the prices of competitors? Second, how variable is the compensation required for firms to engage in such price competition? Third, when experimentally incentivized to undercut their competitor’s prices, do entrepreneurs update their beliefs about the social costs of competition? Treated firms are financially incentivized to sell maize flour at prices that undercut nearby competitors and must publicly post their selling price. My analysis leads to three main findings. First, firms are hesitant to undercut their competitors even when doing so is guaranteed to raise profits. At baseline, only 33% of retailers are willing to undercut others; unwilling retailers substantially overestimate the anger that others have towards undercutting. Second, firm beliefs about the severity of social sanctions vary widely. Among those that are willing to undercut, the required compensation varies from a 25 − 520% increase in their maize flour profit margin. Third, firms seem to learn via the experiment that social sanctions are less severe than they initially believed. After the first round, 33% more firms are willing to undercut others in a second round of treatment, and the subsidies they require are 30 − 39% smaller on average. These findings suggest that social concerns impede price competition among small firms, but that those concerns can be partially overcome with temporary experimentation.

title: Business Failure Prediction Model using Accounting Anomaly and Corporate Governance Indicators: A Qualitative Approach
affiliations: Islamic Azad University

detail.title: Business Failure Prediction Model using Accounting Anomaly and Corporate Governance Indicators: A Qualitative Approach

detail.abstract: This paper presents a qualitative investigation into developing a comprehensive business failure prediction model by integrating accounting anomaly and corporate governance indicators. While traditional prediction models predominantly rely on historical financial ratios, they often overlook early warning signals embedded in accounting irregularities and governance structures. This study addresses this gap by employing a grounded theory approach to explore the perspectives of experts. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 experts in the fields of accounting and corporate governance. Through open, axial, and selective coding of the interview data, a conceptual model was developed. The findings reveal that key corporate governance components for predicting business failure include auditor-specific characteristics, the audit process, audit results, duality of duties, ownership concentration, board independence, board size, and institutional ownership. Furthermore, crucial accounting anomaly components encompass the number of shares, profitability, asset growth, earnings management, firm size, book-to-market ratio, investments, financing, and market efficiency. This qualitative phase provides a foundational framework for understanding how these multifaceted factors interact to signal potential business failure, offering a more holistic perspective for researchers, practitioners, and regulators.

title: The Unobserved Source of Latent Worker Types

detail.title: The Unobserved Source of Latent Worker Types
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the unobserved source underlying three latent worker types, clustered using K-means. The Stable type accounts for 55% of the labor force, with 85% of employment spells longer than 2 years, a 99% participation rate, a 0.02% unemployment rate, and a 37% job-switch rate. The Turnover type accounts for 18% of the labor force, with more than 95% employment and nonparticipation spells shorter than 2 years, a 23% unemployment rate, and a 74% job-switch rate. The OLF (out-of-labor-force) type accounts for 27% of the labor force, with more than 60% of nonparticipation spells lasting more than 2 years, a 9% participation rate, and a 10% job-switch rate. Demographic observables can't explain these latent types. Instead, the divergent life-cycle wage profiles imply that the worker types are more closely associated with unobserved worker heterogeneity. To explain the empirical findings, I develop a directed search model with on-the-job search and human capital accumulation. The model assumes no ex-ante worker heterogeneity and generates worker types endogenously through human capital accumulation. The calibrated model successfully replicates key characteristics of worker types and their divergent life-cycle wage profiles. These findings establish human capital accumulation as a primary source of worker types and demonstrate that ex-ante heterogeneity is not necessary to account for observed labor market stratification, which is essential for interacting policies and unobserved worker heterogeneity.

title: Trading with Uncertainty about Signals and Price Impact
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics and Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Trading with Uncertainty about Signals and Price Impact
detail.abstract: We study optimal trading with uncertainty about both trading signals and price impact. Rather than treating all models within a prespecified class as equally plausible, we penalize less likely ones according to their distance from a reference model. In the limit of small uncertainty aversion, this yields closed-form expressions for the optimal robust trading strategy. In a simulation study with noisy parameter estimates, we find that optimal regularization via uncertainty aversion markedly improves performance compared to plug-in strategies based on point estimates only. For weak signals, impact uncertainty only plays a secondary role but rapidly becomes dominant as signal strength increases.

title: By Design
affiliations: University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law

detail.title: By Design
detail.abstract:
In recent years, scholars and policymakers have increasingly embraced regulation “by design” to address new problems, especially those caused by new technologies. These approaches go by various names, like privacy by design, security by design, even the rule of law by design. Despite the popularity of these approaches, though, describing what goes into regulation “by design” is surprisingly challenging. Different speakers use the term in strikingly different ways, with little consensus about why design is important, how design and new technologies interact, or how design can be harnessed to deliver policy results.

Design exists along multiple dimensions: process versus result, plan versus creation, form versus function. While the literature on regulation and design has recognized and grappled (sometimes implicitly) with the first two dimensions, the third has been unappreciated. Yet this is where the most critical regulatory problems arise. Design can refer both to how something looks and is experienced by a user—its form—or how it works and what it does under the surface—its function. In the physical world, though, these two conceptions of design are connected, since an object’s form is inherently limited by its function. That’s why a padlock is hard and chunky and made of metal: Without that form, it could not accomplish its function of keeping things secure. So, people have come, over the centuries, to associate form and function and to infer function from form.

Software, however, decouples these two conceptions of design, since a computer can show one thing to a user while doing something else entirely. Some of the most pervasive regulatory problems, like online tracking and profiling, stem from this misalignment between form and function, because companies can collect, use, and disseminate information without any formal indication that that will occur. Recognizing this third dimension of design, then, can help policymakers identify these problems and fashion reforms directed at inducing realignment.

title: Overreaction as an Indicator for Momentum in Algorithmic Trading: A Case of AAPL Stocks
affiliations: University of Warsaw, University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences and University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences

detail.title: Overreaction as an Indicator for Momentum in Algorithmic Trading: A Case of AAPL Stocks
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether short-term market overreactions can be systematically predicted and monetized as momentum signals using high-frequency emotional information and modern machine learning methods. Focusing on Apple Inc. (AAPL), we construct a comprehensive intraday dataset that combines volatilitynormalized returns with transformer-based emotion features extracted from Twitter messages. Overreactions are defined as extreme return realizations relative to contemporaneous volatility and transaction costs and are modeled as a three-class prediction problem. We evaluate the performance of several nonlinear classifiers-including XGBoost, Random Forests, Deep Neural Networks, and Bidirectional LSTMs-across multiple intraday frequencies (1-, 5-, 10-, and 15-minute data). Model outputs are translated into trading strategies and assessed using risk-adjusted performance measures and formal statistical tests. The results show that machine learning models significantly outperform benchmark overreaction rules at ultra-short horizons, while classical behavioral momentum effects dominate at intermediate frequencies, particularly around 10 minutes. Explainability analysis based on SHAP reveals that volatility and negative emotions-especially fear and sadness-play a central role in driving predicted overreactions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that emotion-driven overreactions contain a predictable structure that can be exploited by machine learning models, offering new insights into the behavioral origins of intraday momentum and the interaction between sentiment, volatility, and algorithmic trading.

title: The Kainji Corridor as an Emerging Geopolitical Threat: Options for Nigeria and its Neighbours
affiliations: Baze University

detail.title: The Kainji Corridor as an Emerging Geopolitical Threat: Options for Nigeria and its Neighbours
detail.abstract: This study examined the evolving trajectory of insecurity along the Kainji corridor and analysed how recurring patterns of violence transformed the axis into an emerging transnational security interface linking Nigeria, the Sahel, and coastal West Africa. Using trend analysis, qualitative content analysis, and pattern-recognition techniques applied to open-source conflict reporting and policy documents between the COVID-19 period and January 2026, the research investigated the convergence of bandit economies, militant diffusion, and mobility-driven threats within forest borderlands. Findings showed that the hydrological and ecological characteristics of the Kainji Lake-forest complex, combined with governance gaps and porous borders, enabled hybrid armed actors to exploit sanctuary terrain and expand operations across administrative and national boundaries. The study further found that government responses-including Operation Savannah Shield, forest governance reforms, and the deployment of over 7,000 forest guards-reflected a shift toward corridor-denial strategies but remained constrained by mobility asymmetry, humanitarian pressures, and institutional coordination challenges. Empirical evidence demonstrated that rising displacement, agricultural disruption, and coordinated attacks signalled a structural transformation of localised violence into a corridor-based threat ecology with regional geopolitical implications. The research concluded that sustainable stabilisation required integrated intelligence fusion, persistent territorial presence, community-based early warning, and synchronised cross-border cooperation rather than episodic military offensives. These findings contributed to early-warning discourse by reframing the Kainji axis as a strategic geopolitical barometer within West Africa's evolving security architecture.

title: Accounting for Structural Breaks in the Hamilton Filter
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Duluth - Department of Economics and Health Care Management and University of Missouri at Saint Louis - Department of Economics

detail.title: Accounting for Structural Breaks in the Hamilton Filter
detail.abstract: This paper reveals that the regression-based trend-cycle decomposition of Hamilton (2018) introduces spurious cyclical dynamics when time series undergo structural breaks. Because the filter relies on an h-step ahead projection, trend adjustment mechanically lags behind regime shifts, inducing bias in the cyclical component. We propose a parsimonious modification using a dummy-variable structure that allows the regression intercept and autoregressive components to adjust to identified breaks. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations show that this approach substantially reduces Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) across a wide class of data-generating processes. These gains are robust to variations in sample size, break timing, location and number, and signal-to-noise ratios, even when break dates are endogenously estimated. An empirical application to the Swiss franc/euro exchange rate demonstrates that our modification avoids the spurious cyclical spikes generated by standard filters during major policy shifts, ensuring a more reliable decomposition for macroeconomic inference.

title: Private Asset Distress and Public Market Volatility
affiliations: pvot.io

detail.title: Private Asset Distress and Public Market Volatility
detail.abstract: Public equity prices are volatile and negatively skewed, and large moves often occur without obvious news about public-firm fundamentals. This paper identifies a 'dark matter' source of this volatility: the vast, leveraged, and illiquid privately held sector that dwarfs public markets roughly ten to one. We develop a two-sector Tobin's q model in which the publicly traded sector has no exogenous technology shocks; all uncertainty originates in a leveraged privately held sector. Private-sector shocks propagate to public equity through (i) general equilibrium effects on aggregate consumption and (ii) a leverage--distress: fixed debt service amplifies cash-flow fluctuations, and a leverage-dependent distress-cost wedge generates nonlinear efficiency losses that reduce aggregate absorption. Because distress costs rise convexly in cash-flow shortfalls, symmetric private shocks generate asymmetric public equity responses and negative return skewness. The amplification is stronger when private assets are large relative to public markets, leverage is high, investment adjustment costs are larger, and risk aversion is higher.

title: Boards as Contracting Intermediaries: Evidence from Board-Interlocking Firms in the Credit Market
affiliations: Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business

detail.title: Boards as Contracting Intermediaries: Evidence from Board-Interlocking Firms in the Credit Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines the contracting intermediary role of corporate boards through the lens of board interlocking. While the traditional literature emphasizes directors' monitoring and advisory functions, their potential to facilitate financing remains underexplored. Using a novel setting, we study cases in which directors link their firms to lenders that already maintain relationships with other firms on whose boards they serve, and find that such connections significantly increase the likelihood of new lending relationships. A counterfactual exercise suggests that aggregate lending to unconnected firm-bank pairs would have been 47.9% higher during the 2007-2008 crisis if they had been connected. Instrumental-variable and quasi-natural-experiment analyses support a causal interpretation. The benefits are most pronounced for informationally opaque firms and during periods of credit market disruption, extending to loan pricing and real outcomes such as employment and investment. Overall, our findings highlight the contracting intermediary role of interlocking directors-effectively acting as informal guarantors or information providers-extending beyond the conventional roles of the board.

title: Nationhood Beyond Borders: Ethical Responsibilities of the Youth in a Connected World
affiliations: University of Delhi

detail.title: Nationhood Beyond Borders: Ethical Responsibilities of the Youth in a Connected World
detail.abstract: In an era of unprecedented global interconnectivity, the concept of nationhood extends beyond traditional territorial borders. Youth today face ethical responsibilities not only towards their own nations but also towards the global community. This paper explores the philosophical underpinnings of ethical responsibility, the role of youth leadership in societal and international contexts, and practical avenues through which young individuals can contribute to nation-building and global welfare. Drawing on historical movements, modern civic initiatives, and philosophical discourse, the study argues that the youth must embrace ethical leadership as both a national and global imperative.

title: The Misinformation Brand
affiliations: DePaul University - College of Law

detail.title: The Misinformation Brand
detail.abstract:
This article examines misinformation in the modern “attention economy” as a marketing problem. What happens if we see the battle between mindsets that favor conspiracy theories and those that promote institutional trust as analogous to competition between PEPSI and COKE? That is, as a battle between competing brands?

Far from trivializing the misinformation problem, this perspective captures a fundamental truth. We often experience information mindsets (and the information choices they drive) as consumption goods to be used or discarded based on the demands of the moment. A person who “trusts the science” and gets a flu shot may still “do their own research” and decide that global warming is a hoax. And unless those choices cause harm to the consumer (and the consumer understands the harm as caused by the choices), these individual decisions—however important in the aggregate—are no more personally consequential than picking a soda.

So how does this brand competition unfold? I apply a model developed by marketing researchers to analyze competition between largely undifferentiated goods. This approach recognizes that people don’t spend their free time thinking about brands; in other words, persuasion is overrated as a means to marketing success. Instead, purchase decisions are driven by whether a brand comes to mind (is mentally available) at a moment of salience (when a purchase is possible) in which the branded good is an option for purchase (is physically available).

Applying this framework to the misinformation problem, we might think of phrases like “trust the science” and “do your own research” as slogans for competing information mindsets. Their success depends on how well they have previously been “marketed” so that the right conditions will cause the consumer to recall them. That result, I posit, sets the stage for follow-up information consumption choices. However cynical this view may seem, it clarifies some of the challenges facing efforts to promote institutional trust and combat the spread of misinformation.

title: A Century in the Making: Port Infrastucture in China

detail.title: A Century in the Making: Port Infrastucture in China
detail.abstract: In his 1921 book "The International Development of China," the "Father of Modern China" Sun Yat-sen planned for Guangzhou to be the "Great Southern Port" along with a "Great Eastern Port" near Hangzhou Bay and a "Great Northern Port" in the Bohai Sea. His objectives for the construction of three world-class ports was to unleash China's economic potential as a major trader and exporter of manufactured goods. While his actual blueprints for the three ports were largely not adhered to by the PRC, China has indeed transformed itself into the leading trader of goods in the world, as well as the location of most of the world's busiest ports. This is in spite of the fact that many of China's top ports like Shanghai and Guangzhou do not have natural deepwater harbors, which is an issue that Sun also highlighted in his book. Thus, this article overviews how the PRC has overcome these natural obstacles to fulfill Sun's vision while staying true to his ambitions for China to possess multiple world-class seaports.

title: From Risk to Buffer: Calibrating the Positive Neutral CCyB Rate
affiliations: Banco de España, European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: From Risk to Buffer: Calibrating the Positive Neutral CCyB Rate

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2544
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Risk-to-Buffer approach for calibrating the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB), with a particular emphasis on the positive neutral (PN) CCyB rate, tailored to the euro area. The proposed methodology is applied in both a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) framework and a macroeconomic time series setting. It estimates the amplification of adverse shocks under varying levels of cyclical systemic risk and calibrates the CCyB to counteract these amplification effects. Using data from 2009 to 2023, the analysis suggests a positive neutral CCyB rate for the euro area ranging between 1% and 1.5%. The findings indicate that output and inflation shocks, which are not directly linked to the materialization of domestic systemic risk, and high degrees of trade openness, warrant a more prominent role of the PN CCyB in the overall CCyB calibration. The exercise to illustrate the methodology is carried out for the euro area. While national calibrations require additional exercises, this approach offers a flexible and complementary framework that can support and enhance national-level analyses.

title: Feasibility of Universal Basic Income(UBI) in the Age of AI: A Comprehensive Simulation with a  16 -Parameter Model
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Feasibility of Universal Basic Income(UBI) in the Age of AI: A Comprehensive Simulation with a  16 -Parameter Model
detail.abstract: This study proposes a new economic model to quantitatively assess the feasibility of Universal Basic Income (UBI), considering the impact of rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the labor market. Unlike conventional static models, this model incorporates a realistic assumption that social security expenditures are dynamically reduced in response to the amount of UBI provided. Based on an analysis using Japan's fiscal data, this paper mathematically demonstrates that while UBI is not feasible under the current conditions due to a negative net fiscal surplus, a monthly UBI of up to ¥ , (in real terms) becomes possible with the rise of AIdriven labor substitution and appropriate tax reforms. Furthermore, this study introduces a novel method called "wide-range rate of change analysis" to quantitatively evaluate the impact of input parameters on the net fiscal surplus. The results reveal that capital income concentration ratio (change width: + ¥. trillion), AI labor substitution rate (change width: +¥. trillion), and personal income tax rate (change width: +¥. trillion) are the most influential factors. These parameters are also classified from the perspective of "policy controllability," clearly distinguishing between short-term feasible policies (tax reforms) and medium-to longterm initiatives (AI investment, economic growth). This finding provides crucial insights for presenting a concrete policy roadmap for UBI implementation.
