detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how prolonged economic necessity can evolve into institutional habit, psychological alignment, and ultimately geopolitical vulnerability between neighboring states. Using the Türkiye-Iran relationship as a structural case study, the analysis argues that sanctions-driven financial cooperation often produces gray-zone dependencies capable of reshaping bureaucratic reflexes, normalizing elevated risk tolerance, and influencing longterm strategic behavior. Rather than interpreting such partnerships solely through the lens of grand strategy, this study suggests they frequently originate from mutual constraint: one state requires liquidity under international isolation, while the other seeks capital inflow and macroeconomic relief. Over time, pragmatic cooperation can harden into a semi-permanent system resistant to disruption. Integrating sociological, psychological, and geopolitical perspectives, the paper contends that the primary long-term risk is not exposure itself but institutional adaptation to operating within ambiguity.

title: A Little Tech Policy Agenda

detail.title: A Little Tech Policy Agenda
detail.abstract: Leaders in Silicon Valley and Washington D.C. want to support "Little Tech." This paper presents an affirmative policy agenda, co-created with conservative and progressive policy experts, academics, and industry leaders at a November 2025 roundtable hosted by the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator. The agenda spans seven discrete policies—from antitrust legislation and enforcement, to public compute infrastructure and open-source support, to procurement reform, noncompete bans, and freedom-to-create laws—that federal and state policymakers can advance to support challengers to Big Tech, startups, and companies not yet founded.

title: Adaptive Model Risk Management for the AI Era: Leveraging SR 11-7 and Global Plugins
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Adaptive Model Risk Management for the AI Era: Leveraging SR 11-7 and Global Plugins
detail.abstract: Effective Model Risk Management (MRM) is fundamental to the safety and soundness of financial institutions. In the US, Supervisory Guidance SR 11-7 (Federal Reserve) / OCC 2011-12 has long served as the blueprint for the MRM frameworks. However, the rapid integration of machine learning, Generative AI, and agentic systems introduces challenges such as explainability, hallucinations, and drift, that strain traditional governance structures. This paper argues that while the core principles of SR 11-7 remain essential, MRM frameworks can be adapted to the specific mechanics of modern AI. It proposes an "Adaptive MRM Framework" that maintains SR 11-7 as the regulatory anchor while strategically scanning for and integrating "best-of-breed" components ("plugins") from existing and emerging US and global guidance, including NIST, OSFI, PRA, ECB, and EU AI Act. Crucially, these enhancements must be applied proportionately: the depth of governance should always be commensurate with the institution’s size and the specific materiality of model risk. By adopting targeted capabilities such as safety metrics, actionable counterfactuals, confabulation controls, Human-in-the-Loop oversight, and differentiation between inherent and residual model risk, financial institutions can reinforce their governance, positioning MRM as a proactive strategic enabler of responsible AI innovation.

title: An Endogenous Moral Formation Game
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU)

detail.title: An Endogenous Moral Formation Game
detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of endogenous moral formation. In a two-stage game, individuals first choose a morality, a function mapping actions to the unit interval that enters each player's payoff, and then choose actions. In equilibrium, morality choices influence everyone's actions, fostering social norms and internalizing externalities.

title: A Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) to Govern Non-linear Dynamics and Uncertainty in AI-Augmented Software Development
affiliations: Valahia University of Targoviste, Valahia University of Targoviste,  and

detail.title: A Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) to Govern Non-linear Dynamics and Uncertainty in AI-Augmented Software Development
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of Large Language Models into the Software Development Life Cycle has given rise to an AI Productivity Paradox, characterized by a structural gap between individual developer speed and aggregate organizational delivery performance. While established frameworks like DORA and SPACE focus on monitoring system health, delivery stability, and multidimensional productivity constructs, they often lack the prescriptive capacity to govern the non-linear dynamics and epistemic uncertainty inherent to AI-mediated work. The main contribution of this paper is the development of a novel Fuzzy Hybrid Decision Support System (DSS) that pivots toward an uncertainty-aware governance model, which is specifically designed to handle the noise and structural ambiguity of AI-assisted engineering. Instead of treating metrics as exact or infallible numbers, this approach uses fuzzy logic to translate complex technical signals into clear, risk-based assessments, helping leaders identify hidden work bottlenecks and quality issues even when data is noisy or incomplete. By operationalizing three specialized constructs, including Delivered Story Points per Deployment (DSPD) to audit value density, Lead Time for Business Features (LTBF) to identify flow constraints in requirements phases often overlooked by standard lead time metrics, and the Acceptance/Churn Duo to predict technical debt, this framework moves beyond measuring mere volume. The study embeds fuzzy logic as the principal inferential mechanism, allowing leaders to manage systemic pathologies such as thrashing and verification saturation by mapping low-level telemetry into high-level probabilistic performance states. The framework introduces a novel socio-technical governance mechanism that utilizes fuzzy logic to formally address the AI-driven development.

title: The Energy Charter Treaty
affiliations: KAPSARC School of Public Policy

detail.title: The Energy Charter Treaty

publicationDetails.detailsText: Elgar Encyclopedia of European Law, Cheltenham, UK and Northampton, MA, USA: Edward Elgar Publishing, 2026

detail.abstract: In 1990, at a European Council meeting in Dublin, Ruud Lubbers, the Dutch Prime Minister, who, at the time, presided over the Council, called for more institutionalized relations with the energy-rich economies in Eurasia following their collapse in order to benefit from their consequent opening-up and orientation towards the global market-based economic order. This led to the adoption of the 1991 European Energy Charter, which is a non-legally binding political declaration embodying key principles of international energy cooperation. The 1991 European Energy Charter paved the way for the negotiation and eventual adoption of the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT) and the Energy Charter Process. Much has happened since then and the 21st century needs a modernized ECT. This article examines three elements that need attention to reach an ECT ready to deliver the challenges of the 21st century: 1) an analysis of the criticisms of the ECT, 2) the modernization process of the ECT, and 3) the relation between European Union (EU) energy security and the ECT regarding the promotion of EU energy security interests at the extra-EU level.

title: Varieties and Mechanisms of Common Ownership: Putting Theory to Practice
affiliations: University of Leeds School of Law

detail.title: Varieties and Mechanisms of Common Ownership: Putting Theory to Practice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/a
declarations.funderStatement: N/a

publicationDetails.detailsText: Marco Corradi and Sam Weinstein (eds.), Research Handbook on Antitrust and Finance (Edward Elgar Publishing, forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
Revolutions come with a bang, not a whimper, paraphrasing the famous lines of T.S. Eliot. They mark the beginning of a new era. Yet rarely they are about theory alone; a transition in thinking is just a preliminary step to real-world action. So it has been with common ownership theory, whose appearance brought shockwaves to the antitrust community. The bold proposition that the simultaneous holding by the same large institutional investors of minority shares in several competing firms in concentrated industries could have significant economic effects or indeed be the “greatest anticompetitive threat of our time” caused radical – both positive and negative – reactions. This new phenomenon seemed particularly concerning in the U.S. context where it has been found to be of increasingly significant and system-wide proportions.

Some went as far as suggesting putting a limit on within-industry diversification or a complete ban on passive funds exercising voting rights in corporate governance. A perplexing tradeoff between product market competition and other laudable objectives came to surface. More moderate voices recommended activating and expanding case-by-case antitrust enforcement to address common ownership concerns that may fall between the cracks of existing antitrust laws and their conservative interpretation. Others questioned the existence of an actual problem and the plausibility of the theory on the argument that “passive” institutional shareholders typically “under-engage” in the corporate governance of their invested firms or calling into question the mechanisms through which common ownership is likely to influence firm behaviour and produce competition concerns. In a previous article, I have responded to this criticism shedding light on the novel “passive mechanisms” through which common ownership may plausibly give rise to material effects.

This debate is well documented but has been rather inconclusive. To be sure, policymakers around the world were alarmed by the news that common minority shareholdings may have underappreciated yet important implications. Given the theoretical controversy, however, and the significant stakes and tradeoffs at play, most of them made a note of developments and took minimal action adopting a “wait-and-see” approach. This state of affairs was true up to one or two years ago. Since then history seems to have taken a different course as antitrust enforcers in certain jurisdictions appear more resolute to act on common ownership matters. With this unexpected turn from theory to practice, the question arises: does this signal the beginning of a real revolution in antitrust enforcement? To properly answer that question, one needs to look more closely into the recently emerging enforcement actions relating to common ownership and map their underlying logic or potential consequences. One thing is for sure, common ownership and minority shareholdings are in vogue again.

Against this backdrop, this paper proceeds as follows. Part II revisits and outlines the basic premises of the unilateral effects theory of common ownership and summarizes the different varieties and supporting mechanisms in which it is said to manifest. Part III discusses ways in which common ownership and minority shareholding can give rise to and support theories of coordinated effects. Part IV presents a range of prominent enforcement actions involving common ownership and minority shareholdings issues in various jurisdictions such as the U.S., Greece and the EU and analyses how well those actions and related decisions may fit existing theories. Part V concludes by offering some short reflections on the progress achieved in translating common ownership theory to antitrust enforcement practice.

title: ADRs, Brazilian Corporations and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002: A Critical Analysis
affiliations: GODKE ADVOGADOS

detail.title: ADRs, Brazilian Corporations and the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002: A Critical Analysis

contentType.other: LLM final paper at Columbia Law School

detail.abstract: At the time of writing, approximately 37 Brazilian corporations were registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), enabling them to be cross-listed in Brazil and the United States simultaneously. That figure suggests that, for these issuers, the benefits of accessing U.S. capital markets outweigh the costs and frictions typically associated with cross-listing. The Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002, however, materially alters this calculus by introducing (and intensifying) corporate-governance, internal-control, certification, and audit-related obligations applicable to all SEC-registered issuers, including Brazilian companies that wish to remain listed on U.S. exchanges. Focusing on American Depositary Receipts (ADRs)—the principal instrument used by Brazilian issuers for U.S. cross-listings—this paper offers a structured overview of the core mechanics of ADR facilities and the corresponding regulatory framework under both U.S. and Brazilian law. It then examines recent Brazilian legislative reforms affecting investor rights and evaluates how these reforms interact with the U.S. securities-law regime. The paper also addresses jurisdiction and conflict-of-laws questions inherent in cross-border listings, and analyzes how the 2002 U.S. reforms reshape compliance expectations for Brazilian issuers and, in turn, the role, risk profile, and workstreams of the Brazilian legal profession. The paper concludes with observations on compliance implications and cross-listing dynamics.

title: genriesz: A Python Package for Automatic Debiased Machine Learning with Generalized Riesz Regression
affiliations: Mizuho-DL Financial Technology Co., Ltd.

detail.title: genriesz: A Python Package for Automatic Debiased Machine Learning with Generalized Riesz Regression
detail.abstract: Efficient estimation of causal and structural parameters can be automated via the Riesz representation theorem and debiased machine learning (DML). We present genriesz, an open-source Python package implementing automatic DML and generalized Riesz regression, a unified framework for estimating Riesz representers by minimizing empirical Bregman divergences. This framework includes covariate balancing, nearest-neighbor matching, and calibrated estimation as special cases. A key design principle of the package is automatic regressor balancing (ARB): given a Bregman generator g and a representer model class, genriesz automatically constructs a compatible link function so that the generalized Riesz regression estimator satisfies balancing (moment-matching) optimality conditions in a user-chosen basis. The package provides a modular interface for specifying (i) the target linear functional through a blackbox evaluation oracle, (ii) the representer model through basis functions (polynomial, RKHS approximations, random forest leaf encodings, neural embeddings, and a nearestneighbor catchment basis), and (iii) the Bregman generator with optional user-supplied derivatives. It returns regression adjustment (RA), Riesz weighting (RW), augmented Riesz weighting (ARW), and TMLE-style estimators with cross-fitting, Wald-type confidence intervals, and p-values. We highlight representative workflows for ATE, ATT, average marginal effects, panel difference-indifferences , and nearest-neighbor matching. The Python package is available at https://github.com/MasaKat0/genriesz and on PyPI.

title: Special Interest Influence and the Interpretability of the Law
affiliations: , Indiana university and University of Surrey

detail.title: Special Interest Influence and the Interpretability of the Law
detail.abstract: Because laws are susceptible to multiple interpretations, interest groups care not only about the choices of lawmakers but also those of interpreters. When institutions restrict groups from directly influencing interpreters, such as judges, they may instead seek to shape the interpretability of laws in ways that advance their interests. Data from the United States show that activities aimed at influencing the interpretability of laws have increased dramatically over the last sixty years and that those involved in these efforts also tend to influence through traditional lobbying. We discuss these ideas within an agency model that links the arenas of influence, lawmaking and law interpretability, and report multiple evidence of complementarities in interest group involvement across both.

title: Dynamic Deposit Betas: An Asymmetric Volatility-Adjusted S-Curve Framework for MMDA Rate Sensitivity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dynamic Deposit Betas: An Asymmetric Volatility-Adjusted S-Curve Framework for MMDA Rate Sensitivity
detail.abstract:
Standard deposit beta models assume banks reprice deposits at a constant rate regardless of the interest rate environment. The Fed’s 2022–2025 tightening cycle exposed the limitations of that assumption.

This paper develops a dynamic beta framework for money market deposit accounts that captures what practitioners already know but rarely formalize: deposit competition intensifies as rates rise, and banks respond to volatility differently depending on whether rates are going up or coming down. The model uses a logistic S-curve to let deposit sensitivity evolve with rate levels, a volatility dampening mechanism that accounts for reduced pass-through during uncertain environments, and an autoregressive smoothing constraint that prevents implausible month-to-month beta jumps. Standard errors are computed using a Huber-White sandwich estimator with Newey-West HAC weighting, properly accounting for the serial dependence inherent in monthly financial data.

The core empirical finding is asymmetric volatility dampening: banks suppress competitive repricing by 25.5% when rates are rising under elevated volatility, but only 22.3% when rates are falling. The data reject the symmetric restriction at 𝑝 < 0.001. Using monthly data from January 2017 through March 2025 (𝑛 = 99), the model achieves an in-sample 𝑅2 of 0.987 and RMSE of 10.3 basis points. Scenario analysis with a Nerlove partial adjustment filter (𝜃 = 0.47) shows that roughly half the gap between the current deposit rate and its model-implied equilibrium closes each month,withfullconvergencewithin12months. A+200bpshockproduces22%moredeposit cost pass-through than a-200bp shock, a structural asymmetry driven by the S-curve’s concavity near the current rate level.

For practitioners, the paper provides effective duration schedules showing that MMDA duration declines from 2.5 years in a 1% rate environment to 1.4 years at 6%, a worked portfolio example quantifying the dollar impact on a $10 billion deposit book, and an implementation checklist for embedding the model in ALM systems. The complete code and data are publicly available.

title: The Political Economy of Financial Fragility: An Institutional Analysis of Liquidity Transmission and Systemic Risk
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Political Economy of Financial Fragility: An Institutional Analysis of Liquidity Transmission and Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: Financial crises are not random events but institutional failures encoded in the parameters governing liquidity transmission. This paper develops an Arithmetico-Geometric Progression (AGP) framework that maps regulatory architecture directly to systemic stability through two institutional variables: transmission efficiency (velocity ν) and structural impediments (friction Φ). The mathematical core reveals cubic fragility near critical thresholds-a non-linear instability that makes catastrophic phase transitions inevitable when efficiency is pushed too far. The empirical puzzle drives the institutional insight: observed U.S. financial system behavior (2016-2026) exhibits only 2% of the feedback intensity predicted by frictionless theory. This isn't model failure-it's quantitative proof that institutions matter. The 98% dampening effect represents the cumulative stabilization from post-2008 regulatory architecture, measuring in closed form what decades of institutional economics argued qualitatively: The market depends on institutions to stabilize. A more concerning finding is that this dampening is politically unstable. Using comparative institutional analysis across crises (1929, S&L, 2008) and countries (US, UK, Canada, China), I show why suboptimal friction persists despite repeated catastrophe. The answer lies in distributional conflict and regulatory capture-banks extract rents from low-Φ regimes and socialize losses. Time inconsistency prevents commitment, memory fades post-crisis, and the cycle repeats. The AGP framework measures beyond fragility to expose the political economy equilibrium that generates it. This paper aims to make financial stability measurable, predictable, and with political adjustment, preventable.

title: Beyond Redistribution: Towards an Ex-Ante Distribution Model for Systemic Financial Inclusion

detail.title: Beyond Redistribution: Towards an Ex-Ante Distribution Model for Systemic Financial Inclusion
detail.abstract:
This article introduces the Folahan Mechanism, a Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) designed to systemically address the limitations of traditional redistribution policies. While ex-post transfer models struggle to sustainably reduce income inequality, this study proposes a paradigm shift toward ex-ante wealth distribution.

The mechanism is built upon the integration of three disruptive pillars: a collaborative economy based on productive co-ownership, the advent of an ethical electronic currency (ECO) to secure essential consumption, and streamlined access to credit by lowering traditional banking barriers. Using rigorous mathematical modeling and an empirical approach conducted in Benin (WAEMU zone), the author demonstrates how transforming consumption flows into capital assets enables a transition from a survival economy to shared abundance. The article details the financial mobilization instruments (DAT, IS, CP, CS) and the four-part governance structure (ADI, FC, DMU, ICF) that ensure the system’s balance and self-regulation. This model provides international institutions with an operational solution to rebuild the social and monetary contract for the 21st century.

title: The Long-term Effects of Crime
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The Long-term Effects of Crime

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Crime shocks are frequent and disruptive, often heightening public concerns about violence and personal safety. Yet little is known about their potential long-term economic implications. This paper studies how historical exposure to crime shapes current perceptions of crime, and how these individual perceptions in turn affect the macroeconomic impacts of new crime shocks. Using cross-country survey data matched with historical crime records, we find that individuals historically exposed to high-crime years are more likely to prioritize fighting crime over other societal goals, such as maintaining a stable economy. This historical link is particularly strong among older and richer individuals, and among parents. A stronger fiscal position, which presumably enhances a country's ability to devote resources to fight crime, helps mitigate the persistence of crime exposure. At the aggregate level, countries where crime concerns are more entrenched experience larger GDP declines in the aftermath of high-crime years, driven mainly by lower consumption, capital accumulation, and productivity, rather than changes in employment.

title: Towards Achieving Sustained Economic Growth in Small Developing States
affiliations: , , International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and

detail.title: Towards Achieving Sustained Economic Growth in Small Developing States

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The small developing states (SDS) have unique economic characteristics and face specific constraints that shape their economic performance. We study a set of key challenges facing SDS using the case of Belize. The empirical analysis centers on (i) improving access to finance; (ii) exploring drivers of labor force participation with a view to increasing the labor force contribution to growth; and (iii) assessing the tourism sector’s capacity constraints, and arrives at the following findings. First, it shows that both demand and supply factors contribute to constraining private sector credit, primarily via the level of lending rates, complex collateral processes, legacy of high NPLs, and extent of regulatory capital above the regulatory minimum. Second, it delves into the relevance of tourism’s share in the services sector, youth’s educational attainment, disparity in labor market outcomes, and availability of childcare for explaining heterogeneity of labor force participation gaps between men and women. Third, it zooms into the critical role of hotel capacity, flight availability, and cost competitiveness in shaping the tourism sector’s prospects.

title: Pandemic-era inflation dynamics in the euro area: the role of policy and non-policy demand and energy and non-energy supply factors
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Pandemic-era inflation dynamics in the euro area: the role of policy and non-policy demand and energy and non-energy supply factors

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We analyze the sources of the pandemic-era inflation surge in the euro area using a Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR) model. By applying narrative, sign, zero, and inequality restrictions,this study is the first that jointly analyzes the inflationary effects of energy and non-energy supply and policy and non-policy demand factors, including fiscal policy, conventional and unconventional monetary policy. Factoring in that energy price dynamics also responded to aggregate demand conditions, we find that the pandemic-era inflation surge in the euro area was driven by a combination of supply and demand factors. Energy-related supply side constraints, even if less important than often estimated, were a key factor in the run up of inflation. Fiscal and monetary policies were accommodative but not the dominant drivers.

title: Modeling The Macroeconomic Dynamics of a Low-Carbon Energy Transition: Where Integrated Assessment Models Fall Short
affiliations: Universidad de las Américas (UDLA), University of Texas at Austin, The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Global Economic Dynamics and the Biosphere, Autonomous University of Barcelona - Institut de Ciència i Tecnologia Ambientals, McMaster University, Dubai Electricity & Water Authority (PJSC), CIRED, International Research Center on Environment & Development, France, , University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna, Mines Paris - PSL, Calvin University - Engineering Department, University of Valladolid, Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3) and Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Modeling The Macroeconomic Dynamics of a Low-Carbon Energy Transition: Where Integrated Assessment Models Fall Short
detail.abstract: Discussions on climate and energy policy are shaped by estimates of the socio-economic requirements and impacts of a low-carbon energy transition. These estimates are obtained from macroeconomic models, predominantly within integrated assessment model (IAM) frameworks. However, we posit that current IAMs insufficiently integrate multiple important concepts and feedbacks, and consequently are not dynamically sensitive enough to structural changes in financial, energy, and materials flows associated with a low-carbon energy transition. This paper highlights five categories of shortcomings within IAMs: equilibrium-based solutions along with inadequate model representation of banking, materials usage, energy and energy efficiency, including the latter two within aggregate production functions of gross domestic product. We discuss the applicability of these shortcomings to a set of ten representative IAMs– five based on neoclassical economic theory, four based on post-Keynesian economic theory, and one combining both. We point out that each model has several important shortcomings, many of them regarding central issues such as the representation of energy itself. Fundamental improvements to these models are needed to more realistically represent the challenges and opportunities of a low-carbon energy transition, and thus inform effective, robust, fair, and more ambitious climate and energy policy. These improvements include more realistic dynamics and linkages among energy, efficiency, materials, and economic output, as well as financial factors such as endogenous money and debt.

title: Liberty Lost: Establishing Constitutional Boundaries for Migrant Detention
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - School of Law

detail.title: Liberty Lost: Establishing Constitutional Boundaries for Migrant Detention
detail.abstract:
Immigration detention numbers in the United States have spiraled upwards out of control alongside dramatic increases in governmental authority to deprive migrants of liberty without justification.  We must take a hard look at the behemoth that detention has become. 

While the Supreme Court countenanced immigration detention more than 100 years ago, the Court has also held that physical deprivations of liberty may only be for:  1) criminal sanction after a full criminal proceeding; or 2) civil detention for limited governmental purposes.  In an effort to apply constitutional limits, scholars have debated for decades whether immigration detention should be best understood as civil or should instead be treated as punitive and therefore criminal in nature.  This Article argues that the debate regarding the civil/criminal dichotomy has obscured a fundamental constitutional problem:  immigration detention, as constituted, does not fall within either of the two constitutionally recognized exceptions to liberty.   

This Article breaks from the grip of the debate and concludes that immigration detention is neither civil nor criminal, at least in any accepted sense of these categories.  It is not imposed as a sanction for behavior deemed criminal, after a criminal proceeding.  Nor does it serve the civil purpose of addressing flight risk or danger.  Instead, it functions as spectacle to stigmatize and exclude.   Since detention as configured does not fit within one of the exceptions to liberty, it cannot continue.  If detention is to be used at all, it must be limited to genuine immigration purposes to fit within constitutional boundaries.  Specifically, detention must be limited to the purpose of facilitating actual deportation once removal from the country is certain.  I call this final-order detention.  Since most migrants in detention do not have a final removal decision, the detention system would shrink substantially on this understanding. 

The Article offers measures for enforcing the boundaries of the newly identified constitutional framework and addresses potential concerns.  It concludes by offering comparative law examples demonstrating the viability of the proffered limitations on detention.

title: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Cognitive Engagement and Academic Integrity in Secondary Education

detail.title: The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Cognitive Engagement and Academic Integrity in Secondary Education
detail.abstract: Research was conducted to investigate the behavioral and cognitive shifts in secondary students following the integration of ChatGPT into academic workflows. Key literature findings indicated that while large language models (LLMs) provided immediate relief from academic stressors, they simultaneously fostered a dependency that threatened critical thinking skills. Major discussion points included the dual-use nature of AI for both legitimate explanation and academic dishonesty, as well as the long-term neuroplastic implications of outsourcing creative tasks. It was concluded that the "shortcut" culture encouraged by AI significantly altered student engagement. The findings are significant as they highlight a critical need for pedagogical reform to maintain cognitive autonomy in an AI-saturated environment.

title: Persistent Influence Theory: A Hierarchical Framework for Structural Persuasion and Information Fidelity
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Persistent Influence Theory: A Hierarchical Framework for Structural Persuasion and Information Fidelity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the developer of BiasClear, the open-source software described in this paper. BiasClear is released under the AGPL-3.0 license. No other conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was self-funded.

detail.abstract: Every major AI governance framework audits models-their training data, weight distributions, and fairness metrics. None audits the text those models produce for structural persuasion: the rhetorical architecture through which manufactured consensus, false urgency, authority substitution, and institutional framing bypass critical evaluation and produce predetermined conclusions. This paper introduces Persistent Influence Theory (PIT), a novel hierarchical framework that models information filtering as a three-tier "throne-net" system: Tier 1 (Ideological Persistence) establishes meta-narrative boundaries via cultural "source code"; Tier 2 (Cognitive and Social Reinforcement) compiles these into personal filters through dissonance resolution and in-group bias; and Tier 3 (Institutional Amplification) executes via media gatekeeping and algorithmic echo systems. PIT's defining contribution is the causal ordering claim: upper tiers precondition lower ones, predicting that single-tier interventions will be systematically undermined by untargeted tiers. The paper presents an operational definition of information fidelity decomposed into four measurable facets, five falsifiable hypotheses, and BiasClear-an open-source computational implementation that operationalizes PIT's tier structure as a structural persuasion detection engine achieving 98.6% F1 accuracy across 34 detection patterns. With the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) mandating bias detection and audit documentation for high-risk AI systems by June 2026, and the EU AI Act imposing similar requirements, PIT and its computational implementation address an emerging regulatory gap: the absence of any framework for detecting structural persuasion in text contentwhether human-authored or machine-generated.

title: Preserving the Ozone Layers: Battling Illegal Trade in Ozone-Depleting Substances

detail.title: Preserving the Ozone Layers: Battling Illegal Trade in Ozone-Depleting Substances

detail.abstract: The depletion of the ozone layer, a vital shield protecting the Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, is now a worldwide environmental concern. Human activities, particularly the release of ozone depleting substances (ODS), have led to the thinning of this protective layer over recent decades. Simultaneously, illegal trade has emerged as a global challenge, giving rise to economic issues, losses of tax revenue, heightened criminal activities, health risks, and environmental hazards. The depletion of the ozone layer, a critical shield protecting the Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, has become a global environmental concern. This paper delves into the legal dimensions surrounding ozone-depleting substances (ODS), their impact on the ozone layer, and the subsequent risk of skin cancer. As countries navigate international agreements, domestic regulations, and enforcement mechanisms, the intricate interplay between legal frameworks and the health implications of ozone layer depletion comes to the forefront. The paper highlights particular instances of illegal trade in ozone depleting substances, drawing from data reported by the parties to the Montreal Protocol. Notably, there are several significant sources of contraband ODS, with countries such as Bulgaria, Lithuania, Poland, and France reporting numerous cases. Analyzing these case instances offers insights into the efficacy of legal frameworks and enforcement measures. The paper offers a comprehensive set of recommendations to strengthen global control and enforcement against the illegal trade of ozone depleting substances. These recommendations span diverse aspects such as production monitoring, customs collaboration, mutual verification, cross-border agreements, public-private partnerships, international cooperation, detection equipment, global regulatory standards, resource allocation, public awareness campaigns, alternative substance development, and controlling the trade at its source. By applying these recommendations and enhancing enforcement measures, we aim to protect the ozone layer and create a healthier and safer world for future generations and achieve sustainable development goals.

title: Shocks and the Determinants of Resilience: Fish and Shrimp Value Chains in Bangladesh after Covid-19
affiliations: , Michigan State University, International Food Policy Research Institute and International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)

detail.title: Shocks and the Determinants of Resilience: Fish and Shrimp Value Chains in Bangladesh after Covid-19

publicationDetails.detailsText: Applied Economic Perspectives and Policy, volume 45, issue 4, 2023[10.1002/aepp.13356]

detail.abstract: There is little systematic evidence on the resilience of South Asian agri-food value chains since the onset of Covid-19. Using two rounds of surveys of 1751 fish and shrimp value chain actors in Bangladesh, this paper undertakes two sets of tasks: (a) analyzes business continuity (closures and resumptions) and its implications for household food security, and (b) adapts a ten-item measure of subjective resilience and examines its predictors: diversity, scope, scale, vertical integration, and cluster effects. Results show that recent closures are linked to Covid-19, suggesting that firms were only able to sustain operations for a period of 8–9 months before folding due to cumulative stresses; and that the degree of resilience varies significantly across value chains and the segments within them. Interestingly, contrary to established stylized facts, clusters appear to be negatively correlated with resilience, indicating that cooperation among value chain actors within a cluster breaks down under large-scale covariate shocks. The implications of these and other key findings are discussed.

title: Strategic and Financial Requirements for a Sovereign AI Infrastructure
affiliations: , Harvard University and

detail.title: Strategic and Financial Requirements for a Sovereign AI Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Sovereign AI refers to the ability to develop, operate, secure, control, and sustain critical AI systems under geopolitical or operational stress-ensuring continuity and growth of AI services even if energy supplies are disrupted, global supply chains fragment, or cloud access is restricted. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integral to business, government, and society, questions on sovereign and defense AI infrastructure have moved to the forefront. This paper points out that achieving AI sovereignty requires sustainable control over key dependencies in the AI stack (such as energy, commodities, computer hardware, cloud platforms, data, algorithms, and information systems). To achieve this, countries need to own an increasingly integrated web of technology, innovation, supply chain, financial infrastructure, information systems, education, and to have adequate governance and political systems in place. We propose a framework of requirements for sovereign AI, outlining the essential measures needed to make AI capabilities resilient against external shocks. This perspective requires an in-depth transformation of economic systems to ensure technological sovereignty for NATO and its allies.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates the effects of a cultural programme on the well-being of older adults through a randomised controlled trial involving four activities— film screenings, guided exposition visits, and expert-led group discussions with informal social time. Compared to controls, treated participants exhibited a 10 percentage point net increase in social relationships and a 22 percentage point net reduction in doctor visits over the intervention period. Unexpectedly, participants reported subjective health declines, which may be explained by heightened self-awareness. Open-ended responses from participant surveys and focus group discussions highlighted the importance of interpersonal interaction, mental stimulation, and physical activation as mechanisms underlying these outcomes. Given its implementation within existing community resources and its positive impacts on social and physical health indicators, this cultural programme offers a promising strategy to support wellbeing and reduce loneliness in ageing societies.

detail.title: The Suspicion We Withhold: Asymmetric Hermeneutics in Critical Technology Scholarship

detail.abstract: This commentary argues that critical technology scholarship has calcified into what Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick diagnosed as paranoid reading: a default interpretive mode that applies suspicious reading, the assumption that surface meanings conceal hidden interests, asymmetrically. While scholars rigorously interrogate how dominant platforms and corporate AI systems embed political interests, they routinely exempt alternatives (including platform cooperatives, open-source AI initiatives, and technological sovereignty projects) from equivalent scrutiny. The diagnosis that “technology is not neutral” is correct. The problem is that this diagnosis functions more as a weapon directed exclusively at political adversaries than as a universal analytical principle. Drawing on Paul Ricoeur’s dual hermeneutics, Sedgwick’s critique of paranoid reading, Bruno Latour’s warning about the weaponisation of critique, and Rita Felski’s postcritical turn, this critical commentary identifies a pattern of one-sided suspicion through close readings of recent scholarship on federated platform governance, open-source AI sovereignty, and decolonial AI. The constructive argument is that postcritical technology scholarship requires not the abandonment of suspicion but its universalisation. Here, polycentric governance epistemology, rooted in institutional analysis and attentive to dispersed knowledge and emergent institutional arrangements, offers analytical resources for understanding what the postcritical literary tradition currently lacks in its critique of technology.

title: The New Emergency Law
affiliations: UC Berkeley School of Law

detail.title: The New Emergency Law
detail.abstract:
The last three presidential administrations invoked delegated emergency authority in novel and expansive ways with substantial domestic effect. Key executive actions like the imposition of global tariffs, removal under the Alien Enemies Act, deployment of the military to major American cities, the construction of a border wall, tech platform regulation, and COVID-19 response relied on statutory emergency authority. 

Courts have traditionally deferred to presidential actions based on statutory emergency delegations, and conventional wisdom maintains that the Supreme Court has largely sided with the President on questions of executive power. Yet this Article argues that the extensive litigation provoked by Presidents Biden and President Trump’s emergency actions marks a significant shift in judicial review of statutory emergency powers. Emergency powers creep and domestication have led the courts to scrutinize executive reliance on emergency statutes closely and impose substantial limits on executive authority in real time.  

This Article also proposes and defends an “authority-matching” canon. The canon requires the executive to rely on specific statutory authority when available instead of broad, nonspecific emergency statutes. The Article argues that an “authority-matching” canon aligns with a longstanding contextual approach to statutory interpretation that accounts for statutory structure. It is a better way to constrain reliance on broad delegated emergency powers than alternatives like the major questions doctrine. And it puts a thumb on the scale against the executive end-running statutory constraints by relying on broad emergency authority, while preserving the President’s ability to act in true emergencies Congress did not legislate for. As presidents leverage and even manufacture emergencies to trigger a sprawling web of expansive delegated powers, the judiciary can harness ordinary statutory construction tools to channel executive action through more constrained non-emergency routes.

detail.abstract: The inheritance of women, children, land and property in Southern Africa has been a common traditional approach to managing the welfare of these, upon the death of the male head of household. However with the ongoing HIV/AIDS pandemic, the male relatives of the deceased are much less willing to inherit wives and children, due to the prospect that these individuals may have AIDS themselves, and the stigma associated with the disease. The male relatives do however continue to inherit the property--land, livestock, farming implements etc; leaving the wives and children homeless and destitute. The partial collapse of this institution of inheritance--refusing to inherit the people but continuing to inherit the property--is known as 'property grabbing' and generates very large numbers of destitute widows and orphans. However in Zambia, AIDS widows have used the current scenario to their advantage--to both escape being inherited, and to retain their land and property to become female headed households able to adequately care for themselves and their children. This chapter examines this 'escape' from female inheritance and the land rights repercussions to this escape.

detail.abstract: The Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF), which was added to the IMF’s lending toolkit in 2022, provides affordable longer-term financing to support countries undertaking macrocritical reforms to reduce risks to prospective BoP stability emanating from extreme weather events and pandemics. This paper draws early lessons from RSF arrangements by exploring whether they have been able to meet one of their core objectives, namely catalyzing financing from other sources. A multipronged approach is used consisting of a survey of country teams, an econometric study, and analysis of non-traditional data. According to a survey of IMF country teams most countries with RSF arrangements received climate finance, mainly from synergies with public sources. The econometric analysis shows that approval of an RSF is associated with increased MDB climate finance and Official Development Assistance (ODA) in low-income countries, thus strengthening the RSF’s link to BoP stability. Non-traditional data drawing from news media and labor market developments point to potential higher financing in the future.

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Consequences of Undermining Central Bank Independence

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic consequences of undermining central bank independence through politically motivated transitions of central bank governors. Leveraging a new panel dataset covering 132 central bank governor transitions in 28 advanced and emerging market economies since 2000, we document the timing, frequency, and political drivers of these leadership changes. Tenures of governors with politically motivated appointments are associated with higher and more volatile inflation, realized and expected. Professional forecasters also tend to expect such governors to be more dovish when responding to shifts in inflation. Using local projections in a difference-in[1]difference setting, we find that following the announcement of a politically motivated governor transition nominal and real short rates decline and expected and realized inflation rise. At the same time, GDP growth increases in the aftermath of such transitions, consistent with an expansionary short-run macroeconomic impulse. These effects are more pronounced when the incoming governor professes unorthodox views on monetary policy, suggesting that political interference in central bank leadership induces a temporary growth–inflation trade-off. Long-term inflation expectations only rise in the case of unorthodox governors with politically motivated appointments, suggesting costs to central bank credibility are much more pronounced in those cases.

title: Corporate Governance and Executive Accountability: The Broader Relevance of Enhanced Accountability Measures in the Financial Sector

detail.title: Corporate Governance and Executive Accountability: The Broader Relevance of Enhanced Accountability Measures in the Financial Sector
detail.abstract: The appropriateness of Australia’s corporate governance and corporate accountability frameworks is a matter of ongoing debate. In particular, concerns have been raised about the accountability of corporate personnel for misconduct and the role of directors in addressing misconduct. This article highlights an important development in the financial sector which it argues should be given greater prominence in this discourse. The development is the Financial Accountability Regime (‘FAR’), an enhanced accountability framework for senior personnel in financial organisations. FAR prescribes core behavioural obligations for such personnel and establishes a novel governance, compliance and consequence framework to support the application, monitoring and enforcement of those obligations. The article contrasts FAR with existing general mechanisms of individual accountability under Australian corporate law which are characterised by their board-centric approach, definitional ambiguity and enforcement challenges. The article argues that there are various theoretical, policy and practical considerations in support of FAR-like strategies being considered for application in the broader corporate sector.

title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How the Epistemology of Ideology Determines the Modality of Power and Post-Crisis Morphology

detail.title: The Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis: How the Epistemology of Ideology Determines the Modality of Power and Post-Crisis Morphology
detail.abstract:
Why did Stalin and Hitler — two leaders facing structurally similar pressures of the 1930s — adopt diametrically opposed strategies for holding power? Why did the Soviet system survive the catastrophic shock of 1941, while the Nazi regime began to fracture from within by 1944? The conventional answer retreats into biography: one was a paranoid bureaucrat, the other a charismatic mystic. This paper argues that this explanation, while not wrong, is insufficient. It reduces macro-historical patterns to the accidents of individual psychology and, in doing so, abandons the search for a generalizable theory of regime behavior.

We propose the Ideological Correspondence Hypothesis. This hypothesis asserts that the epistemological architecture of a regime's dominant ideology — whether it treats reality as a mechanism to be engineered or as a myth to be embodied — functions as the cognitive operating system of its ruling elite, structurally determining its governance strategy and predicting its characteristic vulnerabilities under crisis conditions. Regimes grounded in materialist-rationalist epistemologies instinctively prioritize Structural Resilience Engineering (SRI), constructing durable institutions and centralizing material control. Regimes grounded in irrationalist-mythic epistemologies prioritize Archetypal Mobilization (AAI), generating intense charismatic loyalty at the cost of institutional coherence. These are not stylistic preferences; they are structural constraints that dictate the specific failure mode of the regime long before the crisis arrives.

The hypothesis is tested against eight historical cases spanning the full ideological spectrum, from Pinochet's neoliberal technocracy to Pol Pot's anti-rationalist primitivism. The longitudinal case of China — from Maoist voluntarism to Dengist pragmatism — provides what approaches a controlled natural experiment: the same party, the same population, the same geopolitical context, producing two inverse trajectories based solely on a shift in its theory of knowledge.
Building on this empirical foundation, the paper generates three falsifiable forecasts for contemporary regimes — Iran, Saudi Arabia, and post-Putin Russia — derived strictly from their epistemological parameters. These predictions are submitted to the historical record as tests of the model's scientific validity.

The paper positions the hypothesis within the canon of social theory, acknowledging its debts to Weber's elective affinity, Foucault's power-knowledge entanglement, and the Platonic tradition of causal idealism, while arguing that it advances beyond each of these frameworks toward a quantifiable, predictive instrument. This paper constitutes a fully integrated module of the Anatomy of Chaos cycle, providing the epistemological depth that complements the cycle's quantitative architecture of systemic crisis, elite depletion, and temporal deformation developed across the preceding volumes. We do not merely assert that ideas matter; we demonstrate that specific epistemological structures produce specific institutional architectures, specific resilience profiles, and specific collapse morphologies — with sufficient regularity to constitute a predictive science of regime behavior.

Pathology is not a matter of evil ideology alone. It is the structural output of a cognitive operating system that has optimized for the wrong dimension of power — and then encountered a crisis that exposed the blind spot it could not see.

detail.title: Sovereign Debt Sustainability and Redistribution

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of sovereign debt sustainability driven by the government’s motive for redistribution. It studies a heterogeneous-agent small open economy in which redistribution relies on distortionary labor taxation and the government lacks commitment in its fiscal policies. Access to international credit markets lowers the cost of redistribution, while default into financial autarky raises it, generating an endogenous cost of default. Quantitatively, the model accounts for the buildup of Italy’s external debt and the positive cross-country correlation between pre-tax income inequality and external debt. Optimal austerity is more gradual when distributional concerns are present.

title: AI Meets Fiscal Policy

detail.title: AI Meets Fiscal Policy

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We build the first global quarterly narrative database of discretionary government spending actions by applying a fixed GPT–4.1 prompt to Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) Country Reports. The resulting series identifies exogenous spending shocks—expansions and contractions—for an unbalanced panel of 64 countries from 1952:Q1 to 2023:Q4. We validate the database by (i) replicating expert narrative coding in Romer and Romer (2019), (ii) showing that the identified shocks predict subsequent movements in measured government spending, and (iii) establishing alignment with action-based consolidation measures in Adler et al. (2024). Using country-by-country proxy SVARs that treat the narrative indicator as an internal instrument, we estimate cumulative government spending multipliers. The median multiplier is about 0.7 at horizons up to two years, with substantial heterogeneity across countries and states. Multipliers are larger in countries that are less open to trade, under fixed exchange rate regimes, during downturns, and at the zero lower bound. Political conditions also matter: multipliers are smaller when broad economic policy uncertainty and fiscal policy-specific uncertainty is high, but weak political support is associated with larger conditional multipliers.

detail.title: Stablecoin Shocks

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We develop novel measures of stablecoin shocks and use them to identify the causal effects of stablecoin adoption on U.S. financial markets. Combining a daily narrative dataset of stablecoin-specific news with changes in the combined market capitalization of USDC and USDT, we measure high-frequency movements in stablecoin market capitalization and implement heteroskedasticity-based identification within an event-study and SVAR-IV framework. Stablecoin demand shocks have triggered persistent declines in short-term Treasury yields, a depreciation of the U.S. dollar, and gradual spillovers into crypto and equity markets. We also document heterogeneous effects across firms: payment providers benefit from greater stablecoin adoption, whereas banks—including community and small banks—show no evidence of priced disintermediation risk. Our findings highlight stablecoin demand as a novel channel of asset-market transmission.

detail.abstract: The subpar quality of labor market data in many parts of the world can hinder economic policymaking. The challenge is exacerbated by a secular decline in response rates to labor force surveys (LFS) observed in numerous countries, which is also captured partially in labor market data issues flagged in the IMF’s Data Adequacy Assessments. This paper documents the evolution of LFS response rates in several countries and explores factors affecting it. By creating a new dataset of LFS characteristics for 39 mostly advanced economies, we find that those with voluntary survey participation have seen the response rates erode 1.5 percentage points per year on average, while the rates have been broadly stable in those with mandatory participation. We also find that survey data collection modalities may affect the response rate. Finally, the paper looks into the effectiveness of various ways in which statistical offices and data users have tried to address the challenges, including adjusting survey methodology and utilizing non-traditional data.

title: The EU’s Energy Transition
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), , International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: The EU’s Energy Transition

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The EU has ambitious goals for climate and energy security. Its targets and policies may have large macroeconomic implications, but investment impacts are particularly uncertain. Detailed "bottom-up" approaches based on sectoral calculations point to investment increases of 2 to 3 percent of GDP annually, while “top down” general equilibrium models often yield negligible aggregate investment effects. Further, the investment and broader macroeconomic impacts of the EU’s energy transition will depend on how carbon pricing revenues are recycled. This paper addresses these issues using a modeling technique that bridges bottom-up and top-down approaches. A New Keynesian general equilibrium model (GMMET) is extended to feature a detailed representation of energy use in key emitting sectors, including buildings, transport and energy-intensive manufacturing. Simulations suggest that achieving the EU’s 2035 climate goals implies an increase in aggregate annual investment of just around 1 percent of GDP. More broadly, the EU’s energy transition only has modest macroeconomic impacts if it combines carbon pricing and green subsidies, partly because these are complementary—green subsidies lower energy prices and inflation and raise output, carbon pricing has opposite effects, and therefore combining both yields small effects on all accounts. The fiscal cost of the transition is modest provided decarbonization relies sufficiently on carbon pricing; while revenues from ETS1 and ETS2 could eventually reach about 1 percent of GDP, the public investment cost of the transition is less than 0.5 percent of GDP annually, leaving net fiscal space that could be used for other policy objectives.
